author_headline: i'm 20 · swe · part time building micro products that i personally use
text:
this is the easiest way to understand Jev:

LLMs generate answers.

Jev makes decisions.

that sounds like a small difference, but it actually changes the entire use case.

say you give a normal LLM this:

“here’s a user, their account history, payment behavior, support chats, device data, etc.

tell me if this looks risky.”

the LLM might reason through it and return:

“yes, this looks high risk.”

maybe in JSON if you ask nicely.

with Jev, you define the possible decisions upfront:

risk:

* low
* medium
* high

manual review:

* yes
* no

and Jev returns something closer to:

risk = high (96%)
manual review = yes (91%)

that’s basically the product.

it’s not trying to be another ChatGPT.

it’s more like an AI-native if statement.

instead of:

if transaction > $10,000:
review()

you can start thinking more like:

if “does this behavior look suspicious?” > 95%:
review()

and that opens up a pretty interesting category of software.

a few assumptions I had at first that turned out to be wrong:

1. “so it’s just a classifier?”

kind of, but that undersells it.

the input can be messy real-world context, and you can ask multiple typed questions about that state at once.

fraud?
churn?
escalate?
eligible?
priority?

all from the same input.

2. “so it replaces GPT / Claude?”

not really.

I actually think the interesting architecture is:

Jev decides WHAT needs to happen

Claude / GPT reason or generate WHEN deeper intelligence is needed

normal code executes the deterministic stuff.

Jev becomes the routing layer.

3. “it can’t hallucinate?”

this one needs nuance.

if your allowed answers are:

LOW
MEDIUM
HIGH

Jev won’t suddenly invent:

“EXTREMELY HIGH 🚨”

the output structure is constrained.

but it can still be wrong.

HIGH at 92% can still be the wrong decision.

so “no hallucinations” doesn’t mean “always correct.”

4. “why not just force an LLM to return JSON?”

you can.

we already do this everywhere.

but you still deal with generation latency, schema validation, retries, weird outputs, confidence estimation and a lot of glue code.

Jev is designed around the decision itself rather than text generation.

5. “why should I care?”

because most software is ultimately a giant tree of:

if this → do that
if this → route here
if this → escalate
if this → reject
if this → ask a human

Jev is basically asking:

what if those if statements could understand messy human context?

that’s a much more interesting framing than “another AI model.”

I can see this being very useful for:

fraud / risk
support routing
moderation
PR / QA automation
lead scoring
compliance
workflow orchestration
agent routing

especially as the cheap + fast decision layer sitting in front of larger reasoning models.

early tech, obviously.

but the category itself makes a lot of sense.

text:
The wrong question is increasingly: Which model should we use? The better question: Which model should make this decision?

Salesforce and TypeSafe each announced a different answer over the last two days. Salesforce introduced Koa, a reasoning model tuned for CRM work such as qualifying leads, routing service cases, updating opportunities, and choosing the next tool in a multi-step workflow. Salesforce says Koa makes 3× fewer errors on its CRM-action benchmark after post-training NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super on synthetic scenarios derived from decades of CRM patterns.

TypeSafe, founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida, announced Jev from a very different direction. Almeida worked on the instruction-following research that led to InstructGPT and ChatGPT. Jev does not generate prose. It returns a decision: a class, score, or yes/no answer with confidence. This makes it suited to high-volume software decisions such as routing, triage, policy checks, and scoring, where generating a paragraph adds little value. TypeSafe reports 70–500 ms responses and large latency and cost gains on those workloads.

Koa and Jev are solving different problems. Koa is built for work that needs context, planning, and tool use. Jev is built for fast, constrained judgment. Frontier models still make sense where the task is broad, ambiguous, or unfamiliar.

Jev + Kimi K3 for fraud detection!

TLDR: Jev classified 100 emails in 1.42 seconds, then I routed the uncertain cases to Kimi K3. The full pipeline got 96/100 correct for only ~$0.07.

Video is not sped up, check out the live run!

Here was my process:

I gave Jev 100 emails to classify (a mix of 50 legit & 50 fraudelent emails). It classified all of them in 1.42 seconds.

An underrated feature about Jev is it will give you the confidence score for a classification, so I routed any prediction under 95% confidence to Kimi K3 to be fully sure.

31 emails fell below that threshold. After routing those to Kimi K3, the combined pipeline reached 96% accuracy.

The full run took 16 seconds & ~$0.07 in inference costs:

- $0.068 from Kimi K3 on @togethercompute
- $0.003 (1/3 of a cent) from Jev on @typesafeai.

I think this is a really interesting pattern: use a fast specialized model like Jev for the narrow task, then route the uncertain cases to a larger LLM.

I feel like this kind of approach could be a game changer for use cases like fraud or anything realtime. You can use the speed & low cost of Jev while having a larger LLM as a fallback to ensure high accuracy.

author_headline: Technical Lead Engineer at Perfios | Building Agentic AI IDP Systems & ML Platforms for Financial Document Processing
text:
The one model I've been excited to try recently is TypeSafe AI's Jev model that skips text generation and returns typed decisions with probabilties instead.

Got access this morning. To test it, I wired it up to play Super Mario Bros. 🎮

World 1-1 completed. 356 decisions and costs just $0.08.

Every 4 game frames, Jev receives RAM-decoded game state: position, velocity, nearby enemies, ceiling clearance, etc.

It answers four questions:
• Move how?
• Start a jump?
• Hop under a low ceiling?
• Keep holding A?

The code turns those decisions directly into controller inputs.
No pixels.
No prose.
No parsing generated text.

The output looks more like:
run_right 0.78 | walk_right 0.16 | brake_left 0.05 | wait 0.01
P(start_jump) 0.07 | P(sustain) 0.68 | P(ceiling_hop) 0.05

So I ran Claude Opus 5 alongside it, on its own emulator, deciding at the same time - same questions, same instructions, same action mapping, same seed.

The results were surprisingly stark:
Jev
→ Finished World 1-1
→ x = 3,161
→ ~600ms/decision
→ $0.08

Opus 5
→ Reached ~11% of the level
→ x = 362
→ ~5,998ms/decision
→ $4.42

That's roughly 10× lower latency and 55× lower total cost in this particular experiment.

And Jev lists at $0.042 per million input tokens, with output free.
But here's the part I found more interesting than the benchmark:
Jev isn't the smarter model.

On TypeSafe's own evaluation, Opus 5 scores higher: ~73.1% vs ~68% for Jev.

What Jev optimizes for is different:
0% structured-output error rate + 70–500ms response times.

For a real-time loop, a slightly better answer arriving six seconds later is the wrong trade. Mario doesn't wait. Decision quality was never the bottleneck - loop rate and cost were. And that's where I think this architecture gets interesting for production systems.
Things like:
• Classification: ticket intent, content categorisation, topic tagging, fraud etc
• Routing: which agent, tool, model or queue should handle a request
• Guardrails: safe/not-safe, on-policy/jailbreak, pass/block
• Relevance grading: does this chunk actually answer the query?
• Scoring: lead priority, risk triage, search/feed re-ranking
• LLM-as-judge: grading every eval run instead of sampling a tiny fraction

They all share the same shape:
bounded answer space → structured decision → program consumes the result

Using a chat model for these tasks often means paying for a generation layer you don't actually need.

Maybe the future isn't just bigger models. It's knowing when you don't need one. For many problems, fast + cheap + good enough beats big + expensive.


(Video is at 3× speed btw. Mario had places to be. Opus apparently did not.) 🍄

text:
Judgment models could become an important layer in enterprise AI. This week TypeSafe released Jev, built to return structured decisions with calibrated probabilities. Salesforce launched Koa, a reasoning model trained specifically for enterprise CRM work. Both point toward a broader shift: more specialized models doing specific cognitive jobs inside the same AI system.

Most enterprise workflows contain hundreds of small decisions. An invoice needs review. A claim looks unusual. An agent needs to know whether it can continue. A customer interaction carries some level of risk. Many of these calls require judgment without needing a large model to generate a long answer.

That opens up a different architecture. An agent can work through a process while smaller models assess its decisions, score confidence, route exceptions and trigger human review when uncertainty gets high.

The economics make this interesting at scale. Cheap judgment can sit inside thousands of workflows and evaluate far more of what enterprise AI does. Calibration will matter enormously. A confidence score becomes useful when the business understands what that score means in practice.

I expect enterprise AI stacks to contain a growing portfolio of specialized models, each built for a particular kind of cognitive work.

author_headline: Co-founder of Standard Agents (🤫). Compulsive open source builder. Creator of dmux, ArrowJS, FormKit, AutoAnimate, Tempo, zodown...
text:
I’ve put a ton of tokens through Jev now, and...I have thoughts.

1. The big labs lost the script

TypeSafe’s intro video says, “We’re building prod, not God” — and can I just say? Hell yeah. @typesafeai built something for engineers like me, so I can build products for people like your mom (she says hi btw). They’re not trying to create “Machines of Loving Grace”; they’re trying to build things that let OTHER HUMAN BEINGS create new types of products.

The proof is in the pudding. When ChatGPT shipped, we were all blown away by…ChatGPT. When Jev shipped, we were all blown away by what everyone was making with it.

I cannot tell you how refreshing this is. It takes a sincere form of humility to believe that you, the creator of a technology, will not be the best at deploying the technology into the marketplace. The big labs, especially Anthropic, have proven not to have this humility…and now everyone hates AI. Thanks, Dario.

I guess what I’m saying is: Diogo for president.

2. Ultra-smart classifiers were genuinely a missing primitive.

I don’t know how this got missed. Diogo calls it “machine-native intelligence,” and that’s really what it is. I cannot tell you how much bending and twisting I've had to do with LLMs to get them to act like a classifier when they just weren’t. I’m absolutely shocked this is the first time this “type” of model has come to market.

These models will unlock AI utility for entire industries: robotics, trucking, aviation, meteorology, finance, defense, retail…even your smart coffee mug is going to use this.

3. It’s still too expensive

Jev is really, really cheap compared to LLMs. But you don’t use it like an LLM. In my full self-driving example, or any robotics example, you’ll be making decisions several times per second continuously. The #1 value proposition of a model like this is speed and cost.

To be clear, at current pricing, the model will still be successful and well integrated. It will be able to replace a number of tasks that were already being performed (poorly) by LLMs. However, to unlock industrial-scale demand (Jevons paradox), I believe it needs to be roughly 10x cheaper.

Currently, Jev is $0.042/M input, which is actually 7x more expensive than a cache read on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.006). If our industrial application requires decisions at 10 Hz and we provide only 10k of context, that would cost $0.0042/second to operate, or $15/hour, $600/week, etc.

The good news is Diogo said on a recent AMA that they have substantial margin at their current pricing and have already considered dropping the cost further. I hope it's a lot further.

4. Latency is a real limiter

I really hope TypeSafe AI works with an edge network provider to improve the co-location of models and reduce network latency. Ultimately, these models really need to run on-device. I would even be willing to pay some kind of recurring license fee to have a great closed model running on my own hardware, just so I can reduce the TTD (Time To Decision) as much as possible. Imagine running a model like this at 60 Hz, or even 120 Hz.

At that point, we’re looking at a new kind of logic gate — we can’t even imagine what that will be like.

In summary, this one really is a game changer for everyone building AI products, and, assuming cost and latency are further improved…it’ll be a game changer for everyone doing anything.

author_headline: Senior Data & AI Engineer.
text:
I put Jev inside a SQL WHERE clause.

WHERE jev_noul(body, 'The customer is asking for their money back') > 0.8

Jev is TypeSafe's new model. It doesn't generate text. You ask a question in plain English and it returns a calibrated probability. That's the whole integration. There's no prompt template or JSON parsing, and no "please respond with only a number".

The setup: 10,000 customer reviews in DuckDB. The question: who wants a refund?

The old way is ILIKE '%refund%', which gets 780 hits. That count includes "no need for a refund, love it" and misses "put the money back on my card".

The new way asks in plain English. Jev judges every review and hands back a probability as an ordinary float column. After that it's just SQL: filter, sort, group.

Result: 913 refund requests, and 595 of them never use the word "refund". Keyword search was blind to two thirds of the queue.

What I like about it as a data engineer:

→ The output is typed. It's a DOUBLE, so I can threshold it, sort by it, aggregate it, and write tests against it.
→ A new business question is a changed string. The last query in the video finds the products that are losing customers, and I only changed the English.
→ Every judgment is cached. The second query in the video costs $0.00.
→ About 4,400 reviews judged in ~20 seconds. The whole demo cost about 4 cents.

Under the hood it's DuckDB Python UDFs calling the Jev API. Because Jev returns probabilities instead of prose, it fits in a WHERE clause and a chatbot doesn't.

Honest notes: the reviews are synthetic. I wrote them so that keyword search fails the way it does on real data. It's a weekend demo, not production. For speed I pack 16 rows per API call, and I measured what that costs: 0.5% of judgments flipped at my threshold.

This would be useful for customer feedback analysis, ticket triage, data quality checks on free-text fields, and lead scoring among many other things.

Where would you put a judgment like this in your pipeline?

author_headline: Building AI Products and Superintelligence | AI Consultant
text:
I spent sometime exploring Jev by TypeSafe AI, and it has genuinely changed how I think about a piece of our internal stack. Most AI agents today generate text first and then you parse that text into structured output, and that extra step quietly adds latency, adds cost, and adds one more place where things can break in production. Jev skips that step entirely, since you give it state and a set of typed questions, and it returns a decision directly, with a confidence score attached to every answer it gives.

We have an internal B2B CRM tool that we built about six months ago, which scores and classifies inbound leads using an LLM agent that produces structured output after a reasoning step, and today I swapped that piece out for Jev and ran it against a real lead to see how it would hold up. The lead was from a pharma company, asking about an AI system for classifying and retrieving roughly 4 million regulatory documents, and the response came back in under 300 milliseconds with everything I needed already in the right shape.

It has something called Noul, which is essentially a true or false judgment with a confidence score attached, and in this case Jev was 95% confident the lead came from an enterprise-scale organization and 98% confident it described a real business need for AI, all without a single sentence to parse or interpret.

It also has Score, which rates something across a range you define instead of forcing a binary answer, and here the budget signal and purchase intent both came back at 2.98 out of 4 with 98% confidence, which gives you an actual number to set thresholds against rather than a vague explanation you have to read into.

And it has Choice, which picks a single option from a list you provide, and in this case it classified the lead as document_intelligence with 100% confidence while correctly ruling out five other service categories in that same call.

What stood out most wasn't really the speed, even though the speed was impressive, but the fact that every single output already matched the exact shape my code was expecting, which meant no JSON parsing, no retry logic for malformed responses, and no extra cleanup call to make the output usable.

I want to be honest that this is one test on one lead and not a proper benchmark, so before this goes anywhere near production I still want to run it across a larger batch of leads and compare it directly against our current agent on both latency and accuracy. But for the narrow job of making small, well-defined decisions inside a larger system, this already feels like the right shaped tool for that job, since not every decision running through your software actually needs a full reasoning model behind it, and some of them just need a fast, typed answer instead.

Curious whether others are experimenting with decision-only models like this instead of routing every small decision through a chat-style LLM.

author_headline: Lead AI Scientist @ Zelara
text:
What's Jev?

I recently had the opportunity to try Jev, TypeSafe’s new model.

The idea behind it is surprisingly simple:

LLMs were designed to produce text for humans. But increasingly, we use them to make decisions for software.

Think about classifying a support ticket, scoring a lead, detecting fraud, routing a request, or deciding whether some condition is true.

With an LLM, we ask a text-generation model to make that judgment, force the result into JSON or another schema, then parse and validate it before our code can use it.

Jev is designed specifically for that second problem.

You give it state, which is the data or context you want it to evaluate, like a support ticket, document, transaction, or user message, and ask small, typed questions about it.

It returns structured, probabilistic judgments through three primitives:

Choice → pick from defined options + probability distribution
Score → evaluate on a defined scale + probability distribution
Noul → probability that something is true

So instead of just getting technical, you might get:

technical: 0.72
billing: 0.22
sales: 0.05
other: 0.01

Your code can then decide what to do with that uncertainty. It can act automatically, apply a threshold, rank alternatives, or escalate when confidence is low.

That makes Jev interesting for things like classification, routing, scoring, moderation, document evaluation, risk signals, and triage, anywhere the output is ultimately meant for software rather than a person.

Most people think AI agents need to “talk” to be smart.

A new model called Jev (by TypeSafe AI) is challenging that assumption by doing the exact opposite: it doesn’t generate words at all.

Here is the quick breakdown of what it is and why it matters:
The Difference in Plain English
• Traditional LLMs (Claude, GPT, Gemini): Like a thoughtful consultant. You ask a question, and they type out a response word-by-word. Brilliant for nuance, but slow and expensive for simple decisions.
• Jev (A Decision Model): Like an instant reflex. It doesn’t write text or chat. It evaluates fixed options simultaneously and makes structured decisions in under 100 milliseconds with calibrated confidence scores.

How This Transforms a RevOps Agent?

Imagine an automated inbound sales pipeline:
1. The Traffic Cop (Jev): A lead submits a form. In ~80ms, Jev evaluates intent and routes it: Enterprise Account Executive vs. Self-Serve Onboarding. Zero JSON syntax errors, zero hallucinations, pure deterministic routing.
2. Safe Autonomy: Because Jev outputs calibrated probabilities, you can enforce hard guardrails: if confidence is >95%, route automatically. If <70%, flag for a human SDR to review.
3. The Writer (LLM): The heavy, generative LLM only wakes up AFTER the decision is made to draft the bespoke, personalized outbound email.

Why Agent Developers Care?

Over 80% of steps in an agent workflow aren't creative writing—they are just traffic control (choosing a tool, validating data, branching logic).

Using a massive, slow LLM for simple routing has always been overkill. Splitting agent stacks into fast decision models for routing and generative LLMs for deep thinking makes pipelines significantly faster, cheaper, and virtually immune to schema crashes.

author_headline: Simplifying LLMs, AI Agents, RAG, and Machine Learning for you! • Co-founder @dailydoseofds_• BITS Pilani • 3 Patents • ex-AI Engineer @ LightningAI
text:
LLMs vs. Jev, clearly explained!

TL;DR

The key difference is not that Jev generates faster.

Jev does not generate text at all.

A traditional LLM receives context and produces an answer one token at a time. Even when the output is a small JSON object, every token depends on those generated before it.

Jev receives the same context but evaluates predefined decisions directly. When those decisions are independent, it can evaluate all of them in parallel.

Consider an agent handling a failed deployment. It may need to determine:

→ Whether the incident is urgent
→ Which team should handle it
→ Whether the proposed command is risky
→ Whether the task is complete

An LLM generates a response containing these answers sequentially. The application then parses and validates it.

With Jev, you define the questions and expected answer types upfront. It evaluates them together and returns typed answers with probabilities.

Jev supports three decision primitives:

1. **Choice** selects from known options, such as engineering, billing, or sales.

2. **Score** places the input on an ordered scale, such as low, medium, or high risk.

3. **Noul** evaluates a yes-or-no condition and returns the probability that it is true.

The probabilities matter as much as the selected answers.

If engineering receives 91% probability and billing receives 9%, automatic routing may be reasonable. If the probabilities are 52% and 48%, the system can escalate, gather more context, or call a stronger model.

This keeps control inside ordinary software.

Code owns the thresholds and consequences. Jev supplies the semantic judgment that a normal `if` statement cannot derive from unstructured text.

It works best when the possible answers are known, the decision depends on meaning, and a careful person could judge the input quickly.

It is not designed for writing, summarization, code generation, arithmetic, or decisions requiring several dependent reasoning steps. Independent questions can run in parallel, but decisions that depend on earlier results must remain sequential.

Jev also cannot return an option outside the declared schema, but it can still select the wrong valid option. Type safety prevents malformed outputs, not incorrect judgments.

The clean mental model is this:

LLMs generate new language when the answer space is open.

Jev evaluates known paths when the answer space is bounded.

I wrote the full breakdown explaining Jev and where it fits.

you can make any open source model behave like jev with just a bit of inference engineering.  

it's shockingly easy. to prove it, we built a new endpoint we're calling deepseek-v4.1-flash-jev. see the demo below. here's how it's done:

sglang (an inference engine) offers a scoring endpoint in addition to the normal generation one. in scoring mode, given an input & set of possible answers, it forces the model to produce probabilities for each one. example:

> input: what is most common letter in abcccde?
> possible answers: a, b, c

for deepseek, you have to add a closing think tag before the response. this forces a direct answer instead of  a reasoning trace. if you want reasoning, you can do that too, but imo that makes things too slow to be worth it.

Jev, a decision model by TypeSafe AI, answered over 5x faster than the next fastest LLM in our Ori Eval benchmark, with no loss in accuracy.

Jev is a new type of model. Instead of writing text, it takes a question and a list of options and returns a typed choice with a probability for every option. After a burst of projects and discussion around it, we put it to the test against popular LLMs on OpenRouter used for classification and judging: GPT-5.6 Luna, GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and Qwen3.8 Flash.

The task: read an incoming request and label it as one of 30 task types. A tightly scoped decision, made constantly in production systems, so latency and cost matter a lot. All five models ran the same 200 cases, sequentially and statelessly.

Speed: Jev was over 5x faster than the next fastest model, and even its slowest requests beat every other model's median.

Accuracy: Jev matched the best LLM in the field, and all five landed within a handful of cases of each other. A decision model was as correct as a full LLM.

Cost: Jev came in second cheapest, just behind Qwen3.8 Flash, and well under the three other LLMs.

Notes: the 200 cases are synthetic, evenly spread across the 30 task types. Reasoning was off for the LLMs, except GLM 5.3 Flash, which requires it and ran at low effort. DeepSeek and GLM were spread across 10 and 16 providers, so their tail latency reflects the mix.

Is anyone trying Jev for scalable oversight?

Seems like it could be useful for helping determine if a model is behaving in an aligned way.

for models whose output is a bounded software decision rather than open-ended prose and follows TypeSafe’s 15 Sept release of Jev, which takes application state plus fixed choices and returns a typed answer with probabilities instead of prose.

This benchmark's score deliberately combines Intelligence, Calibration, Speed and Cost because deployment can fail even when raw accuracy is high.

text:
How does Jev work?

Jev takes two things: your input and an output schema.

The schema gives the structure of the answer you want.

I send an email. 

My schema asks for two fields: is spam, and a category from marketing, finance, or spam.

Jev returns:
- is spam: 0.90
- category: spam

That is a 90% chance of spam.

Jev selects the category only from the list I give it. It writes no sentences. 

The 0.90 is a number object, so my code can use it immediately without extra processing.

Jev shows no reasoning. You get the answer and nothing more, so some people do not trust it.

Use Jev for choices your code must make fast and at low cost: spam or normal, buy or no buy, reply or escalate.
Jev makes things like RLS even easier!

🚨 A New AI Model Called “JEV” Is Taking a Very Different Approach

We’ve become familiar with Large Language Models (LLMs).

You give them a prompt, and they predict the next token—again and again—to generate text, write code, reason through problems, and power AI assistants.
Models like GPT, Claude, Gemini, Kimi, and GLM broadly follow this paradigm.

But JEV, a new model from TypeSafe, takes a different approach.

And if you're building AI-powered products or software, it’s worth paying attention to.
Instead of generating a long textual response—a blog post, an explanation, or a block of code 
JEV is designed to produce weighted scores and probabilities.

Think about use cases like:
→ Is this sales prospect a strong fit?
→ Which candidate should be prioritized?
→ Is this transaction potentially risky?
→ Which product should we recommend?
→ What action should the system take next?

TypeSafe describes this as a “System 1” model, inspired by the idea of fast, automatic human decision-making.

The interesting part?

For the right workloads, this approach could reportedly be 20x–200x faster, while also reducing cost.


That could be significant.

text:
I’ve been testing Jev AI alongside my existing lead-scoring workflow.The similarity between the scores is interesting, but it isn’t really the main point.

What interests me more is how the two systems arrive at their answers and where each approach might make sense.

My lead workflow is built in n8n. When a new enquiry arrives, the data is cleaned, checked and redacted before the same lead is sent to two scorers in parallel.

The first is my private Codex node.  Codex produces a detailed lead score, explains its reasoning, writes a short note for the sales team and then passes its result into my own deterministic rules. At the moment, this remains the score that controls whether a lead is sent to sales, held for review or suppressed.

The second scorer is Jev, which I’ve added in shadow mode. Jev returns a much leaner, structured classification. It is not currently allowed to change anything in the workflow. Its result is simply added to the lead email and scoring sheet alongside the Codex result so that I can compare them over time.

On one recent anonymised lead:
Private Codex node: 96/100
Strong lead - send to sales
Jev: 92/100

High purchase intent
Both arrived at essentially the same outcome.  The important difference is that Jev reached its classification with a much smaller token footprint.

For my current workflow, that advantage doesn’t matter enormously. Codex is already included in my existing setup, so the marginal cost to me is effectively zero. I also value the richer reasoning and sales notes it produces.

This is therefore not a case of replacing Codex with Jev.  However, I can see where Jev’s approach could become useful.

If I were processing high volumes of events in real time perhaps as part of a server-side tracking setup the balance would be different. You might need to classify a lead or session immediately before deciding whether to forward it to a CRM, analytics system, advertising platform or another model.

In that situation, speed, predictable structured output and token efficiency could be more valuable than a detailed explanation.

That feels like the more interesting potential use case for Jev: a focused classification layer sitting inside a fast server-side data flow.

For now, I’m only testing it. Codex remains the decision-maker, while both results are recorded and sent to me.  I’ll be particularly interested in the leads where the two systems disagree, because those cases should reveal far more than the ones where both produce similar scores.

Early days, but an interesting idea.   I think definitely worth it if you're running server-side Google Analytics and sending events like that.    I think Stripe, Taggrs, and Tracklution et al will add something like this at some point

-> SET your confidence threshold BEFORE you ship, not after the first incident. the calibrated probability is the actual feature here. no threshold means you built a fast oracle and then trusted it exactly as blindly as the slow one.

-> LOG the confidence next to the real outcome, every time. a calibration score that drifts is invisible until you have the paired data. "it was 0.9 confident" means nothing if you never checked what 0.9 cashed out to.

-> TREAT the benchmarks as marketing until someone else runs them. the speed numbers are self-reported and the accuracy reference is an AVERAGE of two frontier models. that is the vendor grading the vendor.

-> STEAL the pattern from fast-jev-compaction, the claude code plugin. it kills the summary step entirely - every tool call and result gets SCORED in one fast request, stale ones dropped or truncated, everything it keeps stays VERBATIM. no summary means no summarization lies. that is the whole shape: decide what survives, do not rewrite it.

author_headline: Head of Data & AI Engineering
text:
🗓️Jev hype check, week 1.

What is it?

LLM: f(text) → text
Jev: f("My card was charged twice", {
  topic: [billing, technical, sales],
  urgent: yes/no
})
→ { topic: billing (0.85), urgent: 0.72 }

Jev is a zero-shot classifier. You declare the possible answers and it returns a confidence for each.

Is there a technical breakthrough? Single-pass zero-shot classifiers already exist (GLiClass). Calibrated confidence isn't new either. Claiming both, with LLM-grade understanding, on labels the model has never seen, would be.


Performance seems to hold up. Early (sampled) tests show 90%+ accuracy. It does seem to struggle a bit more with specific or ambiguous tasks, the model stays confident where it shouldn’t. Measure the model before you threshold on it.

By design it's a black box: a probability, no explanation. The old explainability problem is back. LLMs answer it post-hoc with a plausible story that changes every run; Jev gives none, just a value and a score.


💡Good fits for Jev are sentiment and intent analysis, tabular data augmentation, and guardrails or routing around LLM agents.

➡️ So where do we stand? Over-hyped, as always. But cheap, fast zero-shot classification with usable confidence and near-LLM understanding carries real substance. Wait and see.

text:
STOP paying "Claude tax" to answer a multiple choice question.

GTM stacks route every decision through a frontier LLM. 
Approve or flag this transaction. 
Is this lead worth a human touch. 
Escalate or auto-resolve this ticket.

That's not reasoning at all. It's a basic lookup with extra steps and a even bigger bill.

TypeSafe AI just launched Jev. 

Built by one of the people behind RLHF, the technique that trained ChatGPT in the first place. And Jev isn't an LLM. 

It doesn't write anything. 

You give it the possible answers up front, approve, flag, escalate, a score, yes or no, and it hands back a probability for each one. Nothing to parse. No hallucination risk on a decision that only had 3 valid answers anyway.

The number that matters - $0.04 per million input tokens. Now compare that to what you're paying Opus or Sonnet to run the same classification, over and over, thousands of times a day.

If your GTM stack has an agent doing any of this, you're overpaying:
➔ Routing leads. Deciding which rep gets which lead, or whether it goes to sales at all.
➔ Scoring intent. Reading a signal (page visit, reply, demo request) and deciding hot, warm, or cold.
➔ Flagging risk. Catching a suspicious signup, a chargeback pattern, a fraud flag before it becomes a problem.
➔ Triaging tickets. Deciding if a support message needs a human now, later, or not at all.

Every one of these is a closed set of answers. You already know what the options are. You don't need a model that can write you a sonnet to pick one of four boxes.

Not every AI task is a conversation. Some of it is just a decision, made fast and cheap, over and over. Keep the expensive model for the calls that actually need judgment. 

Send the rest somewhere built to just decide.

In-call coaching exists today. It shows up 30 seconds late and says something generic. The reason is physics. To answer during a live call, you have to check the conversation every few seconds and respond within one. Reasoning models take ten seconds or more, and every check costs money. So teams cut the context down to a low thousand tokens, and the reasoning budget is limited, and the result is a tool that tells the rep to "ask about budget" half a minute after the buyer moved on.

Our memory decides what matters in this call, Jev decides whether it has happened yet, and our code puts the answer on the seller's screen while the buyer is still talking. The team built that over the past few days.
So for the first time, in-call coaching can run with everything the system knows, at the speed a conversation moves.

Lot's of chat this last week about Jev, an interesting new kind of AI model from TypeSafe.

https://lnkd.in/gaFHewN5

Unlike a normal LLM, it is not designed to generate text. You give it some text and a set of fixed questions, and it returns structured answers with probabilities.

Think of it as a very intelligent switch statement.

The ideal use case is a simple judgement where:
* the possible answers are already known
* the information needed is in the input
* the task mostly requires understanding English
* you do not need deep knowledge or multi-step reasoning

That makes it interesting for things like intent classification, urgency, relevance, sentiment, moderation, routing and deciding what should happen next.

A few practical examples stood out.

Ryan Vogel used Jev to classify 1,500 of his own emails. This is almost the perfect problem: Is this important? Does it require action? Is it sales, support, finance or noise?
https://lnkd.in/gMXkWdJ7

Hassan, used Jev as the first stage of fraud detection. Jev classified 100 emails, then only the lower-confidence cases were sent to Kimi K3. The interesting pattern here is broader: use Jev for the obvious cases and only pay for a large reasoning model when the decision is genuinely difficult.
https://lnkd.in/gXNS8JTQ

Sydney Runkle and the LangChain team have explored using Jev inside agents. One particularly good use case is deciding which tool an agent needs before calling the main LLM. Does this request need web search, a database, code execution, another tool, or nothing at all?
https://lnkd.in/gSCX_-tQ

Mike Taylor also used Jev as a very cheap quality checker across large amounts of writing: does this sound promotional, hostile, vague or inconsistent with a style guide?
https://lnkd.in/gtzh9XXX

The common theme is that Jev probably does not replace an LLM.

It replaces the surprisingly large number of LLM calls where all we really needed was a small semantic judgement.

Use TypeSafe AI's Jev model with Pinecone to rerank results with natural language criteria!

Usually with rerankers, it's hard to cleanly specify what should and shouldn't be returned in results.

Jev resolves this by refactoring the problem into evaluating against distinct binary criteria, which pairs great with Pinecone retrieval!

In this demo, we compare using Jev and Claude to rerank 200 returned candidates from Pinecone. Jev returns a reranked list in about a second — 830 to 1,300 ms across eight test queries. Claude Opus 5, doing the same job in one long-context call, takes 4.2 to 6.8 seconds.
That's roughly 5x faster, and about 43x cheaper: $0.004 per query against $0.18.

Try it out, here!

For years the story has been that models are superhuman at chat, so where is all the automation? TypeSafe's answer, out of two years of stealth this week, is that we've been asking the wrong kind of model.

Meet Jev, the first public System One Model. Founder Diogo Almeida, who worked on the instruction-following research behind ChatGPT at OpenAI, built a new class of frontier model that doesn't generate prose at all. You hand it unstructured state and typed questions. It hands back decisions your code can act on directly: a yes/no probability (Noul), a label with a probability for every option (Choice), or an expected value on a rubric you define (Score).

Giving up strings buys a lot. Zero type errors, by construction. Calibrated probabilities instead of vibes, from a training method TypeSafe calls RLCD, reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions. And speed: 70 to 500 ms end to end, which TypeSafe puts at 40 to 200x faster than frontier LLMs at the same intelligence, at $0.042 per million input tokens with output free. Their workflow evals go as high as 193x faster and 444x cheaper.

That's not a cheaper LLM. That's the Jevons paradox TypeSafe named it after: drop the cost of a decision by two orders of magnitude and every conditional in your software becomes a place you can afford to put intelligence. Routing, guardrails, classification, verification of LLM output, map-reduce over a data lake. Things you would never wait three seconds or pay a cent per call for.

Which is exactly why the decisions need to be observable. When a 142 ms judge is gating what your agent sends to customers, you want to see the judgment where it happened: inside the agent's trace, next to the tool call and the draft it was judging.

So we shipped OpenInference instrumentation for the TypeSafe SDK, Python and JS. Every Jev call is an LLM span in Phoenix with the state, the questions, the chosen answers, the full probability distribution, the confidence, the model version, and the token counts. Plain OpenTelemetry, so it goes to Phoenix, Arize AX, or any OTLP collector you already run. No vendor SDK wrapping your client.

text:
I got to play with Jev today, TypeSafe AI's small AI model that answers yes/no, pick-one and score questions. I threw my real work at it. Thanks to Ezequiel C. and Kinan Hamwi for putting Jev on my radar! 

But what even IS Jev, Andres? You send it text and a question through an API, and It sends back a yes/no, pick-one or score answer, plus how confident it is. How is it different from a chat model like Claude Sonnet 5? Sonnet answers with text you read. Jev answers with a fixed answer (yes/no, a bucket or a number) plus a confidence. 

Sonnet (and like models) are/is best at open-ended work like writing, code and strategy. Jev is best at narrow judgments phrased as a question. You can use both in tandem to get the best of each model and get more consistent output. 

On two small tests (23 job postings and 28 direct messages, DMs), it matched my own labels 40 of 51 times, about 78%. Each run took a couple of seconds, and the whole 51 cost well under a cent. Usually that's ~0.24 cents on Sonnet 5 for me. 

Where Jev fits: yes/no calls, sorting into buckets, scoring against a rubric, and ranking a list. 

Where it doesn't: writing, arithmetic and dates, working out the question, and long, messy documents.

Five ways I'd use it for myself and my clients:

1. Score job postings. Five yes/no questions (is the scope bounded, is it a stack I work in, do I get to pick the tools, is there a named contact, is the client mission-driven), then your own rule turns the yes count into apply, negotiate or skip. Matched my labels on 18 of 23 postings on first pass.

2. Sort inbound DMs into reply, ask back or skip. A bare "hi" goes to "ask back," so a real lead isn't dropped. Matched my labels on 22 of 28 DMs on first pass.

3. Check alt text. Alt text is the description a screen reader reads aloud for an image. Checkers catch it when it's missing. Jev judges whether the words say anything.

4. Screen form submissions. Jev ranks new form entries by spam score. A person approves before anything goes live.

5. Rank case studies for a visitor on a website. The visitor describes their need in one sentence. One yes/no question per case study ("relevant to their sector?"), then sort by how likely each is a yes.

Much to think about but I love the possibilities. What are you excited about using Jev for?

I think most are building AI systems wrong.  Most are building how they are being told. 

Intelligence should not be the runtime for everything.

I’ve been pushing this idea through AI SDLC for a while:

First figure out what actually requires intelligence.

Then figure out what should just be software.

Because if the answer is deterministic…

WRITE THE DAMN CODE.

Don’t ask an LLM the same question 10 million times.

Don’t spend tokens rediscovering something software already knows how to do perfectly.

Don’t use intelligence where automation works.

Automation is cheaper than intelligence.

And with serverless, deterministic execution can be ridiculously cheap.

That alone changes the economics of AI.

But now another layer is emerging.

Decision models like Jev.

They don’t need to write an essay.

They don’t necessarily need to reason through the entire problem.

They need to make a decision.

Which model?

Which tool?

Which workflow?

Continue or stop?

Escalate or don’t?

Safe or unsafe?

Complete or incomplete?

So I increasingly think about AI architecture as three different computational layers:

1. DETERMINISTIC → CODE

Known problem. Known rules. Repeatable outcome.

Automate it.

2. DECISION → SMALL, CHEAP INTELLIGENCE

Route it. Classify it. Score it. Choose.

Don’t summon a giant model just to pick Door #3.

3. REASONING → FRONTIER INTELLIGENCE

Ambiguity. Novelty. Synthesis. Judgment. Creation.

Spend the tokens here.

That’s the architecture.

Code → Decide → Think.

Not:

LLM → EVERYTHING.

That distinction becomes enormous when you start talking about agents.

An agent may perform millions of actions.

If every action requires a frontier-model inference, the economics get ugly very quickly.

But what if 90% of those actions can become deterministic software?

What if most of the remaining orchestration can be handled by extremely cheap decision intelligence?

And only a small fraction actually requires frontier reasoning?

Now the economics completely change.

And AI SDLC makes this even more interesting.

Use intelligence to discover, design and write the deterministic system.

Then stop paying intelligence to execute what it already figured out.

Intelligence creates the automation.
Automation replaces the intelligence.

That is a very different economic model.

Serverless makes the deterministic layer stupid cheap.

Decision models make orchestration stupid cheap.

Frontier models become the scarce resource you invoke when actual intelligence is required.

I’ve spent much of my career optimizing compute.

I think we’re entering an era where we optimize intelligence consumption the same way.

How much intelligence does this transaction actually require?

That’s going to become an architectural question.

And eventually a financial one.

The cheapest token is the one you never needed to generate.

author_headline: Fintech Professional | AI Solution Architect | Real Time Data, Ontologies | AI / Palantir FDE | Quantum Computing | VQE, QEC, FTQC | Exploring AI Beyond LLMs/DL/RL 🥷
text:
Today is a sad day for AI...

Because Jev shows that apparently most of the field knows jack.. I see people with AI lead titles at some of the biggest orgs genuinely confused by its performance and by why it takes so 'few tokens', as if useful computation somehow has to involve a giant LLM generating thousands of tokens. 

You do not need tokens to compute that 2 + 2 = 4. You do not need to sample the answer. You do not need a probabilistic language model to establish the fact, and you definitely do not need to consume a lake of water doing it. Some things are simply known, computed, estimated or decided directly. That applies to a huge class of the statistical functions covered by Jev. Probability functions, confidence estimates, thresholding, scoring, optimization, regression, state evaluation, tree based methods, statistical inference and bounded decision functions have existed for decades. There is an enormous mathematical and machine learning toolbox for doing exactly this kind of work without asking an LLM to generate a book about it first.

Yet somehow we spent the last few years routing every little thing through LLMs. Instead of asking what existing lightweight statistical function actually solves the problem, we started asking how to prompt an LLM to approximate it with tokens. Then we wrapped more software around the transformer, spent even more tokens managing the context, and eventually forgot there was ever another way to compute anything.. Now Jev comes along and people are shocked. Oh my God, how is it so fast? How does it use so few tokens? How can these tiny models make decisions without asking a giant LLM every single time?

Because you never needed an LLM for those functions in the first place.

That is what makes the industry reaction depressing. A bunch of people can take techniques from statistics and machine learning that have existed since the 1980s or even 1900s, apply them where they actually belong, and suddenly half the industry acts like it has witnessed some new fundamental breakthrough in AI. If by progress we mean finally stopping the use of an LLM for every problem whether it belongs there or not, then sure, that is progress.

But this is not some magical post LLM discovery. It is the industry going in circles again. A new generation arrives, forgets the previous generation of techniques, spends years forcing everything through the fashionable architecture, eventually rediscovers the old tools and then celebrates the rediscovery as if somebody just invented computation. 'internet moment' 😭😭😭🤡

That is the sad part.

Jev did not reveal some mysterious new law of AI.

It revealed how many people working in AI apparently know jack..

Also this is why alternatives have such a hard time gaining traction and why we cant have nice things.. bc LLMs is all anyone knows.

Jev is slowly going to take your job away 😞😞

One of the biggest challenges with AI has always been cost.

Think about a simple support ticket:

“My payment failed.”

If you use a large LLM just to decide whether this ticket should go to the Payments, Sales, or Marketing team, you're potentially spending money on a capability that doesn't require that much reasoning.

This is where ultra-cheap, fast models like Jev become interesting.

For simple, repetitive tasks like classification, routing, extraction, and basic decisions, you may not need an expensive frontier model every time.

Jev doesn’t charges for output tokens and even very less for input tokens

Now we are back to optimizing AI costs, let’s see how far this all will go

#dev #jev #ai

Every few weeks, a new model claims the top spot on a benchmark or announces a breakthrough. Just last week, TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, its first public model, which the company claims delivers comparable intelligence on decision-making tasks at up to 200 times the speed and a fraction of the cost of traditional LLMs. 

Teams are then left to figure out whether these advances actually translate into better results for their work. CNBC recently called this “model fatigue.”

The bigger problem is that there is no single best model. Most leading models can search, reason, code, and generate content. What varies is the quality, latency, and cost for a specific task. One model may be better for coding. Another may be faster for search. Another may produce better artifacts but cost a lot more.

Generic benchmarks can’t capture these differences. Models need to be evaluated against the real work people do.

The goal is to understand the Pareto frontier: which model offers the best tradeoff between quality, latency, and cost for each task. 

At Glean, we built Waldo, a specialized model that gathers enterprise context before handing the work to a frontier model. The signals it produces help the system determine how much reasoning the task requires. A simple search shouldn’t take the same path as debugging code or creating a complex artifact.

And when a new model is released, customers shouldn’t have to retest every workload. The system should determine where it performs better and update its routing accordingly.

The best model will keep changing. The platform’s job is to absorb that complexity so model fatigue doesn’t become the user’s problem.

The most interesting AI talent announcement I've seen this year came from a venture capital firm launching a "Sales Combine."

The existence of First Round Capital's "NFL but make it sales" combine matters less than the assumptions behind it. VCs' moves tend to reveal how they think about the future. In this case, how they see markets, moats, talent and GTM evolving. 

Five thoughts:

1) Tech moats keep eroding overnight in AI-driven markets (e.g., Jev and Grok Bot’s rise to startup popularity in days and weeks). Having a killer product is just not enough anymore.

2) GTM talent/distribution are a need-to-have source of competitive advantage now. It’s literally part of the moat. GTM operators in hyper-competitive markets have felt this for a while now, but it’s different when VC decides to put resources behind it at the early stages of company formation. It’s a signal about where they believe market value creation will occur in their next generation of AI companies.

3) SaaS sales talent and skills don’t translate to AI-native sales talent. This is a big emerging narrative. It’s not news that AI companies are struggling to find talent (especially in markets like NYC and SF). It is news that the traditional proxies of years of experience in SaaS are less predictive of success. Raw attributes like judgement, curiosity, agency, coachability, leaning velocity, storytelling > smashing your number in ZIRP era sales teams. 

4) VCs see owned IC talent supply chains as critical to manufacture better portfolio returns. VCs usually place execs; moving into Individual Contributor workforce formation is new, and crucially they probably just think they’re better at it than the founders. What I find so compelling here is that it’s all about placing coachable talent with raw attributes and skills. A signal for the broader AI-native GTM labor market. 

5) This is a big bet that great sellers become even more valuable in the AI era, a counterpoint to a lot of the GTM AI narratives out there claiming you need less reps. My take here is that while yes, AI is changing exactly what a rep is responsible for on a day-to-day basis, we're about to see a renaissance in the craft of selling. The stuff buried in books from the 90s is what a VC is betting a new generation of sellers need to be taught.

For what it's worth, I think this is awesome and I hope more VCs follow suit.

If you’re like me and have been seeing “Jev” everywhere on X, but don’t fully get how it’s useful, here’s the non-technical, simplified summary:

1) The problem with LLMs in a lot of product work is that we force them to “write” an answer every time. It’s like asking someone to write a full paragraph just to say yes or no.
2) Then the app has to read that paragraph, pick out the answer, and hope the model didn’t invent something weird.
3) Jev skips the writing, time, and latency. Think AI multiple choice, not AI essay writing. More like a smart decision button your app can press a thousand times.

Built by the TypeSafe AI team (one of them, Diogo, co-created ChatGPT). You give it a situation, ask a clear question with clear options, and it comes back with a decision plus how confident it is.

It’s taking off online because the comparisons vs LLMs are wild:
- up to 200x faster
- up to 400x cheaper
- Output tokens are FREE

The potential here is that you can keep the big model for the hard thinking and writing and use Jev for the rapid-fire decisions in between.

For Supademo, there are some clear use cases that map cleanly onto our AI Demo Agents:
1) Is this visitor exploring alone, or evaluating for a team rollout?
2) Guided walkthrough, sandbox, or short clip first?
3) Are they stuck on setup, or ready to create their first demo?

Instead of hard-coded if/else trees, you get continuous judgment inside the product without paying full LLM latency on every tiny call.

LLMs made software really good at generating and reasoning. Now, lightweight models like Jev could make software much better at making millions of small contextual decisions in real time.

If that works, AI stops being a feature bolted on top and becomes native to the product itself.

Everyone has been impressed by TypeSafe AI’s Jev — I wanted to see for myself how good it is — and how useful it could be for a product like Lightfield.

I started with text understanding, because it is the foundation of everything a decision model does: it has to understand the input, and it has to understand and follow the instructions you give it. 

The short takeaway:  TypeSafe's tiny "Jev" classifier is surprisingly good — roughly on the level of Claude Sonnet on classification tasks, while being a couple of orders of magnitude cheaper to run. 

I looked at two kinds of work. First, general text understanding: three widely used reading-comprehension and commonsense benchmarks, where Jev performed on par with Opus. Because those may well sit in Jev's training data, I also hand-authored a fresh benchmark over a single random Wikipedia article — every wrong option drawn from the text, so nothing could be memorized. There, Jev landed alongside Sonnet and Opus (it tops CommonsenseQA and MMLU-CF, ties Opus on RACE-H, and is ~150× cheaper and ~10× faster on long-context questions).

Then I tried tasks closer to sales and customer relationships. There aren't many good public benchmarks, so I dug up older customer-service and negotiation datasets. On those, Jev is a bit better than Claude Haiku and slightly below Sonnet 5. Big caveat: none of these come from real B2B sales, so the findings are directional rather than a description of what we actually do at Lightfield.

Overall, the results look good enough that I think small, inexpensive classification models like Jev will have real uses, including in our own product.

We tested three setups on the same Milvus shortlist: 𝗻𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗾𝘄𝗲𝗻𝟯.𝟳-𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁-𝗿𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗸, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗝𝗲𝘃.

On 80 SciFact queries, qwen3.7-text-rerank improved nDCG@10 by 𝟬.𝟬𝟰𝟰𝟲 over no reranking, while Jev improved it by 𝟬.𝟬𝟳𝟳𝟴. Jev ranked best of the three, but its P50 reranking latency was 𝟭𝟬.𝟮× 𝗵𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗾𝘄𝗲𝗻, with an estimated cost per run of 𝟲.𝟳×.

Why does Jev behave differently?
Its interface is built around 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲 + 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀. For reranking, we keep the relevance question fixed and change the state for each query-candidate pair: “𝗜𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝗿𝘆?” Jev returns a structured Yes/No judgment with probabilities, and we use 𝗣(𝗬𝗲𝘀) as the relevance score for sorting.

In this experiment, 30 candidates meant 30 independent Jev requests running concurrently, so the latency includes that API overhead.

We also tested using probability directly for filtering. At a 𝟬.𝟱 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗱, top-5 precision reached 𝟰𝟵.𝟰%, but 𝟭𝟴.𝟴% 𝗼𝗳 𝗴𝗼𝗹𝗱-𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗲𝘃𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝘂𝘁. That makes Jev attractive for offline retrieval, data cleaning, and evaluation, but much harder to use as-is for latency-sensitive online RAG.

Next, we’re testing whether batching multiple candidate questions into one Jev request can bring that latency down.

The nerd herd is talking about Jev (and similar models).

What is it? Should we care? Here's the simplest breakdown I can make. Jev and similar models (Laya, etc.) are fundamentally small, lightweight, very, very fast classifiers. They take in text and return one of three outputs:

1. A choice from a list.
2. A score.
3. A yes/no binary output.

That's all they do, and they do it at very high speeds because they expect you to provide all the information. For example, suppose you wanted to do social media sentiment scoring. You'd provide a scoring rubric and a post, and the model would return a score based on your rubric.

Or you wanted to classify whether or not a decision was a good idea. You'd provide the decision context and request a yes/no output.

Or you wanted to label a dataset. You'd provide rows of data, one by one, along with a list to choose from, and it would return the appropriate choice per row.

Why are people talking about it? Because it's very fast and very cheap, orders of magnitude cheaper than using a frontier model for the same task. But it's not new. Laya, a competing project, is more than a year old now. And creating your own version of this that's totally free (and usable on almost every computer because the underlying models are so small) is a weekend's coding project with your favorite frontier AI.

So do I care? It's a great concept, and I've learned a lot rolling my own over the weekend. I don't need to get on Jev's waitlist when I have my own (built with Qwen 3.5 0.8B), and I get much better accuracy with my own because I tuned it on my own data. 

What I do think is important is that it gets into people's heads that you don't need the biggest, baddest, bulkiest AI model for a lot of tasks, and a lot of tasks fit in this classification schema. You can use a very fast, very small decision system like this to do a lot of work up front in your pipeline, reserving frontier models (which are slower, expensive, and consume a lot of resources) for when they're truly needed.

Many of our decisions really are classification decisions. Which is the better choice? What should I make for dinner? Did someone use an AI bot in the comments? Those aren't decisions that need frontier reasoning as long as you have sufficient examples - and what's missing from a lot of conversation about Jev is that you have to provide the data and context. It's not going to do that for you.

If you're doing a ton of classification work, Jev and similar models are for you.

Just rewired our renewals agent's "Next Best Action" flow using Jev. The flow came out 4.5× cheaper and 2× faster - accuracy holding, and a whole class of routing middleware deleted. 
 
The "Next best action" flow is the most used flow in our renewal agent: do account research utilizing 15+ tools -> map to expected outcomes based on a list of 18 playbooks -> generate the offer and messaging. We took our eval set of synthetic account scenarios and put the Jev-aided flow to the test.
 
What Jev improved:
1️⃣Tool calls & arguments - Jev picks from a candidate set, so it can't invent a tool or a parameter that doesn't exist. That deletes middleware we built to catch fabricated syntax and elaborate tool-rejection/self-heal loops. The entire tool call - reason - validate loop is more reliable, quicker and cheaper.  
2️⃣Deterministic "Next Best Action" - it reads the current playbook set and routes to the right plays, matching GPT-5.4's recall at twice the speed, one fifth the cost. Our playbooks and routing logic are written as markdown files instead of code scripts - a trade-off we made to gain explainability against deterministic decision making. We just won that determinism back. 
 
Lot of people dismiss Jev as just another classifier model. We've known classifier models do great at predicting the next best action. Interestingly, Laya - Jev's open-source equivalent, was originally built for sales conversion forecasting and predicting next best action. While Laya needs fine-tuning per task and temperature-calibration before it's useful, Jev does great zero-shot. Generalization is what they've nailed: producing probabilities and choices from one paragraph of context in English, not millions of rows of historical data or code that needs maintaining. 
 
Zooming out - most of our GTM stack (and I'd bet most Clay-style orchestration) is a pile of small sequential decisions dressed up as hardcoded rules: which data provider to look up, when to fall back, how to score accounts, what to do next. That's where Jev comes in, as a new powerful decision layer for those flows.

Most AI you've used works the same way. You ask it something, and it writes out the answer word by word, even when the answer is just "yes." That's how ChatGPT works, and it's how most tools built on top of it work too.

author_headline: CTO & CIO at Seyfor d.o.o.; PhD in Computer Science
text:
Jev is attracting attention as a fast, inexpensive alternative to LLMs for certain text-analysis tasks. I think it's worth exploring, but some context matters.

Machine learning has classified documents, detected intent and analysed sentiment for decades. More recent approaches can also classify text from category descriptions, without training on examples for that particular task. Jev surely didn't invent classification.

A conventional LLM can perform these tasks too, but produces its answer token by token. Jev doesn't generate text. It evaluates questions you define and returns structured results with probability estimates.

As an example, for a customer support ticket, its three output types could be used like this:
- Choice: Select a team from a list you provide, such as billing, product support, technical support, or sales.
- Score: Rate urgency on a scale you define, such as low, medium, or high.
- Noul: Estimate the probability that the answer to your yes/no question is yes - for example, "Is this customer requesting a refund?"

Application code then decides how to route the ticket, whether it needs human review, or whether an LLM should draft a reply.

Its potential appeal lies in combining instructions written in ordinary language, parallel evaluation of independent questions, and low processing costs. TypeSafe, the company behind Jev, also emphasizes training for calibrated probabilities. For example, among comparable cases assigned an 80% probability of containing a customer refund request, roughly 80% should actually contain one.

These are familiar language-processing tasks. The practical question is whether Jev handles them with a better balance of accuracy, speed, cost, and integration effort than the alternatives - including existing classifiers, not just large language models.

A result can fit the required format and still be wrong. You need to test both accuracy and probability calibration on your own data. Interpreting a customer's message also doesn't make Jev a replacement for, e.g., models validated to predict loan defaults or insurance losses.

For me, the interesting part is the potential to make flexible text classification and scoring easier to integrate into everyday software. That could be valuable.

text:
Jev.... (ala Jevons paradox)

Most of your AI bill is not “intelligence.”

It is an LLM writing a paragraph so your code can throw it away and keep one label.

That is the gap TypeSafe’s Jev is built for.

https://lnkd.in/dwhdMU8V 

Jev does not chat. It does not summarize. It does not write code. You hand it messy state — a ticket, a command, a document, an agent trace — plus a closed set of questions. It returns a typed decision: pick one option, score it on your rubric, or give you a yes/no probability. Seventy to five hundred milliseconds. Output tokens are free. Your application branches on the value.

If you run platform, architecture, or IT operations, the useful question is not “is this the next ChatGPT?” It is “where are we already classifying things with a generative model because we never had a cheap general-purpose chooser?”

Four placements that hold up in real systems:

• **Shim** — sit it between messy intake and software that already knows what “billing,” “legal,” or “P1” means.  
• **Rank** — do not ask it to solve the research problem. Ask it which of 10,000 items deserves a human hour.  
• **Gate** — put it in the agent outer loop. Continue, retry, ask a person, or stop. The LLM still writes. Jev decides whether the next expensive step is allowed.  
• **Interface** — urgency and sentiment as a column, not a chatbot bolted onto the side of the CRM.

What it is not: a replacement for frontier models, a local open-weight box, or a promise of correctness. “No hallucinations” means it cannot invent a label you did not supply. It can still pick the wrong one. Treat confidence as a threshold in *your* policy, not as a warranty.

The only experiment worth running this week is a substitution test. Take one existing LLM classification call. Measure accuracy, latency, cost, and how often you would have acted on the score. If it does not beat that call, leave the architecture alone.

Cheap judgment will not shrink AI. It will put intelligence in a thousand places that were never worth a paragraph.

If you lead engineering or architecture: where in your stack are you still generating text for a decision that only needed a label?

Traditional ML teams train a classifier around a fixed label set. Fraud or not fraud. Route A, B or C. Churn risk high, medium or low. The output is constrained, fast and easy for software to consume, but every new task usually needs its own data and training loop.

TypeSafe AI's Jev is trying to keep that interface and replace the task-specific training.

The useful analogy is zero-shot classification with a production contract around it.

- route an inbound account using the form, enrichment and product activity together
- score whether a support thread is actually a churn risk
- extract the buying committee from messy CRM notes
- branch an AEO workflow based on which buyer question disappeared from an answer engine

The surrounding code still owns the workflow. Jev supplies the fuzzy decision where hand-written rules become brittle.

TypeSafe reports 70-500ms response times, $0.042 per million input tokens and typed outputs with no schema errors. author_headline: Simplifying LLMs, AI Agents, RAG, and Machine Learning for you! • Co-founder @dailydoseofds_• BITS Pilani • 3 Patents • ex-AI Engineer @ LightningAI
text:
The Jev sweet spot.

(when to use it, and when not to)

Jev lives between rules and LLMs.

The easiest mistake is treating Jev as a faster replacement for an LLM.

It is better to think of Jev as the missing layer between deterministic software and open-ended generation.

The graphic below maps that boundary using two dimensions. One is how constrained the answer space is. The other is how frequently the decision must be made.

↳ Use ordinary code when the rule is exact.

↳ Use an LLM when the answer must be created through writing, planning, explanation, or deeper reasoning.

↳ Use Jev when the possible answers are known, but choosing among them requires semantic judgment.

A decision belongs in that sweet spot when four conditions are true.

→ The valid answers can be defined in advance. Jev should choose from known labels, ordered scores, or a yes-or-no decision.

→ The input is difficult to express as deterministic rules. A person could judge it quickly, but an if-statement cannot reliably understand its meaning.

→ The decision happens frequently. Model routing, ticket triage, retrieval reranking, guardrails, and high-volume labelling repeat often enough for latency and cost to compound.

→ Uncertainty should change what happens next. High-confidence results can continue automatically. Ambiguous results can be sent to a stronger model or a person.

Consider support-ticket routing.

The possible owners are already known. They might be engineering, billing, or sales. But customer messages arrive as unstructured language rather than clean database fields.

An LLM can classify them, but generating and parsing text for every ticket is unnecessary. Deterministic rules are cheaper, but become brittle as the wording changes.

Jev handles the fuzzy judgment and returns probabilities that application code can use.

The same framework explains where Jev does not fit.

If the task requires writing or multi-step reasoning, use an LLM. If arithmetic or an exact rule can determine the answer, keep it in code. If the possible answers cannot be defined in advance, Jev is the wrong interface.

The practical rule is simple.

Use Jev when code understands the possible values but not the meaning of the input.

text:
JEV DOESN'T REPLACE YOUR MODEL. IT REPLACES YOUR GATEKEEPER.

Every agent stack I've looked at this month has the same waste in it.

A $9 GPT call answering a question that's really just "A, B, or C."

That's not intelligence. That's a router pretending to be a decision maker.

Here's the actual doctrine for fixing it, not the marketing version.

RULE ONE: Cheap model decides, expensive model executes.

If the output is a choice, not a paragraph, it doesn't need your frontier model.
Write the option list yourself. Never let a model invent its own menu.
Keep your old call wired in as a fallback behind a flag you can flip in one line.

RULE TWO: One big question is a worse test than five small ones.

Every benchmark I've seen this year makes the same mistake. Ask a model one giant judgment call and grade it on that.
Split it into the sub questions a human actually checks first, run them in parallel, and weight the answers yourself in code.
The model gets smarter. Your code got smarter. Not the same thing, and only one of them is free to iterate on.

RULE THREE: Never let a model self report its own uncertainty.

"Do you have enough information" is a trap question. Every model says yes to it, almost every time, because it's answering about itself.
A confidence score is not the same as a self assessment. Route on the score. Ignore the self report entirely.

RULE FOUR: Ship it in shadow mode before it touches production.

Old system stays in charge. New model runs silently next to it for a week. You log both answers and only look at the rows where they disagreed.
That disagreement list is your real test set, and your existing traffic builds it for free, no labeling budget required.

None of this is Jev specific. It's the same architecture I'd want in front of any model that's 40x the cost.

The mistake isn't picking the wrong model.

It's asking a $9 model a $0.0004 question and calling that engineering.

You can't make those calls on every lead by hand, so most campaigns skip them and find out from the reply rate. Jev makes every one of them, on every lead and every message, before anything goes live, for cents.

So we built GTM Bot on it. It tiers the leads in your @heyreach_io lists, scores every message variant, locks the best one to each person, builds the campaigns in HeyReach, and self-improves based on your campaign performance.

Here's the full setup:

1. Two keys and one small file. A TypeSafe key for Jev, a HeyReach key from Settings, Integrations, API. Then a config that says what you sell: one sentence on the product, one on the problem, your target roles, the company type, who to skip. That's all it knows about you, so make it sharp.

4. Write 2 or 3 first messages, not one. It needs options to pick from.

5. Score the leads. Every lead gets asked: right role, senior enough, right company, how close is the signal to the problem you solve, and the disqualifiers (sells what you sell, open to work, on your exclude list). Tier A, B, C or Skip.

6. Score the messages. Every message gets asked: about them or about you, does it use the signal, does it pitch, does it ask for a meeting on first touch, stock phrasing, a merge tag still unfilled. Score and reply chance per variant.

7. Lock the best message to each lead. No more random split putting your best lead on your worst message. Every one of those is a Jev call, and that's where the 2.59 seconds go.

8. Push it into HeyReach. One list and one campaign per tier-and-variant pair. A and B get campaigns, C and Skip don't. Every lead lands with its verdict on it as custom fields, so you can see why it's there. Preview it first, then let it build.

9. The sequence is set for you. Blank connection request, then the message 3 hours after they accept. Blank requests get accepted 27% of the time, ones with a note 22%, and 3 hours is the rule from our 96,051-campaign report. People you're already connected to skip the request and get the message.

10. Launch. In HeyReach, or do what I do: open Claude with the HeyReach MCP and say "start the [GTM] campaigns".

11. Let the inbox teach it. At 30+ conversations it reads the ones you started, scores the lead and the first message behind each one, and learns which ones got a reply on YOUR account. It also prints what moves your replies, habit by habit: using the signal, asking for a meeting too early, going over 60 words.

12. Every Monday: learn from last week, score the new list, build, launch. Each week it knows a bit more about who answers you.

text:
Are humans trained with RLHF, DPO, RLVR, or something like Jev?
Watching the launch of Jev, I found myself asking a more interesting question:
How are humans trained to think?
RLHF: As children and professionals, we receive social feedback. People reward answers that are helpful, acceptable, or persuasive. But social approval does not necessarily mean objective truth.
DPO: We also learn from comparisons. "This response was better than that one." We gradually internalize preferences without needing someone to assign a precise numerical reward to every action.
RLVR: Some learning comes from consequences that can be objectively checked. The calculation balances, the code runs, the bridge holds, or it does not. Here, preference matters less than verifiable correctness.
Jev/RLCD: Much of everyday human behaviour does not involve writing an explanation or consciously reasoning through every possibility. We classify, score, route, and act rapidly: Is this situation dangerous? Is this person upset? Should I continue, stop, or ask for help? This resembles Jev’s positioning around fast, typed, probabilistic decisions more than open-ended language generation. Jev evaluates predefined outcomes and returns probabilities, although the company has not publicly disclosed the full architecture or detailed RLCD mechanism. 
But humans are not any one of these systems.
We combine:
social preference
comparative learning
verifiable outcomes
rapid probabilistic judgement
slower conscious reasoning
That leads to a potentially important architecture question:
Have we been asking one generative model to perform too many fundamentally different cognitive jobs?
An effective AI system should not use an expensive autoregressive LLM for every decision. A fast, calibrated decision model could handle routing, scoring, confidence and control flow, while a generative reasoning model handles ambiguity, explanation and novel problem-solving.
Jev’s real significance is larger than speed or cost.
It challenges the assumption that intelligence must always speak before it acts.
Humans usually do not generate an essay before deciding. We often make an uncertain decision first, consciously reason only when necessary, and seek external verification when the consequences demand it.
The future, therefore, is not Jev versus LLMs, or RLCD versus RLHF, DPO and RLVR.
Perhaps it is a cognitive architecture that knows:
when to decide, when to verify, when to reason, and when to ask a human.
