text:
Jev may be the missing decision layer in enterprise AI.

Not because it replaces LLMs.

And not because every enterprise workflow suddenly needs another AI model.

The interesting part is the gap it addresses.

Today, many AI systems jump too quickly from:

deterministic rules → large language model

But a lot of enterprise work sits somewhere in between.

Some decisions are too dynamic for fixed IF/ELSE logic, but too simple to justify calling a frontier LLM every time.

That is where a decision model like Jev becomes interesting.

A practical enterprise stack could look like this:

Python + Jev + Hermes + Skills

Each layer has a different responsibility.
Python handles deterministic controls.

Things that must remain explicit, predictable, and inspectable:
- approval thresholds
- compliance gates
- access rules
- hard business constraints
- mandatory workflow conditions


If a payment above a certain value requires human approval, that should remain deterministic.

Jev handles bounded decisions.

For example:
- route or escalate?
- retry or stop?
- which workflow path should run?
- which worker or model should handle the task?
- does this case require deeper reasoning?

The important part is that Jev is not deciding anything it wants.

It chooses among predefined alternatives.

Hermes handles orchestration.

It coordinates the workflow, keeps context, invokes the right capability, and moves the process forward.

Skills perform the actual enterprise work.

For example:
- CRM updates
- ERP transactions
- finance workflows
- procurement actions
- sales operations
- customer service processes
- document handling
- reporting
- approvals
- notifications
- cross-system coordination

And when the problem is genuinely ambiguous or requires deeper reasoning, Hermes can escalate to a larger LLM.

So the architecture becomes:

Blueprint / Workflow
↓
Hermes
↓
Python deterministic controls + Jev decision layer
↓
LLM reasoning when needed
↓
Enterprise Skills
↓
Execution

This is what I find compelling.
Not “AI replacing software.”

More like software becoming more selective about where intelligence is actually needed.

Python enforces what MUST happen.

Jev helps decide what SHOULD happen among bounded alternatives.

LLMs handle ambiguity and deeper reasoning.

Hermes orchestrates.

Skills perform the business work.

Of course, not every system needs all of this.

For a narrow workflow, Python may be enough.

For simple classification, conventional ML may already solve the problem.

Adding more AI layers without a real need only creates more complexity, more dependencies, and more operational risk.

But in large, evolving enterprise workflows, the space between rigid rules and “send everything to a frontier LLM” is real.

Jev may be one useful way to fill that space.

text:
What if your AI agent didn't need an LLM for every decision?

A new AI model called Jev was released last week by TypeSafe AI.

And I think the interesting part isn't the model itself.

It's what it suggests about how we should be building AI-powered systems.

Today, we use LLMs for almost everything.

We ask them to research companies, classify prospects, qualify leads, identify buying signals, write emails, decide what to do next, and trigger workflows.

But here's the question:
➡️ Do we really need a general-purpose LLM to make every small decision?

Consider a GTM workflow.

You've identified 10,000 companies.

For each company, you need to answer:

* Does this company fit our ICP?
* Is there evidence of a relevant buying signal?
* Which campaign should this prospect enter?
* Does this prospect need additional research?
* Should we send it to a human for review?

These are decisions.

They don't necessarily require an AI model to generate paragraphs of text.

And that's exactly the problem Jev is designed to address.

Instead of generating text, Jev takes information and predefined questions as input and returns structured decisions with probability estimates.

For example:

INPUT: A company's website, description, and recent news.

OUTPUT:

ICP fit: Yes

Relevant buying signal: No

Campaign: Nurture

Additional research required: Yes

Your application can then use those decisions to determine what happens next.

No generated explanation is required for every classification.

And according to TypeSafe, Jev can process these decisions in 70-500 milliseconds, at an input price of $0.042 per million tokens.

Those are the company's published figures, not independently verified performance guarantees.

But the architecture is what interests me.

I think the next generation of AI agents will increasingly separate reasoning, decision-making, and execution.

Of course, there are caveats.

Jev is new. Its real-world accuracy, reliability, and economics need to be tested against existing LLM-based approaches.

And a structured answer isn't necessarily a correct answer.

An AI model can confidently classify a prospect incorrectly, regardless of how fast or cheaply it produces that classification.

LLMs can also return structured outputs today. Jev's value will depend on whether its specialization delivers meaningful improvements in specific workloads.

But the broader principle is worth thinking about.

The goal isn't to maximize how much AI you use.

It's to build a GTM system that makes better decisions, at the right cost, and actually gets the work done.

#GTMEngineering #AI #AIAgents #RevOps #SalesAutomation

𝗪𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗝𝗲𝘃 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻-𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮.

First, in 𝗗𝗲𝗲𝗽𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗿, we used Jev to decide whether an Agentic Search workflow had gathered enough evidence to stop. Across 100 multi-hop questions, Jev matched DeepSeek V4 Flash at 93.25% Recall@5. Yet median decision latency fell from 2.23s to 0.55s, with estimated API cost at roughly one-seventh.

Second, in 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗦𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵, we tested coding-agent memory reranking on 2,172 private Chinese and English queries. Jev improved Recall@5 from 74.71% to 79.41%, but remained behind the specialist Voyage rerank-3 at 81.87%.

Third, in 𝗩𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗚𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗵 𝗥𝗔𝗚, Jev reranked and filtered candidate relationships for multi-hop retrieval. It outperformed GPT-4o-mini, but trailed GPT-5-mini—by just 1 point on HotpotQA and 4.13 points on the harder MuSiQue benchmark.

Jev is compelling for frequent, bounded judgments such as search stopping, filtering, routing, and simpler reranking.

But as tasks become more domain-specific or reasoning-heavy, stronger generative models and specialist rerankers still earn their place.

What is the Jev AI Model?

Let's learn together ↓

Jev is a “System One” model: built for quick, focused judgments.

Most generative LLMs produce text one token at a time. Useful for explanations and code. But that generation adds latency when all you need is a decision.

Jev gives up free-form text generation in exchange for fast, structured judgments.

How does it work?

① Provide context: a support ticket, document, or conversation.
② Define your questions and possible answers.
③ Jev evaluates those questions in parallel against the same context.
④ Your code uses the results to decide what happens next.

What does it output?

→ Choice: Which team should handle this? Billing, technical, or sales.
→ Score: How frustrated is the customer? Rate against a defined rubric.
→ Yes/no probability: Is the customer requesting a refund?

Instead of a paragraph, you get structured results with probabilities.

Where is this useful?

• Routing support tickets
• Classifying customer intent
• Scoring leads against a rubric
• Deciding which tool an AI agent should use
• Flagging uncertain cases for human review

The important distinction: structured doesn’t mean correct.

Jev can identify a refund request. Your code still needs to check whether the customer qualifies.

Use Jev for the judgment, code for the rules, and a generative LLM when you need to write the reply.

Grok Bot + TypeSafe’s Jev for GTM (what it is, and where it actually fits)

LinkedIn is loud about both right now. Here’s the simple version, plus where we’re putting them.

Most AI you already use writes sentences. Jev doesn’t. TypeSafe’s model takes some material (a reply, a company description, a job post) and typed questions you define. It returns decisions, labels, scores, and confidence that software can actually act on. In short, chat models generate text. Jev *judges* text.

On any qualification job I’ve run so far, it was also ~60x cheaper than gpt-4o and ran much faster. We do love speed, which (beyond saving money) is my favorite thing about Jev.

For us, all of the cold replies hit n8n from Smartlead and HeyReach. A first-pass model tags them, and the hot ones go to the client. Grok Bot runs a daily check on what got misfiled, then re-ships the normal Slack card. Jev is now doing the qualification across that board.

Where we also started using it through Grok Bot:

→ “Is this a SaaS?” from a company description, or any other yes/no / score-style qualification judged off whatever data we already have on the row
→ Keeping sub-agents from burning a week of tokens on judgment calls. Jev pricing = basically free, so I’d rather spend a few dollars there than have our GTMEs blow their weekly usage
→ Sweeping campaigns across clients to check whether each one still has at least 3,000 fresh contacts
→ Reading scraped job descriptions for keyword presence (the boring but useful “does this JD actually say the thing we care about”)

Thus far, Jev hasn’t been a game-changer for us in terms of workflows. It has made the cost of what we generally toss tokens at significantly less meaningful, and we can often justify speed more easily.

It fits well for most things where the output is not a bunch of text, but (for now) it mostly just replaces the model you’re already uses in some cases so you can save some $, generally get better outputs, and do it faster.

I’ve also read it’s better for English inputs (I think TypeSafe said this, but we’ve been running it across multiple languages in Europe and there hasn’t been a drop.

text:
TypeSafe launched a model called Jev last week and it could change how we use AI for GTM.

The reason there’s a lot of hype around Jev is that it’s a ‘System 1’ model which is a frame from the (great) book Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman.

For us normal people, it just means it runs purely on deterministic decisions rather than on reasoning, like the frontier LLMs do.

This is interesting because their reasoning is often overly complex and useful for solving mathematical problems, but not for making quick decisions affordably.

Here’s how I would suggest thinking about splitting work between decision models like Jev and reasoning models like Claude, GPT or Gemini.

System 1 use cases: decision models like Jev

1️⃣ Account prioritization
↳ Put every account's data on one record: deals, product use, and news
↳ Decide which accounts to call first, and what to do next

2️⃣ Lead scoring and ideal customer fit
↳ Let simple rules answer the easy facts: is there already a deal, did they start a trial
↳ Send Jev only the harder calls, like how good a fit someone is

3️⃣ Sorting replies
↳ Give Jev the reply and its date, so it knows what's fresh
↳ Decide which replies need a person right now, and which can wait

System 2 use cases: reasoning models like Claude, GPT and Gemini

1️⃣ Account research
↳ The model reads the website, customers, case studies, recent news, and job posts
↳ Every company is different, so it has to find and piece the answer together

2️⃣ Copywriting
↳ The model writes the email around one real signal, like a hire or funding round
↳ It judges which signal matters, then says it plainly in the buyer's words

3️⃣ Meeting briefs
↳ The model reads the CRM history, call recordings, and fresh research, then writes a prep card
↳ It decides what to ask, in what order, and which objections to expect

author_headline: Co-founder & CEO @ HeyReach | Helping teams turn LinkedIn into their best outbound channel | $18M+ ARR with 7,500+ customers (bootstrapped)
text:
Your best LinkedIn lead can still get your worst message.

You qualify the list, write a few variants, then let the campaign assign them at random.

We built a bot on Jev + @heyreach_io that checks each lead and message, then picks the best-scoring match before you launch.

Here's how to set it up:

1. Tell it who you're selling to.

Connect your TypeSafe and HeyReach API keys, then fill in what you sell, the problem it solves, target roles, company size and who to exclude. Be specific. These are the instructions it uses to judge every lead.

2. Give each lead a reason to hear from you.

Import your Sales Navigator or Clay leads into HeyReach, or give the bot a CSV. Add what the person actually did and when: wrote about a problem, changed roles, asked about a competitor.

Jev checks their fit and how relevant that signal is to your offer. Review the tiers it assigns. Someone working at the right company can still be the wrong person.

3. Give it a few messages to choose from.

Write 2 or 3 first messages. Try a question about their situation or an offer to send something useful. Jev evaluates the drafts you give it.

It flags stock openers, premature meeting asks, product pitches and personalization that only swaps a name. Fix those and score the messages again.

For me, the first message has one job: get them to write back.

4. Match the message to the person.

The bot picks the variant with the highest estimated reply chance for each lead. Preview the setup before creating campaigns. Check who made the cut, why they're there and exactly what they'll receive.

By default, it builds campaigns for the A and B tiers, grouped by the message selected.

5. Check the sequence, then launch.

For new connections, the draft uses a blank request, then the chosen message with a three-hour delay after acceptance. Leads pulled from your first-degree network get a message-only sequence. Match those campaigns to the sender already connected to those leads.

The campaigns arrive as drafts in HeyReach. Check the messages, merge fields and senders, add a useful follow-up if needed, then hit Start.

6. Use the replies for the next round.

Once you have enough reply history, the bot can learn from who answered and which first message they received. Run that again each week before scoring your next list.

Keep tracking positive replies and meetings separately. Someone writing back doesn't automatically mean you've found a buyer.

A new AI model called Jev just scored 68% on its own maker's benchmark. The best frontier model scored 74%.

And it is still the most important AI launch this month.

Because Jev is not trying to be the smartest model in the room. It is the fastest and cheapest classifier you can already put into your production workflows.

Here is the number that made me pay attention. Where a traditional LLM takes real time and real money to process every single email, Jev classified 1,700 emails for 18 cents. 25 times faster. 580 times cheaper.

But cheap and fast does not mean you swap it in everywhere.

Jev is not for coding or writing. In fact it does not write a single word. It only decides. It picks from the options you hand it, and it gives you a confidence score with the answer.

That is the whole product, and it is why the benchmark number is the wrong way to judge it. You are not asking it to reason. You are asking it to sort, at a price where sorting stops being a line item.

So this model does not replace your LLM. It sits underneath it.

If you have a categorization use case in your application, something like:

1. Email triage
2. Lead scoring
3. Routing between multiple agents

and you have been trying to optimize for cost and latency, then Jev is for you.

Everywhere else, keep the model that can actually think.

Where in your stack are you currently paying frontier model prices for what is really just a sorting decision?

#AIEngineering #LLM #MachineLearning #AIAgents #BuildInPublic

Jev is 13.6x faster and 2.7x cheaper than GPT Luna 6 for Tessl verifiers.

We ran our full verifier test suite through both models: six projects and approximately 2,725 verifier-file pairs, with every judgment generated fresh.

Tessl verifiers let you check rules that require judgment, not just syntax. For example: does an error message give the user a concrete next step? Does a change follow the architecture in your design document?

text:
There’s a lot of excitement about JEV at the moment.

Our R&D team had a play. Here’s what we think it means for AI-native GTM 👇

Most AI workflows today look something like:

Context → LLM → Answer → Action

JEV points to something different.

Imagine you have 100,000 accounts in your market. Your GTM operation is constantly making small decisions:

→ Is this actually ICP?
→ Is there a buying window?
→ Does this signal matter?
→ Should we engage now?
→ What should happen next?

Today, we increasingly throw these questions at LLMs.

But many aren’t language problems.
They’re decision problems.

JEV takes State and a defined set of outcomes and returns decisions with probabilities.

State → Decision → Probability.

That matters because if models become incredibly cheap and fast at making millions of these decisions, the bottleneck moves.

The harder problem becomes maintaining the context they decide against:

What is true right now?
What changed?
What does our company know?
What action should follow?
When should a human intervene?
What did we learn from the outcome?

This is why we’ve become obsessed with State at Revenue Labs.

CRM history. Calls. Emails. People. Engagement. External signals. Product behaviour. Company knowledge.

Continuously assembled into a representation of commercial reality.

The architecture becomes less:

Data → Prompt → LLM → Output

And more:

Evidence → State → Decision → Action → Outcome → Learning

Different intelligence can sit inside that loop.

Frontier models for complex reasoning. Specialist models like JEV for high-volume decisions. Deterministic systems where appropriate. Humans where consequence or uncertainty requires judgement.

The model becomes a component of the operation, rather than the operation itself.

That’s the shift from AI-assisted to AI-native GTM.

JEV is early. But what it represents is more interesting than any individual model.

LLMs gave software the ability to generate.

Now we’re giving software the ability to continuously decide.

The missing layer is the system those decisions operate against.

That’s what we’re building at Revenue Labs.

text:
𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 $𝟮𝟵𝟵 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮 "𝗝𝗘𝗩 𝗠𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘆" 𝗰𝗼𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁 — 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗵𝗼𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲. 🙃
No email gate, no "comment JEV and I'll DM you". It's attached. 👇

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺
A grounded assistant that cites its sources can still invent a policy clause that never existed. Retrieval reduces that, it does not remove it. The only way to know is to compare the draft against the passages retrieved for that turn — before the user sees it.
That is a classification problem, not a generation problem. Which is what JEV is for.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗮𝗰𝗵
A policy-grounded support assistant on LangGraph, with a typed decision model as a guardrail lane on both sides of the LLM.
Inbound, before retrieval: in scope, jailbreak attempt, personal data, would answering need another tenant's data.

Outbound, before release: is every claim supported by the retrieved passages, does every citation exist, does the draft promise a refund or an exception, does it repeat an identifier.
Pass releases. Soft fail regenerates once. Hard fail goes to a human.

𝗧𝗲𝗿𝗺𝘀 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗵 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗴
𝗧𝘆𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 — the answer type is declared before the call, so a verdict cannot return malformed. No parsing step, no broken JSON.
𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗯𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 — 0.8 means roughly eight in ten. That is what makes a threshold a decision rather than a superstition.
𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 — whether a claim is supported by the text retrieved for that turn, not the corpus in general.

And the one people misread: 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘂𝗰𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗲 means the output always matches the declared type. It can still be wrong. It will just be wrong as a perfectly formed boolean.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴

In an independent test the same model scored 62.6% asked as one composite judgement, and 95.0% split into five typed questions. Same model, same data. The question is the hyperparameter.

𝗜𝗻𝘀𝗶𝗱𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗰𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
The graph and its state. The contract between application and verifier. Both payloads, question by question. How to derive thresholds instead of asserting them. Degradation paths for every dependency. The latency budget — 230 ms inside a 2,200 ms target. The cost model at 50,000 turns a month: model calls $135, human review $1,650. A phased rollout from shadow to enforcement. And the boundary — no model decides an irreversible action, at any confidence.

Almost no code, deliberately. It ships prompts instead, so the implementation lands in your stack rather than mine.

𝗧𝘄𝗼 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 if you run a grounded assistant:
What share of your answers contain a claim your retrieval never supported?

And if your verifier is the same model that wrote the draft, what is it actually checking?

text:
I came across something called Laya, and compared to Jev, two things stand out: it's faster, and it's open source.

Most AI pipelines default to throwing an LLM at everything, even when the task isn't "write something" - it's "pick one of a few known outcomes."

Routing a ticket. Scoring urgency. Flagging churn risk. These aren't writing tasks. They're decisions.

For example:
"Hi, we were billed twice for March. Please refund the duplicate today or we will cancel our plan."

Instead of:
LLM → Generate text → Parse output → Take a decision

Laya runs it through a single forward pass and returns:
Department → billing (94%)
Urgency → 1.84 / 2.0
Churn risk → 89%
Refund requested → yes

No generation. No parsing. Just a typed answer: choice, score, or probability.

Why it's interesting:
1. Speed - 33ms for one question, ~7ms/question batched. Jev is published at 236-276ms p50. That's 6-7x faster on single questions.
2. Open source - Apache 2.0, self-hosted, $0 per token. Jev is a closed API at $0.042/1M tokens.
3. Multilingual - a built-in Router auto-detects language and dispatches to the right checkpoint across 100+ languages.
4. Calibrated - trained with RLCD against proper scoring rules, so confidence scores actually mean something.

To be fair, Jev still leads when you have 50+ label options in a single question, and its soft probability distributions match a teacher model more closely. But for most decision-layer use cases - routing, triage, urgency scoring, guardrails - Laya is faster, cheaper, and yours to run:

Laya decides → Agent acts → Tools execute

Repo: https://lnkd.in/gKMeCGD6

Jev is 13.6x faster and 2.7x cheaper than GPT Luna 6 for Tessl verifiers.

We ran our full verifier test suite through both models: six projects and approximately 2,725 verifier-file pairs, with every judgment generated fresh.

The results:

• @typesafeai's Jev completed the suite in 32 seconds, compared with 436.5 seconds for GPT Luna 6

• Jev cost $0.24 per 1,000 targets, compared with an illustrative $0.64 for GPT Luna 6

• The two models agreed on 85.9% of verifier decisions

Jev tended to be more lenient on rules about comment structure and content. On warn-level code rules, the models were much closer. That’s why we recommend testing judges against examples from your own codebase, rather than choosing on speed or aggregate agreement alone.

Tessl verifiers let you check rules that require judgment, not just syntax. For example: does an error message give the user a concrete next step? Does a change follow the architecture in your design document?

Jev and GPT Luna 6 are both available in the Tessl CLI. You can compare them on your own rules today.

step 1 → split the responsibilities: the LLM generates, Jev makes bounded semantic decisions and deterministic code keeps authority

step 2 → build the state: give Jev the current request, relevant evidence, policy and proposed action instead of sending the entire conversation

step 9 → batch independent decisions: ask multiple Choice, Score and Noul questions over one shared state instead of creating another LLM call for every judgment

step 10 → record the complete decision receipt: state version, question, probabilities, selected route, model, latency, outcome and human override

Jev vs. LLM as Judge, clearly explained.

Imagine a support agent says, “Done. I issued your refund.”

The trace shows that the agent looked up the order, but never completed the refund. An evaluator now needs to decide whether the answer is grounded, honest, and useful.

Both an LLM judge and Jev can make those judgments. The difference is how they produce them.

→ Both need the same evidence

The customer request, policy, tool results, and agent answer must be included. A judge cannot evaluate evidence it has not seen.

→ An LLM judge generates an evaluation

You describe the rubric in a prompt and specify the desired output. The model then generates a verdict, score, structured JSON, or written explanation one token at a time.

This works well when the evaluation needs detailed reasoning, an explanation, or an answer outside a predefined set.

→ Jev returns structured decisions

You provide the evidence once, then define separate questions with predefined answer formats.

For a yes-or-no criterion, Jev returns the probability that the statement is true. For an ordered criterion, it returns a rating and a separate confidence value.

The Jev calls these formats Noul and Score, but the core idea is simple. The possible answers are defined before the evaluation runs.

Jev evaluates independent questions against the shared evidence in parallel. Your code receives values it can immediately use for thresholds, routing, or review.

→ The workload determines the better interface

Use an LLM judge when you need open-ended reasoning or a written rationale.

Use Jev when you repeatedly need focused judgments such as whether an answer is grounded, whether an action claim is honest, or how actionable the response is.

Multiple LLM judge calls can also run concurrently. The important distinction is not concurrency between calls. It is token-by-token generation versus parallel structured judgments within one request.

That distinction matters at scale. When every agent run needs several checks, a faster and cheaper evaluator can help you inspect more traces, measure more dimensions, and catch failures earlier.

Jev does not replace every LLM judge. It gives bounded evaluation workloads a more direct interface.

The agent generates the answer. The judge should only generate when the judgment requires it.

I also published the complete evaluation workflow using Jev and Comet’s open-source Opik platform. The repository includes frozen agent traces, structured rubrics, result mapping, and the experiment runner.

What is JEV?
JEV vs LLMs, and why does it matter?

In short JEV is a model built for decision-making. JEV still fundamentally an LLM, just cleverly used as a one-shot classifier. It extracts output probabilities (in a single forward pass rather than generating tokens sequentially). 

It's crazy cheap and really intelligent (Benchmarks place it near GPT Terra)

Today we use an LLM for almost everything:
Read → reason → generate → parse → validate → execute 

But a lot of what happens inside an AI agent isn’t actually text generation.
It’s decision-making:
- Which tool should I call?
- Should I retry?
- Which workflow should I use?
- Is this request relevant?
- Which branch should the agent take?
- Am I done?

text:
Stop generating text when all you need is a decision!

Jev is TypeSafe AI’s first “System One” model, built for a part of AI systems that we currently keep forcing generative LLMs to handle: making bounded decisions inside software.

Think about what happens during an agent run. The main model may be writing code, researching, planning, or reasoning through a problem, but the system around it is constantly making smaller decisions. Which model should handle the next step? Does this tool call need approval? Is the agent still making progress? Is the task actually complete?

Today, we often send those questions back to another generative LLM.

Even with structured outputs, the model is still generating tokens sequentially and constraining them into the schema we asked for. The application then takes that generated output and turns it back into the decision it needed in the first place.

Jev removes string generation from that loop.

You give it the current state and define the decisions you care about. Those can be a yes/no judgment, a choice between predefined options, or a score across an ordered scale. Jev returns typed answers with probabilities that the application can use directly.

That distinction becomes useful when these decisions sit everywhere inside an agent harness.

A coding agent can use the main LLM to understand a repository and write a fix, while Jev handles model routing, tool gating, risk checks, progress evaluation, or deciding whether another iteration is actually necessary.

And Jev should not become the permission system either. A probability that an action is safe is still a model judgment. Permissions, spend limits, allowlists, and other hard constraints should remain deterministic.

The architecture I find more interesting is the separation itself: generative models do the open-ended work, decision models handle fuzzy but bounded judgments around that work, and the runtime decides what is actually allowed to happen.

As agents become longer-running, the number of these small decisions only increases.

Using a full generative model for every one of them may turn out to be a very expensive abstraction.

84%: verify the result. Low-confidence or failed outputs loop back through fallback instead of silently continuing.

Here's the breakdown for non-tech people.

Let's start with this: most work inside a company isn't writing, it's deciding.

Is this lead a fit? 
Is this invoice fraud? 
Does this contract need legal review? 
Is this support ticket urgent? 
Which supplier do we flag?
Do I need to add more examples so my post performs better? 

And every decision kinda looks the same: 
information in → choice out

For decades, software did this with if-statements.
↳ If employees > 200 and industry = SaaS → good lead

That's fast and cheap but brittle (it only works when you have clear inputs you can map to clearly defined rules, which in reality is rarely the case).

Then came machine learning
↳ tldr: flexible, but you needed data and a data scientist for every single decision.

So LLMs (AI) came along: flexible, no training needed.

But LLMs are built to write, not decide.

They're slow (seconds per answer), expensive at scale, they can hallucinate, and when they say "90% sure" that number doesn't really mean anything.

Jev is a new kind of AI, built to fix exactly that for decisions.

The core of how it works: 
information in → a choice out (from options you define) → plus how confident it is.

(And that confidence is calibrated, not just a random number)

70–500ms per decision, at a fraction of LLM cost

It's basically a smart if-statement.

What it can't do though: write. 

It only picks from the options you give it.

So it doesn't replace LLMs, it sits next to them. 

Jev handles the thousands of small decisions, the LLM handles the few things that actually need writing or deep thinking (especially when options aren't predefined) 

Take a support team getting 10,000 tickets a day;
Is it urgent? 
Which team? 
Is this customer about to churn? 

That's three decisions per ticket, on every ticket, in under a second. 

Only the ones that need a real answer go to the LLM (or a human).

TL;DR
LLMs write, Jev decides.

TypeSafe founder Diogo Almeida introduced Jev, and the field I would inspect first in any agent built around it is not model. It is state

An agent can have room for a long conversation and still miss the one line that matters. 

A refund request needs the current order, the charge record and the policy that applies today. It does not need twelve earlier attempts to sound helpful

Here is the state packet I would put in front of Jev:

step 1 → name the decision the code needs to make now, not the entire job the agent was given

step 2 → pull facts from the system of record: order status, amounts, timestamps and permissions

step 3 → include the customer's actual words as evidence, without asking Jev to reconstruct the whole conversation

step 4 → state the constraints that can change the route, such as a refund window or an account hold

step 5 → build the available actions from live code, so a closed account never appears as a valid destination

step 6 → put the question in the question field. State is evidence, not a second prompt hiding instructions

step 7 → leave the sums and date arithmetic to code, then send Jev the result it needs to judge

step 8 → keep the exact packet with the answer, because you cannot debug a decision from its label alone

The point is not to compress everything until it looks clever. The point is to make it obvious which piece of evidence could change the answer

text:
I have spent the last several days digging into Jev, where it actually came from, what TypeSafe AI may have done differently, and what has happened since the open community started pulling the idea apart.

The deeper I went, the less this looked like a simple “Jev vs. LLM” story. BERT, zero-shot classification, rerankers, calibration research and newer systems like GLiClass all form part of the technical lineage. At the same time, the open implementations appearing now show that developers are already exploring several very different ways to build fast, bounded decision models.

The question I came away with is much bigger: have we been using large generative models for decisions that never required generation in the first place?

text:
Here's everything you need to know about Jev (no, really)

WHAT IT IS
──────────

Jev is a neural network built to make decisions. It does not generate text. Think of it as a smart if statement.

It comes from TypeSafe, the company Diogo Almeida started after leaving OpenAI in 2024. They call it a system one model.

System one is fast, automatic, intuitive. System two is slow and deliberate. Claude and GPT are system two: great at reasoning, and they generate text. Jev is system one: fast, structured decisions for your code.

You hand it a schema and you always get back a value that fits the schema. That's what TypeSafe means when they say it doesn't hallucinate. It can't return an invalid value.

It was trained with reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions (RLCD). Diogo's thesis is that RLHF and verifiable rewards push LLMs toward answers that please people, which is not the same as making good business decisions. Jev is the first model built on that idea.

THE THREE PRIMITIVES
────────────────────

Jev can answer exactly three kinds of question:

1/ Noul. True or false. "Is this spam?"

2/ Choice. Pick one from a set. "Billing, tech support, security or sales?"

3/ Score. A point on an ordered scale. "Low, medium, high or critical?"

That's the whole API surface. You pass a state (your data) and a dict of questions to client.system_one, and read the answers back.

WHY IT FEELS FAMILIAR
─────────────────────

For people who are familiar with classic ML, this type of model does not seem like anything "new" (in fact, it is. I'll explain why below)

I wrote The Applied Data Science Workshop back in 2017, and my first reaction was that "it's just a classifier". Naive Bayes was doing spam filtering a long time ago. Decision trees, SVMs and XGBoost could do everything in this demo. But there's a catch...

The difference is they'd each need a training set and a model per question. Jev works zero-shot, out of the box.

(side note: reportedly it was trained entirely on synthetic data)

PITFALLS OF JEV
───────────────

1/ We don't yet know how far to trust its probabilities

2/ It has no web search, so niche or brand-new topics are a blind spot. TypeSafe has ways to fine-tune it for your task, and that's a future video.

I'm building a short Jev course in my Skool next: the basics, then a Jev extension for the Pi agent harness, then real-world use cases that aren't just hype. Members get an early access discount (I'll email you once it's ready)

text:
NVIDIA and Stanford just challenged Jev.

(their new System 1 architecture runs up to 9x faster.)

It is called a Contrastive Language Model, or CLM.

Like Jev, CLM is not designed to generate text. It handles the small, repeated decisions inside AI systems, such as choosing a tool, ranking a patch, routing a request, or selecting the next action.

But CLM reaches those decisions differently.

Instead of generating an answer token by token, it treats decision-making as a retrieval problem.

Here is how it works.

1) Encode the state

CLM takes the current situation, such as an agent’s context or the state of a game, and converts it into a vector.

It uses a frozen Qwen3-8B model with a small trainable state projection head.

2) Encode every possible action

A separate action head converts each candidate into the same vector space.

In the Mario example, the candidates are left, jump, and right run. CLM does not invent a fourth option. It only evaluates the actions supplied by the application.

3) Learn which states and actions belong together

During training, the correct state-action pair is pulled closer while incorrect pairs are pushed apart.

A batch of B examples produces a B × B similarity matrix. The matching pairs sit on the diagonal. Every other pairing becomes a negative example.

This contrastive training uses InfoNCE, the same general mechanism behind systems such as CLIP and dense retrieval.

4) Turn similarity into a decision

At inference, CLM measures the cosine similarity between the state and every candidate action.

A softmax converts those scores into a probability distribution. The application can choose the winner, apply a confidence threshold, or escalate an uncertain result.

The real speed advantage comes from separating states and actions.

Actions can be embedded once and cached. If an agent repeatedly chooses between the same tools, CLM only needs to encode the changing state and compare it with stored action vectors.

That replaces repeated generation with one embedding pass and a set of cheap dot products.

The researchers report that CLM-8B matches Jev across computer-use, gaming, and tool-calling evaluations while reaching up to 9x lower latency. The improvement is largest when actions repeat or the candidate set grows.

CLM still has limits. It cannot generate new actions, its probabilities are relative to the supplied candidates, and its strongest verifier results require task-specific fine-tuning.

But its central idea is powerful.

The entire research is open-source, including the code.

Read more here: https://t.co/I9kPwMPI7B

text:
Turn any open LLM into a Jev-style model:

Researchers just open-sourced AnyJev, a Python library that extracts typed choices, yes/no judgments, scores, and probabilities from causal LLMs.

Beyond its raw baseline, AnyJev offers three levels depending on how much labeled data and calibration you need:

- L0 requires no labels. It rotates the answer options to reduce position bias, but its probabilities remain uncalibrated.

- L1 uses 100-500 labeled examples per question to calibrate those probabilities through temperature scaling. It improves confidence estimates without changing the answer ranking.

- L2 uses 100-300 labels to fit a closed-form head on an intermediate hidden state. It leaves model weights untouched and can stop inference before the full forward pass completes.

The main constraint is model access. AnyJev requires access to logits or hidden states, so it is built for open models. L2 heads are also specific to a model and question.

It is compatible with several open causal LLMs.

text:
The classical AI winter is here..

Everybody is running around with Jev or RLCD like it is the new kid on the block. Fast decisions, probabilities, confidence, structured outputs. No giant stream of generated tokens. Ooooh, ahhhh! Lol.. 

RLCD stands for Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions. But strip away the marketing and it is the familiar machine learning and statistics.. train a model so its predicted probabilities are calibrated against observed outcomes. But probability calibration is not a new concept. Neither are classifiers, scorers, discriminative models, confidence estimation, structured prediction or decision functions.

Yet somehow AI changed generations and forgot its own field. 

Of course a system designed to make bounded decisions can outperform an LLM at bounded decision making. LLMs were never designed to be stable autonomous decision engines in the first place. Go back to Attention Is All You Need. It was not a paper about AGI, autonomous intelligence or a universal cognitive architecture. The Transformer was introduced as a sequence transduction architecture and demonstrated on machine translation. Then we became hypnotized by fluency at scale.. Hyperscale it enough, feed it enough human output, and the statistical continuation over bullshit became so convincing that an entire industry started confusing linguistic competence with intelligence.. Then we wrapped it in tools, memory, RAG, planning loops and agent harnesses and tried to turn a probabilistic sequence generator into an autonomous cognitive system.

And the industry response to Jev is hilarious. We are rediscovering classification, scoring, regression, state estimation, structured prediction and bounded probabilistic decision making all over again when we already had all of this for decades if not a century(!!).

Jev may be useful engineering. Yet everybody is acting shocked that direct decision computation can be faster and more stable than asking a giant autoregressive LLM to generate tokens about the decision first.

It feels like the AI industry is suffering from dementia.. It went through machine learning, neural networks, reinforcement learning, probabilistic models, expert systems, cognitive architectures, search and planning.. Transformers came around, scale exploded, and somehow everybody forgot where we had already been.. Now we are walking around the same tracks in circle and calling it major progress. 

The deeper problem is simple. 

Hyperscaling did not breach the intelligence wall. It gave us extraordinary generative NLP, structured coding and generally better learned distributions through curated human labeled datasets.. But scaling the NLP did not magically turn it into a fundamentally different form of intelligence or superduper AGI.. Stable autonomy under uncertainty is still out of reach for GenAI.

So now the industry is moving backward while calling it 'forward' or Jev.. and that, my bros, is your standard classical AI winter.

Jev is an interesting bet on what we actually need AI models to do at work.

A huge amount of work involves reading something and deciding what happens next. An email needs a destination. A support ticket needs a priority. A lead needs to be qualified before it reaches sales.

These are small decisions, but they determine whether an automation can move forward or has to wait for a person.

That’s where Jev fits. It makes structured decisions and returns a confidence score for each one. With Zapier, those decisions can trigger the next action across your apps.

I’ve been using Zapier to build workflows for my AI-native team, where many of us come from non-developer backgrounds. Inbox triage is one example: Jev decides how to categorize an email and whether it’s urgent, then Zapier routes it to the right person or triggers an alert. Decisions below a confidence threshold can go to a human for review.

I think we’ll see more specialized models built around jobs like this. 

There’s a lot of room for AI that does a narrow task well enough to become a dependable step in a larger workflow.

I have added a guidebook for you to checkout below 👇 

#ZapierPartner

Introducing typesafe/jev-router: a cache-aware model router powered by Jev and TypeSafe AI

The Jev Router picks the best model and reasoning effort for each request, balancing quality, speed, and cost.

On four agent benchmarks, Jev Router solved 82% more tasks than our Auto Router (237 vs 130 of 423). On five agent benchmarks, Jev Router had a faster median time to first token than every other router we tested.

Most routers pick a model based on each message. Each switch loses the cached chat, so you pay full price for the new model to reread the whole conversation. Most routers also route on the task type, not the difficulty. Easy and hard coding tasks get the same model.

Jev Router runs on Jev, TypeSafe's first Decision / System One model. Before each turn, Jev reads your prompt and scores it on difficulty and precision. It also checks whether a bigger model or more effort would help, whether a cheaper model is enough, and whether the task changed.

Jev Router keeps a model that works for the rest of the session. It can raise or lower effort without switching models. It switches only when the expected gain is larger than the cost, including the cached chat it would lose.

Jev reads the conversation text only to pick the model and effort. It runs under zero data retention (ZDR) terms, so nothing is stored or trained on. Attachments are never sent to Jev, and requests with "zdr: true" work with Jev Router.

If the Jev call times out or returns invalid output, the request fails instead of falling back to another router. Each response includes routing metadata with the reason for the choice.

You can see Jev Router decide in OpenRouter Chat. The routing insights panel shows the model it picked for each turn and the scores behind it, like task, difficulty, precision, and larger model benefit.

Try it now using "typesafe/jev-router" in your app, or in OpenRouter Chat.

author_headline: Catching the AI signal
text:
MOST PEOPLE WIRING JEV INTO THEIR AGENTS ARE SENDING IT THE WRONG TASKS

Jev doesn't write. It picks. A probability for every option you give it, in ~200ms, and output is free.

So before a task goes anywhere, it goes through one sort:

CODE → Anything with exactly one right answer:
→ totals, taxes, discounts
→ date math and deadlines
→ regex, IDs, format checks
→ permissions and hard rules
→ counting rows

JEV → A judgment between answers you already know:
→ is this ticket urgent (yes / no)
→ which tool does this step need
→ refund, replace or escalate
→ does this diff actually match the task
→ is this lead worth a reply (0 to 10)

LLM → Anything that needs new words:
→ the reply the customer reads
→ summaries and reports
→ writing the code itself
→ planning a task nobody scoped yet
→ explaining why something broke

Then there's a gate inside the Jev lane:
→ read-only actions run at 0.5 confidence
→ anything you can't undo waits for 0.9
→ everything below bounces to Opus or a human

Three questions before you send anything to Jev:
1. Can code answer it exactly? Then it's code.
2. Can you list every possible answer upfront? Then it's Jev.
3. Does the answer need sentences? Then it's an LLM.

Most of what an agent does all day is lane two. Small decisions, over and over, each one paid at frontier prices.

The rule in one line:

Code computes. Jev decides. The LLM writes.

text:
Jev founder Diogo Almeida introduced Jev, and its docs describe a small architecture change that matters more than another model benchmark:

- send one state, ask several independent questions and let code decide which answers it needs

Most agents do the opposite. They ask whether a ticket is urgent, wait, send the same ticket again to choose a team, wait, then send it a third time to check whether it needs approval

The repeated state is doing nothing except adding time and cost

Here is the batch I would build:

step 1 → assemble one frozen view of the ticket, account and current policy

step 2 → ask Choice for the destination team from a list built from live routes

step 3 → ask Score for urgency against levels you defined before the request

step 4 → ask Noul whether the message explicitly requests a refund

step 5 → include a question the code may not use, such as bug severity; discard that answer if the ticket is not a bug

step 6 → send those independent questions together, because each reads the same state

step 7 → make a second request only when an earlier answer changes the evidence or the options for the next one

step 8 → compose the answers in code and measure the batch against the serial version on your own traffic

This is not a trick for getting Jev to reason through a chain in parallel. It cannot see one answer while producing another in the same request

That limitation is useful: it forces the dependencies into the program where you can inspect them

The document below draws the two request shapes. 

The article shows how to turn the cheaper shape into a workflow that is still understandable when something goes wrong

Most of what we call "agentic AI" is a string of tiny decisions. Which tool gets called. Which document matters. Which request gets routed where. Whether a message trips a guardrail.

And we keep handing those decisions to giant models that write a paragraph of reasoning before picking option B.

That's slow, it's expensive, and at high volume it adds up fast. I've built enough integrations to know the bottleneck usually isn't intelligence. It's latency and cost on the hundreds of small calls nobody budgets for.

So I've been looking at Drex, a new small model from https://t.co/OoD4pVoE5f built for exactly this job. It doesn't generate text. It looks at the options you give it and returns calibrated probabilities over them in a single pass. No long reasoning trace, no token bill for thinking out loud.

The numbers they're reporting: #1 on the Decision Index 0.1, beating Jev 1.13.0. 136ms response time. Up to 32K context. Up to 1.5x faster than Jev.

Under the hood it's a diffusion architecture trained with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback loops, which is a very different bet than scaling up another chat model.

Where I'd actually use it: agent routing and tool selection, reranking search results, document classification, compliance and policy checks, security guardrails, and risk flags. Basically any step in a pipeline where you need a fast, confident pick instead of an essay.

The fun part is they dropped it into Chess, DOOM, StarCraft, and Lemmings to show it making calls in real time. Worth a look if you want to see what 136ms decisions feel like.

They're giving 250M free tokens to the first 10,000 builders. If you run agents or routing layers, test it on your own workload and see where it beats what you've got.

TypeSafe AI launched Jev with claims that were hard to ignore: 193.6× faster, 444.6× cheaper, and an AI model that “can’t hallucinate.”

Our team went back through the launch material, the benchmark conditions, OpenRouter’s Banking77 test, LangChain’s early agent experiments, and TypeSafe’s own integration guidance.

Once the headlines are narrowed to what the evidence actually supports, Jev becomes more interesting, not less.

A few things stood out:
▪️Typed output is not truth. Jev can guarantee the shape of an answer and still choose the wrong valid answer.
▪️The speed advantage appears real on bounded tasks, but the evidence is narrower than the headline. On Banking77, Jev was substantially faster and cheaper than Opus 5, but also less accurate. And Banking77 is classification, not coding.
▪️Confidence is useful, but it is not authority. A high-confidence wrong answer can be more dangerous than an uncertain one because the system has less reason to escalate it.
▪️Jev’s relevance to coding may sit around the agent rather than inside code generation itself. LangChain has already experimented with it for model routing, pre-execution tool-risk gating, and repeated agent evaluation.
▪️And then there is the question I found harder to dismiss: what if the state being judged is already wrong?

A README can be stale. A trace can belong to another run. Documentation and runtime behavior can disagree.

In that situation, a model may judge what it sees perfectly reasonably and still reach the wrong operational conclusion because something upstream handed it the wrong version of reality.

That is also the boundary our team wants to test.

We are preparing a small shadow-mode experiment at Flamehaven where Jev handles narrow semantic judgments: whether evidence supports a claim, whether runtime observations contradict documentation, which cases deserve deeper review, and when ambiguity should be escalated.

It will not modify files or approve consequential actions. Missing evidence gets an explicit insufficient-evidence path rather than being forced into a yes/no judgment. Ambiguous cases move to a stronger reasoning model or a human.

We do not yet know whether this will work well enough to keep.

That is the point of the experiment.

The new newsletter looks at the launch claims, the benchmark caveats, the early agent evidence, and the deeper problem underneath all of them:

Is Jev a New Generation of Code AI? What Survives the Debunking
If you are building agent workflows, I’m curious where you draw the boundary.

What would you let a fast decision model judge, and what would you never let it decide?

text:
The Missing Layer: Jev, System 1 Thinking, and What It Means for Enterprise Architecture
 
 Kahneman's Thinking, Fast and Slow splits thinking in two. System 1 is fast, automatic, near-free - you see a face and know instantly it's angry. System 2 is slow and deliberate - multiplying 19 by 26, reasoning through a trade-off. His point wasn't that one is better. It's that using the wrong one costs you either way.

We spent a decade on BI answering "what happened." We're now building a Decision Intelligence layer on top of it - health scores, risk flags, intake classification, routing. Honestly, it's still in flight. Parts of it work, parts of it are scaffolding, and we're learning what the layer even wants to be as we build it. But one thing is already clear: almost every decision in it runs on a generative LLM. Not because that was the right fit - because it was the only tool in the box.

Then Jev shipped last week. No text generation at all. Send it a state and typed questions, get calibrated probabilities back in under half a second. TypeSafe calls it a "System One model" - a direct nod to Kahneman.
Which reframes the whole thing for me as a Data Lader. How much of what we're building is System 1 work - bounded answer space, consumed by software - running on a System 2 engine at System 2 prices?

I wrote up where I think it lands - governance gates, streaming pipelines, AI Gateway routing and tool-risk gating. And where I'd pump the brakes - a probability with no reasoning trail is harder to audit, not easier.
Perspective, not a recommendation. Week-old product, single vendor. But the category feels structural.

every marketer needs a content research agent that plugs into a social media brain

an agent that watches TikTok, Instagram and YouTube Shorts for you, pulls from a database of 13.2M+ viral videos, and uses Jev to decide in 200 milliseconds if each one is worth your time

i used it to get:
- 500K views on social media in 3 days
- $3,057 in a SINGLE day
- just under 1,000 new leads

here's exactly how to set it up for content marketing:

1️⃣ understand what your judge actually does

Jev is a judge. you give it a video plus the answers you allow, and it hands back a decision with a confidence score attached.

three ways to ask it:
- Choice: pick one from your list. "is this a tutorial, a review, or a storytime format?"
- Score: rate it on your scale. "how strong/viral is this hook, from 1 to 10?"
- Noul: yes or no, as a probability. "is this video about the niche it's hashtagged under?"

ask all three in one request and the response time barely moves

2️⃣ give your content research agent a niche

your judge can only rate what your agent collects. set the agent up across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube Shorts with:
- your niche
- your brand name
- your competitors' names
- the platforms you post on

brand and competitor names pull the strongest results. start there, then add intent phrases

3️⃣ make every video pass 2 checks before you trust it

hashtags lie. one off-topic video in the sample and every benchmark after it is off.
- does it match the niche? judged from the caption, the hashtags AND the transcript
- are the hashtags lying? a video can tag its way into a niche it has nothing to do with

this is the step most setups skip, because a reasoning model makes it expensive. i ran the same 15,200 batches on both: $115.07 on Gemini, $4.54 on Jev

4️⃣ benchmark the survivors on 80 intelligence signals

for example: a hook only means something if it's performing better than the other hooks in its niche.

so i group the signals into 6 intelligence categories:
- hooks
- formats and topics
- visual
- production
- sound (transcript + video audio)
- product and sales (CTA type and frequency)

📌 pro tip: Jev decides which videos get counted, and the tagging is a separate job. mixing the two up is the most common mistake in every Jevslop post this week

5️⃣ route every call by confidence

- high confidence: act on it
- shaky: escalate it to a stronger model or a person

Jev is trained to be honest about its confidence. say 90%, be right 90% of the time, which is why you can run it on AUTOPILOT

6️⃣ write the judge's question like a brief

this ONE sentence is the best thing i learned.

early on, Jev treated every detail of my research brief as a hard rule: the format, the tone, even the audience.
- mirroring the brief's exact wording back at it: 16 of 44 right
- one line saying the topic is the only requirement and everything else is a preference: 33 of 44

same test set, one sentence, and 16 became 33.

7️⃣ turn the top result into a script

a ranked list still needs turning into something you can film. give Claude the top results and have it:
→ group them by how each one opens: a question, a bold claim, or a before-and-after
→ pick the outlier that fits your brand best
→ write a beat-by-beat script modeled on its opening, pacing and structure
→ adapt it, never copy it word for word

run step 3 first, so every script starts from a video that's actually in your niche

9️⃣ test it against your current judge before you hand it the keys

before switching from Gemini, i ran mine head-to-head:
- 44 human-labeled videos across 6 research intents: Jev 33, my existing judge 30
- on the videos where the two disagreed, Jev was right 3 out of 4 times

author_headline:
まだ早い — still too early.
Someone posts a number about a token, a repo or a model.
I read whatever issued it. Corrections public.
text:
A video going round this week says Opus 5 took 34 minutes and $23 to sort 1,400 YouTube comments into five buckets, and that a new model did the same class of job for a cent.

I priced both halves against the published rate cards. The cheap half is honest. The $23 is about 43 times too high.

Opus 5 is $5 per million input tokens. $23 buys 4.6 million of them. Spread over 1,400 comments that is 3,286 tokens per comment. A YouTube comment is 20 to 60 tokens.

Read it the other way and it is worse: at $25 per million output, $23 is 657 output tokens per comment, for a job whose output is one word out of five.

Same job, same model, priced at the card:

1,400 comments -> 50 per call -> 28 calls -> 64,400 input + 8,400 output -> $0.53

Through the Batch API, $0.27.

So the honest version of that slide is not Jev versus Opus. It is Jev versus one particular way of driving Opus: an agent loop that re-reads its own context, one comment at a time, while also writing a CSV and building a dashboard. That is a real cost and he really paid it. It is just not what Opus costs to classify 1,400 comments.

Now the part that goes the other way, because I checked it too.

Every Jev figure in the video holds up. TypeSafe publishes $0.042 per million input tokens, output free. Work backwards from each claim:

250 leads for 1 cent -> 952 tokens per lead
203 members for 1 cent -> 1,173 per member
1,300 posts for 4 cents -> 733 per post
227 call transcripts for 7 cents -> 7,342 per transcript
443 browser screens for 1 cent -> 537 per screen

Those are the right sizes for what each of those things is. A call transcript really is ten times a forum post. Nothing there is rounded in his favour.

So the model is as cheap as he says. The comparison is the thing that is broken, and it is broken in the direction that makes the video's case.

Two assumptions in my arithmetic, stated so you can attack them. I assumed a comment is 20 to 60 tokens, and I priced classification only, while his $23 run also produced a spreadsheet and a dashboard. Halve my estimate or double it and the gap is still two orders of magnitude.

The rule this leaves you with: when a post compares a new tool against an old one, check whether the old one was being used properly. Most of the difference in these threads is not the tool. It is the batching.

author_headline:
I test AI workflows that save time or make money. 
Builds, costs, prompts and failure points.
text:
A viral post claims that GPT-6 Sol, Jev and four Grok Bots can perform an entire team’s work for “pocket change.”

The architecture is real.

The conclusion is exaggerated.

Each component serves a different purpose:

GPT-6 Sol handles complex reasoning and writing.

Jev performs fast, inexpensive classification and routing.

Grok Bots operate computers and interact with connected applications.

Combining them can create a useful workflow:

Plan the task.

Collect potential leads.

Filter them cheaply.

Draft personalized messages.

Request approval.

Then send the approved outreach.

But the headline numbers require context.

The widely repeated test involving 3,412 leads, 20,472 decisions, 15.7 seconds and a $0.41 bill measured Jev’s filtering stage.

It did not demonstrate that the complete system found every lead, researched every company, wrote every message and closed sales in 15.7 seconds.

The “six hours of work” comparison is also self-reported—not an independent benchmark.

And the advertised cost does not necessarily include:

Lead acquisition.

GPT-6 Sol generation.

Grok Bot usage.

External services.

Infrastructure.

Setup and maintenance.

Human review.

Or the cost of mistakes.

Calling four configured bots a four-person team creates another illusion.

They are not independent employees.

They are automated roles operating inside one workflow designed, connected and supervised by a person.

This setup could still save substantial time.

Cheap routing can prevent expensive reasoning models from processing thousands of irrelevant records, while approval gates can keep humans in control of external actions.

That is the genuine innovation.

Not replacing an entire company for cents.

But using inexpensive models to decide when the expensive models—and the human—actually need to become involved.

author_headline: Building AI agents inside enterprise Salesforce, where security review and governor limits decides what ships. Daily notes on what breaks.
text:
One of RLHF's co-inventors co-founded a company whose AI won't write a sentence.

The company is TypeSafe and the model is Jev. Their manifesto fits the idea into five words, "building prod, not God," and the bet behind it is that roughly 99% of AI traffic will be software talking to software. Software doesn't want a paragraph; it wants something it can branch on.

So Jev doesn't chat. RLHF taught models to talk and RLVR taught them to reason, but TypeSafe trains Jev for calibrated decisions, which means you ask it to pick an option, rate something on a scale or answer yes/no, and it hands back a typed answer with a probability attached. When it says 0.8, it should be right about eight times in ten across many answers, so your code finally knows when the model isn't sure.

I wired it into a Salesforce dev org last week. A typical call came back in 209 ms from inside the org, and the Agentforce guardrail I built got 8 of 8 decisions right. One hotel case still went to a person because Jev was only 0.53 sure how frustrated the guest was, and I kept that rule on purpose; for anything about trust I'd rather over-review.

The surprise was Salesforce itself. Its built-in layer caught a pasted card number, a stalking question and a message from someone in crisis before my agent saw them, then gave all three the same canned reply. Stopping them early is right, but those three need different answers, and telling review, block and support apart is where Jev earns its place.

It isn't for everything. Anything whose output is a paragraph belongs to an LLM, and if you need data kept in India, that isn't documented yet.

The full Deep Dive video lands next: case triage routed by a Flow with no AI in it, the guardrail, and a guarded Agentforce agent that can't file a case until Jev says pass.

author_headline: Partner at Menlo Ventures
text:
The economics of a Neolab.

A neolab is loosely defined as a startup of AI researchers who raises a lot of money pre-production to be able to finance GPU compute to take on a large AI problem.

To buy 1000 GB300s or ~14 NVL72 racks will set you back $125-150M for 3yrs with 15-30% upfront. That’s about ~2-2.5MW. 

Thats about enough to do 10^25 flops a quarter and get to a GPT-4 level model which is 1-2 OOMs off frontier for pretraining.

If you post-train on a great open source model, you have a better chance of getting to frontier. The risks are a) you need to spend millions on RL environments too and b) being lapped by another model release while being tied to a base model.

For this to payback, you need to give your customers a better and ideally cheaper inference service than a base model and serve them for long enough to recoup your large investment. Even at 50% margin on inference, to recoup $10M in training means serving ~10T tokens (!) if you price like Fable / Astra given a standard cache read / input / output split ($2/M blended). And you have to justify being better than a release like Opus 5.5 which is even cheaper. Often, you end up charging your customers a huge premium in terms of platform fees and compute fees on top of pure inference.

Meanwhile, every hour you’re not utilizing your GPUs you are burning money so you typically resell this compute back to a broker or run inference for open models / resell spot instances. At below a ~60% utilization on spot, you will still lose money.

Add to that insane cost of talent.

So what can you do with the compute?
- Not play the model game at all.
- Play an entirely different model game (Jev, World Labs) that if big labs played, would either a) cannibalize their business or b) be incrementally not significant revenue c) would cause too much distraction from the main main thing
- Acquire a proprietary data set (Peridodic Labs) in enough volume in a domain of usefulness to eclipse frontier quality. Often happens in robotics, biology, chemistry.

If you do overcome the challenge of building a model that is useful and well priced beyond big labs models, given the huge price of compute, you still need to play in an area where the revenue / compute ratio is signficant and market demand is large enough to payback your compute spend. 

It is a difficult game.

A model that makes useful decisions without writing an entire response has plenty of work to do in an AI application.

If you've heard about Jev but aren't quite sure where it fits, here's how I'd explain it.

1/ What Jev does

Jev is a model from TypeSafe AI built for structured decisions.

You give it context and define the question:

→ Which of these options fits?
→ How does this score against my criteria?
→ How likely is this statement to be true?

It returns structured values and probabilities your code can use directly. Choice and Score also include confidence estimates.

That makes it useful for specific, bounded judgments inside a larger workflow.

2/ Why model routing is an interesting use case

An incoming request doesn't always need your most capable model.

Your application needs to decide where to send it:

→ A small, fast model for a straightforward request.
→ A more capable reasoning model for a complex task.
→ A fallback when the routing decision is uncertain.

Jev can assess the request, and your code applies the routing rules using its outputs and confidence.

If you're already using a smaller language model purely to choose a route, this is a step where I'd evaluate Jev. Compare the routing accuracy, response time, and cost on your own requests.

3/ Where reranking comes in

Say your retrieval pipeline returns 20 chunks.

You still need to decide which ones are useful for answering the question. Jev can assess each chunk's relevance, and your code can use those scores to reorder or filter the results.

The workflow becomes:

Retrieve chunks → assess relevance with Jev → rank or filter → send the selected context to the LLM.

The LLM still writes the answer.

I don't see this as another “LLMs are being replaced” moment.

We're optimizing the balance between intelligence and determinism in our applications. Jev supplies a judgment; code controls how that judgment translates into an action.

There's room for that alongside the language generation and deeper reasoning we use LLMs for. Each step needs a model suited to the job, and the decisions still need evaluation.

Arvind and I have been talking about Jev, and we're planning a deep dive session on it. I'd love to spend more time exploring these use cases together.

If you've read this far, thank you. Congratulations, your attention span is doing pretty well 🫶

Ad tech has a layer that still runs on rules and people, and the first model built for it went public this month.

Generative LLMs already write the brief, draft the creative, and summarize the report. Almost none of that makes the decisions that move the money. The LLM drafts and proposes. A person, a rule, or a ranking model still decides. Is this creative compliant? Does this package fit this brief? Does this page suit this brand?

The new agent protocols, AdCP and IAB Tech Lab's AAMP, built the pipes between buyer and seller agents. Both stop for a human before spend. Neither one decides. The gap between the protocols and the auction is what I call the decision layer.

Jev, from TypeSafe, is the first model built for that layer. You send it the creative or the brief and a question with a fixed set of answers, and it returns an answer with a probability instead of a paragraph. Code keeps the rules and the thresholds. The model supplies the judgment.

It is not for the bidding path. It is for creative review, RFP response, and brand suitability, the decisions that run today on hand-written rules and review queues.

I think that by mid 2027 the first production uses will be approval gates and creative review, not bidding, and that review queues will shrink before CPMs rise.

Should a model that can't write a single sentence make your business decisions?

I ran ~3,600 test calls comparing TypeSafe's new decision model with GPT-6 Luna across multiple test cases. What stood out:

> ~3-6× faster than Luna, at ~2-2.6× lower cost (prompt caching at play for Luna)
> Its confidence score is quite usable: more trustworthy than an LLM's token probabilities (logprobs), though a reasoning model's self-reported confidence did about as well.
> Without a "can't tell" option, it guessed a hidden die roll at 0.83 confidence, every time
> Wording steers it: changing the "role" label changed which tool it picked
> With reasoning on, Luna never got a case wrong that Jev got right

My takeaway: Jev is a true "System 1" model. Fast, consistent, and best used with precomputed inputs and a confidence threshold, or as the first layer of a cascade.

author_headline: Curating the future of AI, autonomous agents & code automation. Deep dives into building next-gen tech stack. Drops & insights daily. 🛠️🤖
text:
Most "AI experts" are teaching you prompt engineering. This guy just leaked the actual architecture.

Jev founder Diogo Almeida dropped a 12-page playbook on running LLMs the way serious engineering teams actually do it — and it makes most paid AI courses look like content marketing.

It's a 10-step blueprint for building an AI system that's faster, cheaper, and actually controllable — works with Claude, Codex, Grok, or whatever model you're running.

Step 1 — Divide the labor. The LLM writes. Jev makes tight, bounded judgment calls. Code stays in charge.

Step 2 — Feed it state, not noise. Give Jev the request, the evidence, the policy, and the proposed action — not the whole chat history.

Step 3 — Pick the right decision type. Choice picks a path. Score ranks against a rubric. Noul returns a probability that something's true.

Step 4 — Kill the mega-prompt. Stop cramming intent, urgency, evidence, risk, and scope into one giant eval. Split them into separate typed calls.

Step 5 — Run Jev before the model. Decide context, tools, provider, and workflow before you burn tokens on a real generation.

Step 6 — Give the LLM a narrow lane. Once Jev picks the route, the model gets only the instructions and tools that branch actually needs.

Step 7 — Run Jev after the model too. Did the output answer the ask? Is it grounded? Did it stay in scope?

Step 8 — Route by confidence, not vibes. High-confidence, low-risk → auto-proceed. Uncertain → pull more context. High-stakes → human review.

Step 9 — Batch your judgments. Fire multiple Choice/Score/Noul questions against one shared state instead of spinning up a new LLM call for every single check.

Step 10 — Log everything. State version, question, probabilities, route taken, model, latency, outcome, human override — the full receipt.

Most courses teach you to write a bigger prompt.

text:
Top 12 agentic use cases for Jev:

(bookmark this)

Jev handles semantic decisions that ordinary code cannot express reliably. It returns typed answers and probabilities, while code continues to cover the workflow.

Here are 12 practical use cases for Jev:

1. Browser next action

> Convert the current DOM state into a bounded action such as click, type, or stop. Code executes only valid operation-target pairs. There are already several open-source Jev web agents.

2. Context compaction

> Decide which events from a long agent trace should remain. The selected text stays verbatim instead of being replaced with a generated summary.

3. Skill and context loading

> Compare the current user turn against the available skills. Load only the instructions needed for that turn instead of filling the context window with every skill.

4. Typed tool-call compilation

> Map a natural-language request to a function and fill its typed arguments. Each argument is evaluated separately before code allows execution.

5. Citation verification

> Check whether a quoted passage exists and whether the surrounding evidence supports the claim. The output can be supported, unsupported, or contradicted.

6. Extraction verification

> Run a cheap extractor first, then use Jev to verify questionable fields. Clean records stay on the fast path while uncertain ones reach a reasoning model.

7. Agent trace evaluation

> Turn raw trajectories into queryable labels such as progress and repetition. This avoids asking another LLM to write a full review of every run.

8. Semantic regression tests

> Replay a trace suite against a new agent build. Semantic checks can then pass or block prompt, model, tool, and policy changes in CI.

9. Jevgrep code search

> Search a codebase by what the code does rather than its exact words. Jev scores candidate snippets and returns the most relevant code first.

10. Entity alignment

> Compare two candidate records and decide whether to merge, review, or keep them separate. Candidate generation remains deterministic while Jev handles semantic identity.

11. Retrieval reranking

> Let embeddings retrieve a broad candidate set, then use Jev to reorder passages by relevance. The generation model receives the most useful evidence first.

12. Memory promotion gate

> Capture a completed agent trace, then judge whether its corrections contain a reusable lesson. Trace-backed lessons can be promoted while task-specific noise is discarded.

If you want to see the final pattern in practice, it is already implemented in the Beacon open-source project.

Beacon captures full sessions across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, and 20+ agent harnesses, and then Jev identifies which workflows and corrections are worth learning from, so that a lesson discovered by one agent can become available to the others.

text:
Brilliant paper from CMU.

If you use Jev/LLM-as-judge, this one is for you.

(bookmark it)

We use LLMs to generate answers, then use another LLM to judge them.

But many evaluations only need a bounded decision.

- Was the answer grounded?
- Did it follow the instruction?
- Which response was better?

This Carnegie Mellon University paper tests whether Jev can make these decisions cheaply, then identifies the cases that need a stronger judge.

The results reveal Jev’s real edge.

→ Jev works well on focused judgments

On ordinary response preferences, evidence-grounded factuality, and final-answer checks, Jev remained within three percentage points of the strongest judge tested.

→ The cost difference is substantial

On the paper’s matched workload, Jev cost only 0.36 percent of the strongest comparator’s fee.

This makes it practical to evaluate more agent responses, across more criteria, without scaling the evaluation bill at the same rate.

→ Confidence becomes a routing mechanism

Jev returns a decision and label probabilities.

When confidence is high, accept its decision. When confidence is low, escalate the case to a stronger LLM.

A frozen version of this cascade retained about 99 percent of GPT-6’s accuracy while using roughly 57 percent of its fee.

→ Jev still has a clear boundary

It fell behind when evaluation required checking complex derivations or resisting an elaborately written wrong answer.

It also struggled with factuality judgments when no reference evidence was provided. In those cases, confidence did not reliably expose the errors.

So the paper is not arguing that Jev should replace every LLM judge.

It presents a more useful architecture.

Code handles exact rules. Jev handles focused semantic judgments. Stronger models or humans handle uncertain and reasoning-heavy cases.

That is also the idea behind the workflow I built.

The agent generates an answer. Jev judges bounded claims against the supplied evidence. Uncertain cases move to review. Opik records the traces, scores, and experiment results.

The paper explains why this architecture works.

Before you add another LLM call, look at what your application actually needs back.
A lot of the time it needs a category, a score, or a yes or no.

I've been looking at Jev, the System One model from TypeSafe AI, for exactly that kind of work. You pass it context and a set of defined questions.
