text:
Your AI agent doesn't always need another LLM.

Sometimes, it just needs to make a decision.

I came across Jev, and the easiest way I found to understand it was to think about all the small decisions happening inside an AI-powered application.

For example, imagine you're building a support system.

A new message comes in:

«“I can't access my account and I need to fix it before my meeting.”»

Your system might need to decide:

→ Is this a support request?
→ What type of issue is it?
→ How urgent is it?
→ Which workflow should handle it?
→ Does it need a human?

You could throw the entire thing at a large LLM.

But that's not always necessary.

This is where a decision-focused system like Jev becomes interesting.

Where could you use it?

1️⃣ Classification

Turn unstructured information into a defined decision.

"Email → Sales / Support / Billing"

"Security alert → Normal / Suspicious / Critical"

"Ticket → Low / Medium / High priority"

---

2️⃣ Routing

You have multiple agents or workflows.

Instead of every request going through the same path:

"Request → Decision → Appropriate agent/workflow"

For example, a coding request could go to a coding agent while a billing request goes somewhere else.

---

3️⃣ Tool selection

An agent might have access to:

🔹 Search
🔹 Database
🔹 Calculator
🔹 CRM
🔹 Email
🔹 Internal APIs

The question becomes:

“Which tool should I use for this situation?”

That's a decision problem.

---

4️⃣ RAG filtering

Imagine your retrieval system returns 20 pieces of information.

Do you really want to pass everything to your expensive LLM?

A decision layer can help determine what is actually relevant before the next step.

---

5️⃣ Security & policy decisions

This is especially interesting for cybersecurity and automation.

For example:

Should this action be allowed?

Does this request require human approval?

Does this activity violate a defined policy?

The decision system doesn't necessarily perform the action.

Your application still controls what happens next.

---

So I think the useful way to look at Jev isn't:

“Can this replace my LLM?”

Instead, ask:

“How many decisions does my application make that don't actually require a generative LLM?”

Because AI applications aren't only about generating text.

They're also constantly deciding:

what to do, where to go, what to ignore, and when to escalate.

And that decision layer is something I think developers should start paying more attention to.

author_headline: Founder and CTO at HubSpot. Helping millions grow better.
text:
There's gold in your LinkedIn Connections and Invites and I'm using the new JEV AI model to mine it in YouSpot (the AI-native CRM for solopreneurs).

You've likely heard JEV the new AI model from a company called TypeSafe.

What makes JEV is interesting is that it is *not* a Large Language Model (LLM) like GPT, Claude and other models you've likely heard of and use.

JEV is a decision model. Instead of entering in a prompt and generating a bunch of tokens (usually words), such as generating a blog post or summarizing an essay, JEV does something much, much simpler.  It basically acts as a classifier with probabilities as outputs. Think of it as answering a multiple choice question with a "confidence level" on its responses.

For example, you could prompt with an article and ask it to categorize the article into pre-defined categories:  marketing, sales, finance, operations, fiction.  What JEV then gives you back is a set of probabilities. That is, this article has an 85% chance that it's about marketing, 10% chance that it's about sales, etc.

Because it's not trying to create/generate something, it's much faster and cheaper (like 200X+ faster/cheaper) than a typical LLM. And it runs in less than a second. 

As a result, you can use JEV for things that using an LLM (even the smaller/faster ones) is just not practical for.

Here's an example:

In YouSpot (promo link with discount in comments), I recently added a feature that's been very popular where you can export your full LinkedIn dataset (connections, invitations and InMail messages) and bring that file into the YouSpot into its Second Brain.

Then you can use YouSpot to analyze, categorize and prioritize your LinkedIn connections and invites to connect.

JEV is what powers this. 

Here's how it works: You describe, in natural language, what kinds of people are of most interest.  

Example (this is mine):  I'm interested in founders and C-level execs at tech companies or high influence people in tech.  Less interested in finance and HR.

YouSpot will then go through all of your connections and invitations and calculate a priority score (0-10) *and* classify/tag them in the categories you specified in your prompt.

You have to use it to truly appreciate how useful it is.  I've already used it to find invitations that were "stuck" in my pending queue. They bubbled to the top of the priority list. 

YouSpot Pro is $10/month (cancel anytime), but there's a link in the comments to get a 20% discount for the next 7 days. 

Let me know what you think -- or if you try it, ideas for how it could be more useful for you.

After a week of leaks and Twitter vagueposting, OpenAI Dev Day finally happened. First, a flex: ChatGPT now has 1.2B weekly users. 4 announcements stood out to me:

(1) Dots: the answer to Muse

Dots are persistent, always-on agents with memory and access to connected apps. OpenAI previewed “specialist dots” for enterprises - agents that can own a particular function. 
If the competitive target wasn’t obvious enough, CFO Sarah Friar accidentally called Dots “Muse” on TV. Freudian slip, AI edition. There is one key difference: Muse is free, while Dots is initially limited to paid accounts. 
The demo left me somewhat underwhelmed. Dots feel like Muse for the narrow set of people whose to-do list spans “book dinner” and “fix GitHub issue.” Too Bay Area coded.
Maybe GPT-6 Astra makes the product dramatically better. But how much model quality does the mass-market user actually need? If Muse is free, ubiquitous, and good enough, the capability gap may matter less than the distribution gap. 

(2) Space: moving from the AI seat to the AI workspace

Space gives teams and agents a shared environment for files and project context. Pages create editable artifacts that humans and agents can work on together. This is a bid to own the workflow and move AI adoption from individual seat to team workspace, a much stickier place to live. 

(3) Decisions: Jev competitor 

A few weeks ago, TypeSafe AI launched Jev, a model designed around the idea that most AI workloads don’t require prose, they require decision-making: approve or reject, route to agent A or B. Jev built for these bounded decisions, optimized around speed and cost, and quickly climbed usage charts. Which raised the question: how long until a frontier lab notices? Answer: apparently a few weeks. 
OpenAI launched Decisions API, addressing the same workload. Being a startup is difficult when the 800lb gorilla still has startup reflexes. 
The key takeaway is that the stack is fragmenting into specialized primitives:
- reasoning models for hard problems
- generative models for content
- embedding models for retrieval
- decision models for cheap, high-volume control flow
With agents, that last category will be massive 

(4) Open models inside Codex

OpenAI announced a partnership with Baseten to serve open models directly inside Codex. Devs can now run models like GLM and Kimi inside OpenAI's coding environment. It’s a classic aggregator move: cede commodity supply, keep the demand side. Better to collect a toll on somebody else’s model than become somebody else’s API call.

This is a hedge against model commoditization.
If frontier models remain differentiated, they win by owning the best models.
If models commoditize, they win because everyone accesses them through OpenAI. 
That is the broader Dev Day strategy.

While Twitter litigates demo quality, OpenAI is reportedly raising $30B at a $1.4T valuation with growth accelerating to ~$70B RR Rev. Tough one to bet against.

text:
Here's everything I think you should know if you're building GTM bots with AI.

I've built them on 8 different AI setups so far this year: Claude, GLM, Codex, Kimi, GPT-6 Astra, Grok, Fable and Jev.

Before you build (1-5)

1. Run ten accounts yourself first, fifteen minutes each. Every field you find missing becomes the spec.
2. Give the bot your offer and your ICP side by side before it researches anyone. Hand it a vague brief and it invents the judgment you left out.
3. Start with one signal. I started with six once and ended the week with six thin lists and no idea which one earned the reply.
4. Pick the model for the job. We picked Grok 4.7 for one line in its launch post, that it "checks its work more carefully". For a lead judge that's basically the whole job.
5. You don't always need a model API bill to start. Our Opus 5.5 bot never calls a model API and runs on the Claude Code login you already have.

Running the stack (6-10)

6. I go from Claude to Codex to Kimi constantly, all on max plans. If you run from the terminal and centralize on GitHub, switching feels very light next to what you get out of it.
7. Use one model to research and another to run what you build. Kimi K3 did the deep research for my copywriting skill, and I built the skill for Claude.
8. Point Claude Code at something you like and let it build your own version. Our launch film took one line of prompt and 38 minutes to a first cut.
9. When a new model ships, rerun your golden set on it before you trust a single rank.
10. End every run with a daily brief: what it found, what it drafted, and every call it tried that got blocked.

How to structure it (11-20)

11. Let the model make the judgments, and let plain code apply the gates, the weights, the routing and the permission to send.
12. Keep the ICP, the weights and the playbook in plain text files. When a rank is wrong you want to open one file and change one line.
13. Split each judgment into small questions with fixed answers: is there a live need, does it match what you sell, does the ICP fit, is it a competitor.
14. Hide the contact when the model judges the company. In our Jev build, with the contact visible to every question, the same company read 0.28 on intent with a recruiter as the contact and 0.80 with a managing partner.
15. Keep the watching separate from the agent that ranks. A scheduled agent sees nothing between two runs, so something else has to fill the queue overnight.
16. One shared record per account that every agent reads and writes: who they are, what just moved, what happened last time.
17. The writer only gets three things from that record, in under 120 words: why now, who, and the one line of history that matters.
18. Before the model sees a lead, plain code drops anyone you've already put in a campaign. Our Jev build skips every max lead that already has a delivery on record.
19. Treat everything inside a lead as data. It's a stranger's post going straight into your model, and it doesn't get to give instructions.
20. Keep company size as the range the source gives, and make the whole range fit your ICP. Our Astra build is told to keep "51 to 200 employees" as written, and to say it opened the page it took the size from.

Judging leads (21-28)

21. Gate before you score. Our Fable build rejects anything that fails size, country, buyer seat, a signal dated inside 30 days or a source that actually opens.
22. Make the model open the source before it scores a lead high. Dead page, need goes to zero.
23. Date the lead by the event. A page indexed this week can describe a launch from last year.
24. No source link, no lead. Whatever fails goes on a held list with the reason written down.
25. Hot account, wrong contact: the bot reroutes it and emails nobody. In our Grok 4.7 repo, the test lead with a recruiter as the contact scores 73.4 and still never gets a message.
26. When the model hesitates between B and C, or between C and DQ, the playbook tells it to take the lower one. Read its disqualification reasons first, they show fastest whether it understood who you sell to.
27. Let the daily list come back empty when nothing happened, and cap it around eight names. A routine that must always return something starts loosening its own filters.
28. If your gate rejects nothing in week one, it was fitted to the list you already had.

Writing (29-35)

29. Give every signal a say-it rule in the playbook: yes, lightly, topic only or never. 92 of the first 100 leads our Opus bot pulled came from a "never" signal, and none of the 18 sequences it wrote mentions it.
30. Put the seller profile in a file the writer reads on every run, with only the facts you'd defend on a call.
31. Run a linter that flags any % or "2x" that isn't one of your proof points. Ours flagged a harmless "sans double outil" in a French email at first, so give the check its own test cases.
32. Make it check each draft before saving: could this opener go to anyone else, and does every claim trace back to the lead or the profile?
33. Keep a never-list per play, and add every dead phrase you catch.
34. Let it write in the prospect's language when the location makes it obvious. Our first Opus run came back in French, German and English.
35. When a reply asks for something that isn't in your facts, the draft should promise the figures and flag the gap. Answering one simulated test reply, ours did that and still slipped in "depends on seats and volume", which isn't in our profile. Every reply draft waits for a human to send it.

Safety (36-43)

36. Default to locked. Going live should be a flag you flip on purpose.
37. Every campaign the bot creates starts switched off. In our Opus test run that was 18 campaigns and zero people enrolled.
38. Keep approving, launching and ICP changes out of the scheduled run.
39. Log every write the bot attempts, allowed or blocked. We tried to break the lock three times on our live workspace: twice with a safety script, once by launching an approved campaign while send mode was locked. The guard blocked 7 calls and the daily brief listed every one.
40. Tag everything the bot creates with one name prefix, so you can list it and delete it in one go.
41. Put a daily cap on anything that costs money or creates something.
42. Make the bot re-check for replies, bounces and opt-outs right before it enrolls anyone. A human review sits between building a campaign and launching it, and people can reply or opt out in between.
43. Read at least 20 sequences in review before you flip send mode to live.

Testing and learning (44-50)

44. Build a small golden set with the traps in it: a recruiter at a hot account, a competitor, a company stacking press releases. On our Jev starter set the ranker gets 10 of 10, the offline baseline gets 7.
45. Write tests for the routing too. Someone who already replied should never land in a new sequence, whatever the model thinks.
46. Make the reason a required field in the outcome log. A bare "no reply" teaches the next run almost nothing.
47. Leave the weights alone until each bucket has 30 real contacts. After its first run our Opus bot called its 15 simulated outcomes "not evidence". Fair.
48. Cap how far a weight can move in a day, and give every signal a floor so the rare ones don't get buried.
49. Route a few leads below your line to a one-touch lane. If the bot only ever contacts the top, you never find out the line is in the wrong place.
50. Change one thing per round. Our Codex build proposes one change at a time as a pull request, and a human merges it.

text:
This is how I make sure I can source 90%+ of a total addressable market.

This is often overlooked, but your foundational data is the highest ROI lever you can pull. 

Everything downstream depends on the data it's founded on and even something that should be as simple as list building can quickly become complex.

Here's how I approach this 👇

COMPANIES

1️⃣ Start from closed-won

We start from our closed-won companies I know fit and check how the databases tag them. They rarely all show up as clean matches under one label. Missing these can already impact your downstream results.

2️⃣ Expand with lookalikes

I run Prospeo's company lookalike search, one domain at a time. Then I add content similarity using Exa.

Prospeo's lookalike finds companies that look like a seed in the database: size, industry, profile.

Exa finds companies whose website text reads like the seed's website.

Both start from the seeds, so the categorization matters less.

3️⃣ Pull wide

Every industry a confirmed fit carries, we pull. Same for Every multi-word keyword from confirmed fits. 

4️⃣ Let AI classify

Let AI classify every company. I write the ICP in one line plus the disqualifiers, and I tune the model on 10 companies at a time until we get 20 records back with zero corrections. Then it scores every company I pulled. It reads each company's website or description and answers yes or no.

One option we are looking at is Jev by TypeSafe, a new kind of classifier that never writes text and returns a yes/no probability in 100 to 300 ms, which is exactly this job.

I QA to make sure these are correct.

5️⃣ Keep expanding

Every confirmed fit becomes a new lookalike to search for. This way we keep expanding until a round adds under 2 to 3% new fits, and make sure the list is close to the 90% aim. 

CONTACTS

6️⃣ Search broad, let AI classify

Also here we recommend searching broad and letting AI do the classification. I can remember very well that we needed to sit inside of Clay and manually QA this every time. Now at least AI can do the first part at scale.

"CCO" also matched account managers, executives and accountants.

Sometimes I search with no title filter at all, then cut down to who belongs in the campaign.

Before I pay, I check which emails are verified. 

Prospeo shows verification status before you export, so you can see what you're actually buying. 

And that is how easy it is to underestimate how much of your TAM you’re missing
Prospeo.io refreshes its whole database every 7 days, so a broad pull stays current.

How good is Jev at detecting threats? Spoiler alert: damn good. But why?

Jev is a decision model. It answers yes-or-no questions you define about a piece of text in milliseconds. This lets you expand deterministic signatures in a way that is impossible otherwise.

Agents are dynamic. Give an agent one task, and it will find seven different ways to accomplish that. Because there isn’t just one way to delete a file.

text:
holy sh*t, Sam Altman launched Dots, but Jev is still the one that decides the fork

Dots does the work while you're away, and Jev makes sure every decision inside your own agent is one you can audit

this is a 6-step blueprint on how Dots and Jev each handle a fork, and when you need which:

step 1 → Dots starts from a goal: you set it once, like "weekly market brief, ask before email", and your dot on GPT-6 Astra runs on its own cloud computer with memory that stays the same in every channel

step 2 → Dots splits the work: background agents research the web and Drive, analyze the numbers and draft the PR in parallel, each one a thread you can open

step 3 → Dots decides with rules: every action passes an automatic review of instructions, permissions, custom rules and safety, then lands in one of four modes: without asking, when you say so, ask first, or hand off to you

step 4 → Jev starts from the state: "the agent wants to run a migration on prod-db" goes in as one packed request

step 5 → Jev decides with numbers: typed questions like "is prod touched?" and "how risky, 0 to 1?" come back as calibrated probabilities in 70–500 ms. risky 0.93 is above the 0.90 deny line, so code blocks it

step 6 → Jev hands the next step back to the LLM: it writes a safer plan, a dry-run on staging, and the result is verified in code, leaving an audit trail for every fork

most people think these two compete

they don't: Dots is the agent you use, and Jev is the layer you build into your own

use Dots when you want the work done while you're away, and use Jev when you're building the agent and need forks you can audit ↓

text:
First day using TypeSafe AI's Jev for my GTM as a non technical dude. 

Heres the thing: 

The most difficult point is to not treat it as an LLM. 

Yesterday I ran research on +300 GTM job postings to qualify companies and find whales. 

Pulling job descriptions was the eazy part. 

I was responsible for the quality of the input + output, so the real work was figuring out which questions actually matter, and which assumptions & distractions to avoid. 

I started with 7 different qualifiers about scope, ownership, responsibilities. 

The results? poor, too many things to judge.

I chopped it down to two: Build/Scale GTM & SMB/Enterprise motion. 

Easier to audit, and the output was more reliable than having more pieces on the puzzle. 

Then the details started to matter: 

1. The wording of your question is your criteria: I first asked whether the role was programmatic outbound. A company that runs enrichment every single day landed in the doubt zone, because the JD talks about enrichment, not outbound. I rephrased the question around enrichment and it moved up. Same data, different question, different answer.

2. Jev sees almost every B2B company as "enterprise deal chaser“: The median score on my does this company sell to enterprise? question was 0.64. With the cutoff at 0.6 I would have thrown out half of my list. At 0.9 only 15%. Look at the distribution before you set a threshold. Don't default to 0.5. 

3. Dont filter by theres positive evidence. That gives you tiny lists. With a strict criteria I got 44 companies out of 227. Flipping it to remove whats clearly bad, then rank the rest gave me around 70 on the exact same list, at no extra cost. 

If you ask me about the main difference with regular LLM workflows: you must be clearer on the picture. 

LLMs its more about working in the abstract, providing data & letting them connect the dots. 

With Jev, you decide what the dots are. 

This will be definitely sharper over time and at such low cost it’s well worth it.

So thats the drill.

 - - - 

You don't need to be a mastermind to determine SaaS niches or business models, use Leadsforge 🏎️, plug it to your AI agent & start pumping today.

Procurar emprego é um problema de GTM. Então tratei como um.
O Jev, novo modelo da TypeSafe AI, foi lançado no dia 15 de setembro. No dia 21 eu já estava rodando o meu radar de vagas com ele. O Jev não gera texto: ele devolve decisões com uma probabilidade calibrada, rápido e barato. Pensei na hora: é exatamente o que falta para triar vaga. 
Porque buscar vaga nunca foi o meu gargalo. O gargalo era decidir quais valiam o meu tempo. 
Esta semana, encontrei o ótimo post do radar de vagas criado pela Kauana Moreira!!!
O que o Jev faz aqui pode ser considerado o próximo passo: triagem e ranqueamento dessas vagas.

O pipeline, a cada rodada: 
→ coleta ~3.500 vagas de 17 fontes (Gupy, Greenhouse, Lever, Workday, boards remotos) e ~115 empresas que acompanho 
→ aplica filtros baratos antes de gastar IA, o que cortou ~48% das chamadas sem perder nenhuma vaga boa 
→ manda cada vaga para o Jev, que devolve uma nota de aderência ao meu currículo e às minhas preferências 
→ corrige com regras fixas onde a IA erra de forma previsível 
→ entrega um ranking em Excel: aplicar agora, avaliar ou não aplicar 

A parte que mais me ensinou: não confiei na nota da IA no achismo. Rotulei um gabarito à mão e medi. A primeira versão acertava 52% da ordenação. Ajustando o que eu mandava para o modelo, chegou a 70%. 
E a IA erra de um jeito interessante. O Jev me deu nota alta para vagas de gerente de contas, porque meu currículo tem muito e-commerce, marketplace e gestão de contas. Só que eu nunca tive carteira de clientes como executivo de vendas. Foi overlap de palavra-chave, não aderência real. Por isso o pipeline tem regras fixas por cima da nota, e por isso eu ainda leio as vagas do topo, ajustando cada vez mais a aderência do modelo ao meu perfil.
Quem trabalha com vendas vai reconhecer tudo isso. A vaga é o lead, meu perfil é o ICP, a nota é o lead score, e filtrar antes de chamar a IA é a mesma lógica de não queimar crédito numa waterfall de enriquecimento.

Detalhe importante: não sou desenvolvedor. Construí tudo junto com o Opus 5.5 da Anthropic. Meu papel foi o de dono do produto: definir o que é uma vaga boa, rotular o gabarito e validar cada rodada.

text:
A few thoughts after yesterday’s @OpenAI DevDay, from an engineering perspective.

The era of subsidized AI may be coming to an end.

OpenAI introducing a $500 plan, after the $200 tier already felt like unusually good value and was eventually constrained, is another signal that frontier intelligence probably won’t remain artificially cheap forever.

As these systems become more capable and more economically useful, we’ll likely start paying closer to their actual cost and value. I wouldn’t be surprised to see @AnthropicAI move in a similar direction.

But the more interesting shift to me is what’s happening to software itself.

OpenAI shipped what is essentially their equivalent of Jev in an incredibly short amount of time.
That should tell us something:
Software is losing its scarcity and big corp can take over your little idea anytime if it's attractive enough.

Products and features that would have required months of engineering, or looked technically unrealistic for a small team, can now be recreated remarkably quickly.

Building the feature is no longer the moat.
And paradoxically, I think this raises the bar for engineers rather than lowers it.

Craft, reliability, taste, performance, and obsessive attention to detail will matter more than ever. When almost anyone can generate functional software, differentiation moves toward how well the product is made and how deeply you understand the people using it.

Learn your audience. Talk to them. Build with them, not just for them.

Engineering > Product
I also don’t think AI kills engineering roles before it changes product roles.
Instead, I think a lot of traditional product thinking gets absorbed directly into engineering.
The strongest engineers will increasingly understand users, design, business, data, and distribution, and be able to execute across the entire loop:

understand the problem → build → ship → observe → talk to users → iterate.

The distinction between “product person” and “engineer” starts becoming much less meaningful when one person can do what previously required an entire team.

And if you’re a solo builder, there’s another skill you absolutely need to learn:

Distribution.

By now, anyone who has seriously built something understands this.
Building has never been cheaper.

When everyone can build, your edge becomes a combination of exceptional product quality, deep understanding of your users, and the ability to get that product in front of them. 
Hint: Think out of the box, way out, marketing has also changed and now Gen Z does it best.

author_headline: Founder, Zeron — Building the Autonomous System for Cybersecurity
text:
I spent this week reading Jev's docs instead of the threads about Jev.

The threads are right that it's impressive. Cheap, fast, typed decisions are a real unlock, and most teams building agents should be using it.

But almost nobody is reading the limitations page. Six things I'd want every security engineer to know before this ends up in a guardrail:

1. It cannot say "I don't know."
Jev cannot abstain. Without an explicit escape option, it picks the least wrong one. That is an unsafe default for anything gating an action. Add a "none of these" member to every enum you route through it.

2. It cannot explain itself.
No reasoning, no rationale, just a typed answer and a probability. For anything that needs an audit trail — regulated workloads, incident review, a customer asking why they were blocked — that is a gap you have to fill somewhere else.

3. Option order changes the answer.
Pydantic's docs note that the order of your enum members is part of what Jev sees, and reordering them can move the verdict. A developer sorts a list alphabetically and a security decision flips. Nothing in the diff looks like a security change.

4. The checker can itself be attacked.
TypeSafe's own limitations page says text written to adversarially steer the model can move the answer. Pydantic says Jev treats the state as data, not as hostile. If you're using it to detect prompt injection, sit with that.

5. Type-safe is not the same as correct.
It cannot return a value outside your schema — TypeSafe calls that guaranteed by construction. But it can still assign high confidence to the wrong option. Type safety narrows the shape of a failure. It does not remove the need to test the judgment.

6. There are no published weights.
You cannot run it locally. Every decision is an outbound call carrying whatever state you passed in. For regulated data, that's a residency question before it's an accuracy question.

None of this makes Jev bad. It makes Jev a sensor.
Sensors inform controls. They are not controls.

Put a deterministic check underneath it, and version your enum ordering and your confidence thresholds the way you'd version a firewall rule. Because that's what they are now.

#Jev #AIAgents #AISecurity #PromptInjection #AgentSecurity #LLMSecurity

The most useful AI model we started using this month can't write a single sentence.

Generating content is cheap now. Judging it is the bottleneck.

So at @23andMe we started using Jev from @typesafeai, a "System One" model. It doesn't generate text. It makes fast, structured judgments about text and tells you how confident it is.

We took hundreds of our published articles and used them to define what great looks like for us: voice, clarity, scientific accuracy, how we talk about health. That became a rubric. Every new piece gets scored against it before an editor sees it. Clear passes move faster. Anything uncertain goes to a person. Anything health-related still goes to our reviewers, always.

Why not just use a frontier model for this?

Cost and speed. LLMs charge by the token. Ask one to grade something and it writes out its reasoning, so you pay for the essay too. Multiply by every draft, every variant, every criterion. The bill compounds and each answer takes seconds.

A #SystemOne model skips the writing. It returns a verdict, not an essay. Almost no output to pay for, answers in under half a second. In Every's independent test, one editorial check with #Jev ran ~25x faster and ~580x cheaper than a frontier model.

That changes the math. Review stops being the expensive step you skip under deadline and becomes something you run on everything. Frontier models still do the writing. Humans still make the final call.

The model is a commodity. Our standards are the asset.

That was my argument on the "AI Leadership and the Metrics That Matter" panel at the @ThinkingAI_io Agentic Growth Summit: the biggest value of AI in marketing isn't making more content. It's checking everything against a source of truth, every time, at a cost that makes skipping review pointless.

LLMs are incredibly powerful for language understanding, reasoning, and open-ended problem solving. But in an agent workflow, many decisions are actually structured and well-defined.

→ Should the agent continue or stop?
→ Which action should have higher priority?

The future of agentic AI may be less about one model doing everything and more about multiple specialized components working together.

Introducing GLiDE, a thinking decision model built for reasoning-intensive decisions.

Using the official Decision Index 0.2.1 scorer, GLiDE scores 64.81, leading Jev by 6.90 skill points and outperforming it across all five evaluation areas, including an 11.5-point lead in Knowledge and Reasoning.

Typically, decision models are designed to score a set of options in one pass. GLiDE takes that process a step further by recognizing when a decision requires more effort.

After producing an initial answer, GLiDE quickly assesses its confidence. When the result is uncertain, the model automatically allocates more compute to thinking further and incorporates that reasoning into its final probabilities.

This allows GLiDE to move beyond straightforward classification into complex, multi-step decisions like selecting from hundreds of tools, choosing the best next action from hundreds of possible paths, or judging and verifying reasoning-intensive model outputs.

With every decision, it returns:

• The selected action
• A corresponding confidence score
• A probability distribution across the available options

→ remember what happened earlier
→ resolve a blurry boundary
→ work out why something happened

In other words, the harder metrics weren’t about spotting something explicit in the transcript. They were about understanding what happened across the conversation.

That gave us a much better rule for designing evals:
Choose the judge based on the shape of the metric.

We broke down all 7, why Jev failed on them, and what we’d do differently.

Bookmark it and enjoy the read over a long weekend :)

THE GUY WHO HELPED BUILD CHATGPT JUST BUILT AN AI THAT CAN'T WRITE A SINGLE WORD.

And developers can't stop talking about it.

It's called Jev.

Diogo Almeida co-invented RLHF, the training behind ChatGPT. Then he disappeared into stealth for 2 years asking one question...

Why are we using chat models to make yes or no decisions?

Is this spam. Approve or reject. Refund or not.

You ask an LLM and it writes you a paragraph. Just to say "yes."

Jev skips the writing completely.

You give it the options → it picks one → it tells you how sure it is.

→ 70 to 500 ms per decision
→ $0.042 per million input tokens
→ Output tokens cost nothing. There aren't any.

But the speed isn't the interesting part.

The confidence score is.

95% accurate is useless if you don't know which 5% is wrong. Jev tells you every time. Sure? Let it run. Unsure? Send it to a human.

That's what makes it usable in production.

Now the catch nobody's reposting.

The 193x faster number is from TypeSafe's own tests. Independent measurements so far land between 1.16x and 6x.

Still faster. Just not 193x.

And their benchmark scores "correct" as agreeing with two frontier LLMs. So it measures agreement, not truth. They say so themselves.

The launch still hit 1,500+ points on Hacker News in a day and briefly knocked their API over from demand.

Because the idea is right even if the headline is loud.

Most of what we pay LLMs to do was never a conversation.

It was a checkbox.

text:
Judging a company just got cheaper than enriching it.

Jev has been all over my feed for two weeks, mostly from teams using it to grade agent outputs. 

Last night 🦾Eric Nowoslawski pointed it at something closer to home: an ICP prompt across every company in the US. Jev cannot write code or a paragraph. It only decides, and it charges almost nothing to do it. That is the whole point.

Three things I am changing about how we build lists after Clay Club NYC.

1 -- Stop trusting the industry filter.

A bank was listed on LinkedIn as a construction company. Industry is self-reported by whoever set up the page, and that person was not thinking about your ICP.

2 -- Pull the trash on purpose.

Take your closed-won accounts, see every industry and keyword they have ever appeared under, and pull it all. Then let a model judge every row. Is this a bank, yes or no?

I came across something called JEV recently, and I think it’s a pretty interesting concept.

We’re all using ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc. for almost everything now.

But here’s the thing I started thinking about:
Do we really need a full-blown LLM for every little decision?

Say a lead comes in.

You might use an LLM to understand the conversation and figure out what the person is asking. But then you still need to make a bunch of smaller decisions:
Is this a qualified lead? How high is the intent? Which salesperson should get it? 

Using a large LLM for every single one of these decisions can be an overkill. This is where JEV gets interesting.

The simplest way I understand it:
LLMs → Think & generate
JEV → Decide
Your software → Execute

So you could have something like:

ChatGPT/Claude → Understand the lead
↓
JEV → Score + classify it
↓
CRM → Assign it
↓
n8n → Trigger the right workflow

And this isn’t just for leads.

It could be:
→ Spam or genuine email?
→ High or low purchase intent?
→ Which support ticket needs escalation?
→ Which workflow should run?
→ Which action should an AI agent take next?

Basically, instead of asking your biggest AI model to do everything, you start giving different parts of the workflow to different models.

I think this is going to become a pretty important way of building AI workflows. That’s what will make building AI workflows lean and cost efficient. Most of us never consider the cost behind building AI workflows, that should be thought about like how costing is important at a steel manufacturing plant.

We shouldn’t be using ChatGPT or Claude for everything.

text:
Jev is a useful reminder for GTM Engineers

Not every AI problem needs a chatbot.

TypeSafe AI's Jev is getting a lot of attention because it works differently from GPT or Claude.

It doesn't write answers at all.
It returns fast typed decisions with a confidence score.

That matters because GTM workflows are full of small judgment calls:
→ Is this account ICP fit?
→ Is this lead worth routing to sales?
→ Is this signal strong enough to act on?
→ Is this title a buyer, influencer, or irrelevant?
→ Should this account go to research, nurture, or ignore?

A lot of teams send all of these to a frontier LLM.
It works, but it's often slow and expensive for a simple yes/no.

A GTM stack could look like:

Formula = deterministic rules
Jev = fast decisions
LLM = deep research or content
Human = approval for risky actions
CRM = source of truth

And the confidence score is the part GTMEs should care about:

High confidence → auto-route
Low confidence → send to an LLM or a human

Jev is still in early access, so I'd test it on accounts you've already labeled before trusting it in production.

The point isn't "Jev replaces GPT."

The point is:
GTMEs need to stop using the most powerful model for every tiny decision.

The future GTM stack will probably be less about one AI model, and more about routing the right task to the right intelligence.

Hey friends! Some of you know I build https://wildpocket.com/ as a passion project to share my love of nature. WildPocket has local species data for 2.5 million places in the US! At that volume, errors slip through. This is a large dataset, and the hard QA question of "is this location useful?" takes semantic (natural language) thinking.

This week I tried TypeSafe's Jev on it. If you haven't seen Jev, think of a multi-class classifier that you configure in plain English. It sits in the middle ground between code, which is fast and cheap but can't judge meaning, and an LLM, which is great with language but slow and expensive. It has an error rate (like any model). TypeSafe calls this a "System One" model. 

I asked Jev to look at 20,000 random places. Total cost $0.95, about 3 minutes to complete. It flagged "places" named Wild Turkey (a wildlife sign), Welcome to Utah (a road sign) and Haunted Picnic Table 29. Accuracy was on par with Claude Haiku, which is ~7-34x the cost and much slower. Jev is cheap and fast enough that setting up this QA pipeline was worth the effort - I can justify re-running it.

Lessons learned:
  - Input tokens add up at scale. I spent almost 2x my original budget because I kept adding questions that looked interesting (Jev can answer many questions from one input). I probably would have been better off with a single "flag anything odd" question.
  - Most hosted LLM APIs rate-limit hard enough that big parallel jobs crawl. Jev let me run 100+ requests a second without hitting a limit.

Happy to share the setup if anyone wants to try this on their own data.

text:
An AI agent’s next command could find a vulnerability or cause an outage. Before it runs, a guardrail has to make a decision: allow or block.  

We wanted to understand where decision models fit into that process.

Can they catch harmful actions quickly enough to check an agent’s next step?

We compared JEV with Grok 4.7 on 200 synthetic cases, repeated three times per model. That’s 1,200 checks covering data deletion, credential leaks, service disruption and actions outside the agreed scope.
We measured three things:

Accuracy: Grok made more accurate decisions on the checks it completed, although some requests timed out.

Speed: JEV’s median response was 324 milliseconds, compared with 16.44 seconds for Grok.

Cost: About $0.084 per 1,000 checks for JEV versus $3.79 for Grok, using published pricing and reported usage respectively. These are different calculations, not verified invoice totals.

author_headline: Researcher @ Applied Compute | Berkeley AI Research
text:
We're adding reward-hacking monitors into AC2. Every RL run gets checked for cheating, and our research agent, Ari, automatically investigates the flags.  

After a model discovers an exploit, it can become its default strategy within a few training steps. We used to hunt for reward hacking manually, reading traces and running one-off agent queries. This was error prone and didn't scale. We decided to automate detection instead.

After each training step, a cheap LLM judge scores sampled traces for reward hacking. Scores above a threshold trigger Ari to investigate run-wide patterns and ping the owner in Slack. In a recent Kimi K3 post-train, the model shimmed the ip package to fake a network route and pass a test. Ari caught it, and we rolled back to a pre-hack checkpoint.

We optimized the monitor prompts for partial AUROC under 10% FPR rather than F1 or full AUROC. Past that, the monitor flags so many benign traces that you stop reading them. In practice, we calibrate the threshold at 2% FPR.

We benchmarked DeepSeek v4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash, GPT 6 Luna, and Jev on real reward hacks from our own runs. At a 2% false positive rate, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash on low reasoning gets nearly the same recall as Luna High at less than half the cost per classification.

text:
I won a silver medal in Kaggle’s Biohub competition and became a Kaggle Competition Expert for the first time! 🥈

Scientists use 3D microscopy to study cells, but making sense of those massive images still takes researchers a lot of time.
The Biohub competition on Kaggle asked us to automate part of that work: find cells in microscope videos, follow their movement, and recognize when one divides into two. This helps researchers build a family tree of the cells.

I started with studying publicly available models, combined predictions, corrected for movement between images, and improved how cells were recognized over time. 
Only some cells and connections were labelled in the training data. Unmarked didn’t mean wrong, so I had to be careful about what I taught the models. In a check on 32 training videos, 37 of 48 missed divisions already had the parent and both daughters detected. Often, one daughter had been assigned to the wrong parent. The cells were there. I needed to reconsider their relationships. I kept the deep learning models for finding cells and suggesting connections. A smaller machine learning model then examined 110 measurements around a possible division: brightness changes, movement, distance, and whether the daughters already appeared separately before the split. Another algorithm compared possible family trees across five consecutive images. Reassigning a daughter meant accounting for the parent losing it too. It could accept a division, keep separate tracks, leave a connection undecided, or preserve the existing result. I also found that later position adjustments could make the correct parent look less likely. I used original positions to decide relationships and refined the final positions separately. 

Some ideas recovered more divisions but added too many false ones. Others changed thousands of positions and gained nothing. I kept an experiment ledger and checked improvements and new mistakes.

Throughout this work, I orchestrated multiple AI agents for research, experiment preparation, coding and review. These tasks continued in parallel while GPU experiments ran.

JEV helped with quick decisions about what to test next and when to submit. Ponytail helped keep the code minimal and understandable. Experiments ran in Colab through Docker; the final solution ran offline on Kaggle.

A San Francisco AI startup just raised a $40M seed round for a model that answers with a choice, not a sentence!

The company is TypeSafe AI and the model is Jev and the founder is Diogo Almeida, a former OpenAI researcher.

So, you give Jev a list of options, it picks one and tells you how confident it is. Developers around the world are already using it for different use cases.

TypeSafe charges $0.042 per million input tokens and its output is free.

At that price, what would TypeSafe need to reach $40M a year?

About 950 trillion input tokens annually!
That's 2.6 trillion a day, 
or around 84,000 decisions every second
if you assume 360 tokens per decision (one third-party test measured that on a routing task).

And that's just revenue. TypeSafe hasn't said what it costs to serve the model, so nobody outside knows how much of it is profit.

So, could 2.6 trillion tokens a day be captured from existing workloads, or created from new ones? Each decision earns TypeSafe about $0.0000151, so cheap pricing has to create a huge amount of new demand. Nobody has shown that yet.

Then there's competition. I think Jev looks more like a capability than a product category. If the demand is real, a bigger lab could build something similar and charge less. 

Maybe it wouldn't be a quick add, since Jev is a different kind of model, but even the threat puts pressure on TypeSafe's pricing. They need a lead that lasts, or a different business model. 

We are yet to see where this goes.

author_headline: Co-Founder & CTO @ Stealth | Cybersecurity x AI | Ex-Fortinet & Check Point
text:
Your AI agent shouldn't be the one deciding when it's safe enough to act.
⠀
ByteByteGo mapped 9 places to use fast decision models like Jev. Three of them are security controls:
⠀
Guardrails: catch prompt injection before it reaches the LLM.
Tool-call gating: decide if an agent's tool call is allowed, needs approval, or gets denied.
Confidence gate: the classifier sets the thresholds, not the LLM. Low confidence goes to a human.
⠀
Picture an agent that can issue refunds. A $20 refund at 0.95 confidence? Let it act. A $5,000 refund at 0.6? That goes to a person, every time.
⠀
That decision shouldn't live inside the LLM.
⠀
But a fast classifier is a first filter, not your only defense. Attackers will test it, and anything that can be classified can be evaded.
⠀
Use it as one layer. Never the only one.

author_headline: Co-Founder & CTO, Simbian (We’re hiring!)
text:
In the last two weeks, three labs shipped the same strange idea: an AI model that makes a decision instead of writing text.

TypeSafe's Jev. OpenAI's Decisions API. Databricks' ai_decide. Hand any of them a pile of state and a typed question, and it returns a decision, a probability or a score, in a few hundred milliseconds for a fraction of a cent. No prose, nothing to parse.

It's a strange thing to get excited about, and it lands harder in security than almost anywhere.

The whole job of a SOC is to attribute intent to a flood of events: was this 2 a.m. directory read malicious, or just Tuesday? Intent is the one thing no sensor records, and judging it has always been slow and costly, so we only ever judge the handful of events a detector already flagged.

Which means the dumbest component in your SOC decides what the smartest one is allowed to look at.

A cheap, fast decision calls that arrangement into question. If judging intent gets nearly free, where should judgment happen?

There is an obvious move once you ask. I'm not sure it's the right one, and the piece spends as much time on where it breaks as on where it helps:

- why "judge everything" is a promise you can't fully keep
- why a model that reads attacker-written fields can be argued with
- why a calibrated score is least trustworthy on the novel attacks you built it to catch

More of an interesting problem than a prescription. Full piece below.

text:
Cloudflare just launched Clef, its first in-house AI models, and says they beat Jev on speed. Here's what you need to know.

Clef is the first model family trained by Cloudflare's Workers AI team. There are two decision models, Clef and Clef-flash. Cloudflare says both top the benchmarks for quality and latency. It also launched a new RL fine-tuning platform alongside them.

Decision models don't write text. They take a state and a schema of typed questions and return decisions, for routing, sorting and classification. Clef is a 27B multimodal model built on a Qwen backbone. It uses a non-autoregressive, prefill-only scoring approach. Jev, from TypeSafe AI, is the model that started this wave.

Cloudflare says Clef leads the evals on the Hugging Face Jev Decision Index. It claims it pushes the pareto frontier on both quality and latency. A live leaderboard and demo are up on a Workers AI site.

Clef is hosted on Workers AI and the weights are on Hugging Face. They are open source under Apache 2.0, so you can run them locally. One early user already ran clef-flash on an M5 Max. Cloudflare also says Replicate's Cog work is now part of how you fine-tune and redeploy models on Workers AI.

Key numbers:
- clef-flash is around 13x faster than Jev
- Trained for 256k context, 64k hosted
- Vision encoder, so it classifies images as well as text
- Drop-in compatible with the Jev API
- License: Apache 2.0

The race is on, and Cloudflare is the first big infrastructure player to ship open decision models that claim to beat Jev.

author_headline: I dig through AI research so you don’t have to.
text:
A 21-YEAR-OLD CHINESE DEVELOPER CUT HIS CLAUDE BILL BY 87% AND ACCIDENTALLY EXPOSED HOW LAZILY MOST AI AGENTS ARE BUILT.

A 21-year-old developer from Shenzhen only noticed the problem because he finally opened his bill at the end of the month and looked at where the money was actually going. His agent worked fine, the team was happy, tasks were getting done faster than before, so nobody had any reason to touch it. But once he went through the logs step by step, the pattern was almost ridiculous: Claude kept getting pulled into decisions that ended a few seconds later with one tiny internal action. Should the agent keep reading this file? Is this actually an error? Which tool should it call? Should the search continue? Is it time to escalate? The strongest model in the stack was repeatedly burning context and reasoning on decisions the user would never even see.

He spent the night going through the logs and by morning realized that most of the cost had very little to do with how difficult the agent's actual work was. The money was disappearing because Claude had become the default answer to every internal question. So he didn't change the model itself. He put a separate decision layer in front of it and made that layer decide whether an expensive Claude call was needed at all. Within a day, the bill dropped 87% while the product behaved almost exactly the same.
That's where this stops being a story about one developer in Shenzhen. The industry spends months arguing about token prices, context windows, new pricing tiers, and which frontier model is currently the smartest, while a huge amount of agent infrastructure may have a much simpler problem sitting one layer above all of that. We're paying expensive models because we made them part of every step by default, including the steps that never needed frontier-level intelligence in the first place.

If you're already using Claude, Codex, or your own agents, the most expensive question may not be which model you should use next. It may be how many of your current model calls should never have existed at all.

JEV ISN'T TRYING TO REPLACE CLAUDE. IT'S TRYING TO STOP YOU FROM CALLING CLAUDE FOR NO REASON.

text:
I'm sure a lot of you have heard of Jev. Well, I also decided to play with it over the weekend.
I built a quick routing tool between two models ("small": Qwen3-4B, "large": Qwen3-32B) and tested it on the HumanEval benchmark (OpenAI, via Hugging Face): a series of short coding problems.

The baselines were 70% solve rate if I always chose the large model, 73% if I always chose the small model, and 86% for the oracle (the best-case scenario). So there was room to improve.
At first, I had Jev try to predict the difficulty of the problem and route it to the large model if it was hard, and the small model if not. If you know a bit about Jev, I used the "Choice" mode for this.

It didn't lead to any improvement over the baselines.
Then I had the small model solve every problem, with Jev deciding ("Noul" mode) whether it thought the answer was correct. If not, the problem was sent to the large model. With a few improvements, I got to a final solve rate of 84%, a big improvement over the baselines.

author_headline: GTM Engineer @ Parsec | MBA Candidate, Rice Business
text:
The most exciting thing about working for Parsec is all of the things we are working on. The hardest thing is keeping my mouth shut. Today I get to finally announce TOD. 

Most support agents spend a frontier LLM call on every turn, even when the turn is just look up this order or start this return. TOD is a small model that takes those turns instead. 

Each turn it does two jobs. It extracts the facts the action needs (order ID, item, address, amounts) from the conversation, and it picks the tool call from the actions your assistant already has. It never writes free text and never invents a tool. 

When it is confident, it serves the turn and your LLM is never called. When it is not, it hands the turn back untouched. Every write (cancel, exchange, return) is offered once, read back in plain language, and executed only on the customers explicit yes. 

Measured on tau2-bench retail, on customers the model never saw in training: 

- The right tool is in its shortlist 96.6% of the time, even on slates of 52+ options
- 84.5% pick accuracy on held-out decisions 
- 94% exact match on the arguments those tools need, against a frontier reference 

Pricing is a flat $0.30 per 1,000 decisions, no matter how long the conversation runs. 

We are still measuring end-to-end solve rate, and I will share it when it lands.

text:
Why the new Jev model matters for information workers.

The new Jev model, by startup TypeSafe AI, took the world — or at least Twitter — by storm. 

It's actually not just hype. Heres why it matters:

Extremely low latency (so you can use it in real-time).
Big context (so you can give it a lot of information to incorporate).
Extremely cheap (so you can use it for even the most minute tasks).
Easy to configure.
Much more control (so you define the possible outputs ahead of time, versus allowing an LLM to freestyle).

Jev is a classifier. You give it something to look at and a set of possible values, and it chooses from those values.

For instance, say youre using an LLM to compose and send responses to your emails. It has access to your personal information. A scammer reaches out asking for your social security number, and your helpful little agent drafts a response with those dangerous nine digits.

Now put Jev between the draft and the send button. You define the possible outputs: send, block, or flag for review. Jev checks the outgoing email for private information and chooses one. Your system can then block or flag the message before those precious nine digits leave you exposed.

You could couple a powerful LLM w a model like Jev so you can check what its doing as it goes. An extra gate that previously wasnt practical from a cost or latency perspective.

Thats just one example. Every outgoing email, every network request, every action an agent takes in production could get another check. There are all these little classification tasks where it previously wasnt worth the expense or the effort of setting something up. Jev makes them fast, cheap, and easy enough to put in places where you previously wouldnt have bothered.

Josh and I discuss Jev and more on the latest episode of Vibes and Benchmarks. Link to full ep in comments.

→ 0.8B model (5× smaller): accuracy of 47% to 90%

→ Created a table of 226 exercises and rendered them in my own logging style, including typos like dumbell and latpulldown
→ Trained each model for 15–20 minutes on a single H100, costing only a few dollars in GPU time

author_headline: Senior Manager, AI @ Loopio | Enterprise RAG, agentic memory & knowledge graphs | Ex-Head of AI @ O.XYZ | Founder: MyLabStory | Author: Lazy Data Science Guide
text:
AnyJev can turn any large language model into a Jev-like System One model, without fine-tuning.

I've been digging into Nokia Applied Research's AnyJev. The useful bit: stop asking the LLM to generate a classification answer, and treat it as a frozen decision engine instead.

Most pipelines still look like LLM → write some text → parse it → map to a class. That works, but generation is often unnecessary, the scores are not always trustworthy, and the answer can flip when you reorder the options.

AnyJev walks that problem in three levels. L0 starts from next-token scores over the allowed answers, cycles option order so first-slot bias does not win, and corrects for label prior, all without training examples for that question. L1 keeps that readout and adds temperature calibration once you have a few hundred labeled examples, so a predicted 0.8 is closer to meaning eighty percent. L2 is the part that stuck with me: freeze the LLM, take a hidden state from a middle layer, fit a tiny LDA/ridge head on about 100–300 labeled examples, and you can early-exit instead of running the whole transformer. So the big model is a shared semantic backbone, and each decision task gets a small head on top.

It’s been a month since I talked about AI stuff—oops, sorry, SI 😂

This post was sitting in my drafts for a while, but here we are!

Let's talk about the system 1 model (Jev)

Initially, I assumed Jev was just another new LLM crushing ChatGPT or Claude across benchmark metrics, which is why it was trending everywhere. Because of that assumption, I didn't dig too deep at first. But once I actually started researching, I realized it was different like jimmy guy—and it is totally different from jimmy guy 😵.
In my last post, I talked about the jimmy guy and hardware-level inference speed. While hardware acceleration gets raw speed, speed alone doesn't guarantee accuracy. That’s where software comes in—and where setups like Tallas + AMD combos might bridge the gap in the future. We need both to deliver the sweet spot: Speed + Correctness.

Enter Jev 💡
I originally assumed Jev was a software-level tweak to sit in that sweet spot. Turns out, it belongs to a completely different category with a unique use case—one that becomes vital in the Agentic Era.

Here is how simply I break down the difference:
LLMs + RLHF: Auto-regressive generation. They generate the next word sequentially, optimizing for human-like.

Jev + RLDF: Non-auto-regressive. It doesn't hunt for sequential words or bluff extra text to keep user attention. Instead, it evaluates scenarios, classifies options, and outputs direct probabilities for decision-making.

"Can't LLMs just do this anyway?" 😏
Technically, yes. we can make an LLM do this if you feed it strict schemas, heavy prompt engineering, and force it to output confidence scores. But it’s slow, expensive, and prone to hallucinations.
Jev shines here because its core job is decision-making and classification. It’s fast, cheap, and accurate (depending on tuning).

The catch: Jev isn't here to replace LLMs. We have to pick the right tool for the job:
Need complex reasoning, deep thinking, or creative generation? LLMs.
Need fast, high-confidence decision-making and classification? Jev

The combo of both will be more efficient.

A perfect use case for these System 1 models like jev and laya? 
Agentic tool calling.

What about ultra-fast inference in auto-regressive models?
I originally thought Jev was the answer 🫩, but that mystery remains unsolved for now. Still yet to discover.

author_headline: Digital social researcher | Lecturer at UC | Director of MonitorSocial.cl
text:
Mucho se está hablando de Jev estos días, como un nuevo tipo de LLM: más rápido, barato y especializado en tomar decisiones. Para mi, su principal interés no está en todo eso, sino en su potencial para el desarrollo de software que oriente rápidamente a organizaciones en urgencias sobre su entorno social.

Jev es una especie de eslabón perdido, y en verdad creo que llena una brecha.

Hasta hace poco, los especialistas en ciencia social computacional tenían dos grandes opciones para analizar textos no estructurados.

1. El aprendizaje automático (usualmente modelos supervisados para procesar lenguaje). Estos modelo tienen un excelente costo y baja latencia computacional, pero necesitan un entrenamiento importante con datos clasificados manualmente. Si necesitas medir variables finas como conflictividad política o matices emocionales en una conversación, y no tienes miles de datos bien etiquetados, no te sirve.

2. Los LLMs (GPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.): capturan el contexto inmediatamente sin necesitar entrenamiento previo, pero usarlos para clasificar o estimar probabilidades suele ser ineficiente. Son lentos, caros y obligan a lidiar con errores de formato o alucinaciones.

Lo interesante de Jev (de la empresa TypeSafe AI) es que atacó justo esa brecha. Al funcionar como un modelo de toma de decisiones directo y no como un generador de texto, no produce prosa ni alucinación. Uno le entrega un texto y hace preguntas cerradas con salidas especificas (opciones, escalas o probabilidades booleanas).

Esto tiene implicaciones muy interesantes para el software de análisis social. A diferencia del aprendizaje automático, nos permite clasificar y asignar probabilidades sobre variables complejas sin necesidad de entrenar o afinar un modelo específico desde cero. No necesitas gran cantidad de trabajo manual.

Y a diferencia de los LLMs, reduce errores operativos, como respuestas fuera de esquema o variaciones en la salida.

Además, retorna probabilidades calibradas, lo que permite conocer y gestionar el nivel de error. Esto lo hace una alternativa más viable que los LLMs para investigación científica.

Sin duda es una alternativa útil para responder preguntas exactas sobre datos sociales (sentimientos, emociones o intensidad de conflicto) en escenarios donde no existe un buen modelo supervisado y donde levantar una muestra de entrenamiento no es viable.

A mi juicio no reemplaza al aprendizaje automático tradicional en volúmenes masivos de datos estructurados, ni a los LLMs para tareas de redacción o razonamiento largo. Pero podría ser una excelente capa intermedia de clasificación en tiempo real.

Para plataformas que clasifican información todo el tiempo parece una buena idea: más barato que los LLM, y sin la necesidad de entrenar un modelo demasiado específico. 

¿Alguien por acá lo está probando directamente en plataformas?

A New Jersey school district is listed on LinkedIn under Retail Luxury Goods & Jewelry. An FDIC-insured bank is filed under Construction.

Those were two of the slides at Clay in NYC last night, a Clay Club NY evening at Clay's office hosted by Andreas Wernicke and Clay's community team ( Munnawar Hashim, Siya Verma🦄✨, Shriya Nevatia). 🦾Eric Nowoslawski (Growth Engine X) dry-ran his Sculpt talk on building the perfect company list, then took 30 minutes of questions.

His opening claim: bad lists aren't the data provider's fault. Industry labels are self-reported, often by whoever set up the company page, so filters fail in both directions at once. They miss real fits (the jewelry-store school district) and they pull in junk. A plain Banking + United States filter returned 16,895 companies; about 10,500 of them weren't banks.

His fix inverts the usual order. Use your customers only to learn which labels they actually use. Pull every one of those industries and keywords, wide on purpose. Then judge every single row with one yes/no question on a cheap decision model, i.e. Jev. His published runs put 900,000+ judgments at about $12.

The receipts, scored against public registries (standard LinkedIn filters → his process):
→ SEC-registered advisers: 31% → 92%
→ New Jersey school districts: 54% → 80%
→ FDIC banks: 79% → 88%

From the seller's seat, here's what I'd take to a CRO:

→ Coverage is a measurable number now, and it belongs on the planning deck next to TAM. Wherever a registry exists (banks, advisers, schools, licensed trades), you can know it instead of guessing.

→ The cost of judging moved from headcount to rounding error. The scarce input is the ICP question itself. Who writes it, who signs off on the edge cases, and how often it gets revisited is a GTM leadership decision, not an ops ticket.

→ Over-pulling stops being waste. Pulling five times the list and judging every row costs less than the rep hours spent on accounts that were never a fit.

One more market signal from the Q&A: even Clay's heaviest power user drifted toward building outside Clay this year, and Clay Audiences is what pulled that work back. Tool loyalty is now earned feature by feature, which is exactly how buyers should want it.

The finding got cheap. The judging is the job now. If you own a TAM: run it against a registry before you trust the filter, and tell me what coverage you got.

author_headline: Senior Full-Stack Engineer | Building Scalable Web & AI Platforms | AI Engineering, Agentic Systems, Distributed Systems
text:
Bounded decisions are becoming an AI primitive. But what happens when they're confidently wrong?

Recently, I ran Jev against Claude Sonnet 5 on 100 frozen routing cases:
Jev: 91/100, Claude Sonnet 5: 90/100, Confidence-gated hybrid: 92/100
At n=100, those differences are within noise. The interesting part wasn't the ranking. It was the failures.

Since then, the decision-model space has moved quickly.
Laya introduced an open-weight approach to bounded decisions, and OpenAI introduced the Decisions API for tasks such as classification, routing, and action selection.

Different approaches, but a similar contract is emerging:
State + bounded choices → decision + probabilities
That may be the bigger shift. The emerging primitive isn't a particular model. It's the contract.

For bounded problems, this can be cleaner than:
Context → LLM → generated output → parse → validate → act
But a cleaner decision interface doesn't solve another problem my experiment exposed:

Who verifies the decision?

I saw three patterns:
Correction: Jev was uncertain and wrong → Claude corrected it.
Regression: Jev was correct → Claude changed it to the wrong route.
Shared error: both models chose the same wrong route.
The clearest case was RC-048. Jev chose the wrong route with 0.99 confidence, so a confidence-gated fallback would never trigger. When I asked Claude separately, it chose the same wrong route.

Two boundaries became clear:
Confidence ≠ Correctness 
Confident errors can pass straight through a threshold-based cascade.

Fallback ≠ Verification 
A second model gives you another decision. It doesn't automatically give you an independent check.

Verification may require something different: deterministic constraints, external ground truth, application policy, or human review. 

So I think bounded decision models raise two architectural questions:
1. Should this step be a generation problem at all?
2. What checks the answer when the model is confidently wrong? 

Decision models can make bounded decisions faster and cleaner. They don't make those decisions verified.

Next: Laya on the same frozen 100 cases, and OpenAI Decisions once I have preview access.

Clef is a 27B multimodal model built on a Chinese open-source model called Qwen. 
This trend started by the release of Jev, a model developed by TypeSafe AI, is considered the pioneer of this wave of decision models.

author_headline: Founder at Haha Systems Limited | Researcher in Artificial Intelligence, Information Security
text:
A lot of people have been raving about TypeSafe AI's #Jev and decision models like it lately, and rightly so. They add a really cool and surprisingly powerful kind of capability for very low cost and extremely low latency.

I haven't had much time to play with it until today, so I’ve been building a tiny experimental world called JevLife (similar in spirit to JaxLife, see comments) to explore how much behaviour can emerge from very simple decision systems.

The setup is deliberately minimal: a couple of simple agents in a Godot-based simulation, a handful of world objects like Tree, Rock, etc., and a Jev/System One decision model choosing between actions based on the agent’s current state.

Tonight, I worked on the first real physiological loop:
body state → need → decision → action → body state

For now, the only need is hydration. As hydration falls, thirst rises. The agent can "see" world objects in a short range and has basic actions like "wander", "wait", or "drink".

The interesting part is what I didn’t program (and yeah I actually wrote the code for this!)

I never explicitly told the agent:
- “drink when thirsty”
- “stop drinking when hydrated”
- “rest after drinking”
- “stay near useful resources”

It discovered the pond by wandering, chose to drink because it was thirsty, kept drinking as thirst remained high, then stopped once hydration was restored.

At that point, I expected it to go back to wandering around, discovering all the wonders of its 2D flatland like the Tree and the Stone. Instead of wandering off aimlessly, it decided that waiting by the pond was the best option. Maybe doomscrolling on JevTok or something.

As it started to get thirsty again, drinking that lovely pond water became the most attractive option again. It actively chose to wait at the pond rather than move away.

Zoomed out, the behaviour looked surprisingly intelligent:
find water → satisfy need → remain near resource → reuse resource

There’s an obvious caveat here: this does not mean the agent is explicitly thinking “I should stay here because I’ll be thirsty later.” At least not yet. It may simply be making a sequence of local decisions where waiting makes more sense than pointless wandering.

But that’s exactly why I find it interesting!

A behavioural pattern emerged that was never represented as an explicit rule.

The next step is memory: allowing agents to remember where resources were after they leave the location, and eventually, being able to communicate those memories to each other.

It’s still very early, but this is exactly the kind of thing I wanted JevLife to explore: how far can you get by combining simple internal pressures, perception, memory, and action selection before you need anything resembling explicit planning?

(And yes, the current research subject affectionately known as "JevBoi" is basically a small white blob who loves a bevvie or five)

If your enterprise is still relying solely on open ended GenAI for application logic, your architecture is already at zero.

The last two weeks have fundamentally shifted how we build AI systems. We saw TypeSafe AI  Jev model emerge from stealth, only for OpenAI to immediately counter at DevDay with their new Decisions API (powered by GPT-6 Luna).

But let’s cut through the "Decision AI" marketing hype. What are we actually looking at? In reality, it is just a highly optimized, bounded classifier.

For the last two years, we’ve been forcing generative models to make deterministic choices prompting them, praying they output the right JSON schema, and parsing the results. It was slow, expensive, and fragile.

Decision AI flips this. It takes a focused state and a strict, developer-defined list of outcomes, and returns a single typed decision in ~150 milliseconds.

Why does this matter for Enterprise Architecture?
The End of Parsing: The pipeline shrinks from ⁠Prompt -> Gen Text -> Parse -> Schema Validation -> Action⁠ to simply ⁠State -> Bounded Decision -> Policy Check -> Action⁠.

 Multi-Agent Governance: If you are building agentic workflows, these models act as the perfect, high-speed supervisor layer to route tasks reliably between sub-agents.
 Semantic Judgment Meets Deterministic Code: The model judges the intent; the code owns the authority.

Generative AI writes the email. Decision AI dictates which queue the email goes to, which agent handles it, and whether it requires human escalation.
Stop building wrappers around open-ended text. Start building deterministic, decision-driven architectures.

Jev vs LLM: Are we building AI that predicts words — or understands what comes next?

Large Language Models (LLMs) have transformed AI by becoming extremely good at predicting the next token.

Give an LLM:

“The cat sat on the…”

and it can predict:

“mat.”

That simple principle, scaled to billions of parameters and massive datasets, has produced remarkably capable systems.

But there is another direction worth watching: Jev.

Instead of focusing primarily on predicting the next piece of text, Jev explores AI around learning structured representations of the world and reasoning over them.

LLMs

→ Learn from massive amounts of language
→ Predict tokens
→ Generate text, code, and other sequences
→ Extremely powerful for language-centric tasks

Jev

→ Focuses more on representations and predictive structure
→ Attempts to model relationships between concepts rather than only surface-level sequences
→ Can be viewed as part of the broader movement toward more world-model-like AI

The key question isn't:

“Will Jev replace LLMs?”

It's:

“Can AI move beyond predicting what comes next to learning representations of what is happening?”

LLMs have shown us how far scale + data + prediction can take us.

The next generation of AI may combine that capability with systems that can build richer internal representations, reason over them, and interact with the world.

We may not be looking at LLM vs Jev.

We may be looking at:

LLM + representation learning + world models + reasoning

👉 How does an AI Agent decide what is actually worth remembering?
Think about a normal human conversation.
You don't remember every sentence.
You remember the important facts, relationships, events, and context — and bring them back when they're relevant.

AI Agent memory needs to work more like that.
That's what I found interesting when looking at the JEV approach to agent memory.
Instead of making the LLM responsible for every memory decision, the architecture separates the responsibilities.

🔴 Before
Query → LLM → LLM → LLM → LLM → Answer
The LLM is repeatedly involved in questions like:
• What should I remember?
• How is this connected?
• What should I retrieve?
• Do I have enough information?
More generation can mean more tokens + more latency.

🟢 With JEV
Query → Memory → JEV → Relevant Evidence → LLM → Answer
The memory layer takes more responsibility for organizing and retrieving information, allowing the LLM to focus on reasoning.
The memory can be viewed through different dimensions:
🧩 Semantic — What does this memory mean?
⏱️ Temporal — When did it happen?
🔗 Causal — What caused what?
👤 Entity — Who or what is involved?

And the overall flow becomes:
Write → Organize → Retrieve → Verify → Score → Reason
💡 The part I find most interesting
The LLM doesn't necessarily have to do everything.
It can focus on the part where it adds the most value:
Reasoning.

Calls to LLMs are pretty common in software systems these days. Write a reply to an email, classify a customer's complaint, decide what to do with a refund request, etc. All typical use cases, and all fine until you notice that half of them are not really "generate some text" problems, which is sort of a big part of what LLMs are for.

Take a bog standard event-driven document pipeline: S3 → Lambda with Textract and an LLM classify call → SQS → downstream processing. You're asking an LLM to do something it's reasonably good at (reasoning), but you end up with a lot of prompting, slow responses, and a bill that gets ugly at high volume.

If you already know a document can only be an invoice, purchase order, or contract, wouldn't it be easier to use something specifically designed to classify into those categories and not an LLM you need to feed yet another JSON template and a lot of CAPITAL LETTERS WITH STRICT INSTRUCTIONS to get its response in the right shape?

Well... Jev launched recently. It's a "System One Model" (yeah, me neither). They describe it as a "smart if statement" though, which I think is a useful way of thinking about it. It's  a specialised probabilistic decision model (not text generator) for cases where the possible outputs are known in advance.

The AI isn't running the workflow here, because that's often overkill and really expensive at scale. You still need to give Jev some context and define the output schema you want, but it's very well set up for machine to machine comms. As for the rest of your code, you still own the branching, the thresholds, and the "what do we do when we're not sure?" paths, and a model like Jev just gets you a programmatic response to your "what kind of doc is this?" question really quickly.

How quickly?

Up to 75x faster than an LLM, and an example on their site has it 238x cheaper than Claude. I don't really write about AI (it's a bit crowded!) and prefer IAC, python, and product stuff, but this is a bit of a step change.
