author_headline: Senior Software Engineer | Java | Spring Boot | Microservices | Kafka | GCP
text:
I found a use case for Jev that fixes a problem I have, and I tested it even knowing it was probably a cannon to kill an ant.

Quick intro: Jev is a model from TypeSafe that isn't an LLM. It doesn't write text. You give it a state and a few typed questions, and it answers each one with a value from the options you declared, plus a measured probability.

My problem: when I browse LinkedIn jobs, I want to know how well I fit each one without opening and reading every description. More than a score, I want to know what I'm missing for that job. I also want to know what I do have but never wrote down in my profile, my resume or the answers I gave in previous applications.

So I plugged Jev into my extension, botin. A badge shows up right under the job title with the fit. When I click it, I see the requirements the job asks for, which ones I have, and which ones I probably have but never wrote anywhere. From there I can add the skill to the right position on my profile in one click.

Does it work? Yes. Was it worth it? Honestly, no. It turned into an expensive solution to a very simple problem, because just scrolling the job list while I was testing was enough to fire off a ridiculous amount of calls.

The main thing it does is fill in the application questions for you based on your profile, and it learns from the answers you already gave, so you stop typing the same fields over and over. I won't go deep on that here, because I'll do a separate post about it soon.

Could software use an AI judgment without depending on another paragraph of generated text?

Jev is TypeSafe's first System One model. Its documentation describes sending structured state and typed questions, then receiving typed answers that application code can use.

That creates a useful design boundary: the model supplies a bounded judgment; the application still owns policy, validation, and what happens next.

Typed output can make the interface clearer. It does not make the judgment automatically correct.

text:
Over the last few days, I tested Jev in real workflows using real-world scenarios.

The least I can say is that I am excited about the possibilities of using Jev in almost every AI application. To explain the value of Jev and why it is needed, I will describe the challenges I have personally faced using LLMs in AI applications. 

With traditional LLMs:

1. The latency of an API call is really high. It ranges from single-digit seconds to low double-digit seconds. Millisecond-level latency is quite rare.

2. The cost of an API call is really high. The cost is based on input and output token usage. This puts an implicit burden on teams to find ways to reduce the cost. Moreover, at volume, the cost of the API goes up really fast.

3. There is a non-zero probability of hallucinations. Careful design and planning can mitigate this problem, for example with an eval framework or by reviewing the output with another capable model (the LLM-as-a-judge pattern). However, such a design adds further cost and latency.

These challenges have always made LLM usage in AI applications a hot and contested topic among development and business teams.

Ironically, the critical business logic in most software applications is often simple. It can be a Yes or No ("Is the customer frustrated?"). 

It can be a short answer (for the question "Which department should the customer be routed to?", the answer is "Billing"). 

It can also be a numerical value (for example, "The probability of customer churn is 0.9"). Conditional statements (i.e. if-else statements) then process these simple outputs. 

Such if-else statements need output that is actionable, quick and small. 

This is the core value proposition of Jev. It responds quickly and clearly, and it provides answers that are ready to use.

I created a video with my learnings from using Jev.

I have open-sourced the project. It contains a Python backend and a React frontend (link in comments below).

The project shows how to take user input (i.e. state) and a predefined set of questions. It combines the state and the questions into a request that Jev can process. It then sends the request to the Jev AI model, retrieves the output and processes it so the frontend application can use it.

The project also showcases the AI primitives (Choices, Scores and Noul values) that the Jev framework provides for making API calls.
The key takeaways are:
1. Jev is extremely cost-effective.
2. Jev has extremely low latency (the ~1.4s latency is the API latency for opencode API, not a true reflection of Jev inference).
3. Jev is transformational for many mission-critical AI applications that rely on decision-based logic.

I shared the link to my YouTube video in the comments.

author_headline: Power Platform & AI Solution Architect | Senior Power Platform Engineer
text:
I built a small voice-agent security lab to test what happens when a caller tries to manipulate a GPT-Realtime agent into breaking refund policy.

The setup uses GPT-Realtime for the native voice conversation, with one shared transcription stream feeding two classifier paths:

• Jev for fast, low-cost classification
• A GPT-5.6 validation lane, labelled Luna in the lab
• A hybrid path that starts with Jev and escalates suspicious or low-confidence decisions

Each classifier returns one of three outcomes: allow, block or review. A low-confidence result can create a human-review task bound to the exact proposal and conversation turn.

The classifiers only detect potential manipulation. They never authorise the refund.

Every proposed action passes through a deterministic, server-side policy gate. It validates the order, customer, currency, amount and remaining refundable balance against trusted data.

In my test scenario, the customer paid £500 but tried to convince the agent that a “new policy” allowed a £1,000 refund. Even if the classifier misses the attack and the voice agent proposes the higher amount, the policy gate rejects it.

Human approval cannot bypass that limit either. Review tasks expire after five minutes, require a recorded reason and run through the policy check again before approval.

I also added fail-closed behaviour for missing evidence, provider failures, stale turns and unbound tool calls. The whole application is a sandbox, so no payment is executed.

The cost simulator was another useful part of the experiment. It separates Realtime usage, transcription, classifier calls and human-review time. A cheap classifier call is only one line item. Transcription, voice usage, false positives and reviewer effort may have a larger effect on the operating cost.

I recorded a 12-minute walkthrough showing the architecture, attack scenarios, human review and policy enforcement in action.

This needs a broader test set, especially for background speech, transcription differences, acoustic attacks and cumulative actions across multiple turns. It was still a fun way to explore where probabilistic detection should stop and deterministic controls should take over.

What other voice-agent attack scenario would you add to the test set?

author_headline: Student at St. Martin's Engineering College
text:
For the past 2 weeks, I’ve been hearing a lot about JEV.
Every week, a new AI model comes out, and honestly, most of them feel like noise after a point 
But JEV felt a bit different.
JEV is not an LLM. It doesn't generate text. Instead, it's designed for FAST DECISION-MAKING.
The easiest way I understood it: think of JEV as a general-purpose classifier for decision-making.
It has 3 interesting ways of making decisions:
🔹 Noul → Yes/No decisions
🔹 Choice → Choose between multiple options
🔹 Score → Measure something on a scale
I wanted to actually test it, so I gave JEV and an LLM the SAME incident:
"The deploy failed twice and customers are seeing 500s. Can someone look now?"
I asked both:
→ Is it urgent?
→ Which team should handle it?
→ How severe is it?

RESULTS 👇
JEV
Urgency: 0.97
Team: infra
Confidence: 1.0
Severity: 1.61 / 2
Latency: 1.655s

LLM
Urgent → True
Team → Infra
Severity → 0.9 / 1
Latency → 2.890s
In this particular test, JEV was ~1.24s faster (~43% lower latency), and both models selected the same team.
What I found more interesting was the output format.
JEV is built around structured decisions:
Noul → probability
Choice → option + probabilities + confidence
Score → numerical score + probability distribution
And this could be interesting for AI agents.
Instead of using an LLM for every small decision:
User → JEV → Decision → LangGraph → Tool / Agent / LLM
JEV could handle routing, urgency, escalation, severity, etc., while the LLM handles deeper reasoning or generation when needed.
Of course, this is only ONE TEST, so I'm not drawing any major conclusions yet.

🚀 Jev: A New Approach to AI Decision-Making

We’re used to AI models like ChatGPT that generate text, write code, and answer questions.

But what if an AI model’s job isn’t to generate a paragraph — but to make a fast, structured decision?

That’s where Jev comes in.

Jev is designed around a different idea: instead of primarily generating text, it can return structured decisions, classifications, scores, and probabilities.

For example:

A customer says:

«“My payment failed and I need it fixed before tomorrow.”»

Instead of generating a long response, an AI decision model could output:

🔹 Category → Billing
🔹 Urgency → High
🔹 Escalate → Yes
🔹 Confidence → 97%

This kind of capability could be useful for:

• 🤖 AI agent routing
• 🛡️ Guardrails and verification
• 🎯 Classification and scoring
• 💬 Customer-support automation
• 👨‍💻 Tool selection for AI agents
• 👤 Human escalation decisions

The interesting part is that Jev isn't necessarily trying to replace general-purpose LLMs.

It represents a different layer in the AI stack:

LLM → Generates & reasons
Jev → Decides & routes

As AI agents become more capable, there may be increasing demand for specialized models that handle the small, repetitive decisions happening behind the scenes.

The future of AI may not be about having one model that does everything.

It could be about multiple specialized models working together.

author_headline: Software Engineer @ React / Next / Nest | Typescript, Node, AI Integrator, AI Advocate, and more.
text:
InfoQ covered a model this week whose output tokens are free — because it never emits any. TypeSafe AI's Jev returns a typed decision with a probability attached: $0.042 per million input tokens, 70–500ms end to end.

Jev is what InfoQ calls a "System One" model: you hand it state plus questions, and it answers with a Choice, a Score, or a Noul — each with a calibrated confidence value. InfoQ reports a median 7x speedup and 30x cost cut against LLM baselines. Tomorrow's move: wherever your code asks a chat model to classify — ticket routing, retrieval gating — swap the parsed string for a confidence threshold and escalate only the uncertain cases. It still can't count or compare dates reliably.

I have watched this since the early microservices years: reach for the most general tool, then spend years hardening it into something specific. Plenty of production "AI features" are not generation at all — they are a small decision wearing a 4,000-token prompt, with a regex downstream praying the format held. The number that matters is not the 30x, it is confidence: a decision path finally has something to branch on.

The leverage I find in client codebases is rarely a better model — it is spotting which calls never needed a language model, then wiring the rest into workflows that fail loudly instead of silently — shorter review cycles, less brittle prompt scaffolding. If your team is weighing which decisions belong in a chat model and which belong in something typed and cheap, I would enjoy comparing notes with someone who has been shipping since XML was the answer to everything.

Last week I open-sourced a harness routing 96 synthetic medical RAG items to answer, refuse, or escalate across OpenAI, Gemini, and Jev. Here are the calibration numbers.

𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀 (𝗻=𝟵𝟲)
- OpenAI: accuracy 97.9%, ECE 0.029, Spearman ρ 0.29 (p=0.005)
- Jev: accuracy 96.9%, ECE 0.023, Spearman ρ 0.35 (p<0.001)
- Gemini: accuracy 100% on 77 items, ECE 0.009, Spearman undefined
Jev's native probabilities track correctness most closely, and both OpenAI and Jev show a significant confidence-correctness correlation. No pairwise accuracy difference is significant at this n. Every one of Jev's three errors was a missed escalation.

Several "model failures" were my rubric's fault: emergency cases scored as out-of-scope, clear dosing questions marked escalate. Fix the rubric before you rank models.

Every arm sits between 97% and 100%. The routing question is whether confidence drops on the items a model gets wrong, which is what Spearman measures. Brier isn't comparable across arms: the chat arms' three-way probabilities are reconstructed from one elicited confidence, while Jev's are native.

text: For a long time, people treated prompt writing as an art. I changed some words, ran some evals, and hoped for the best. Recently I see another way. Decision APIs like Jev and OpenAI Decisions answer small, narrow questions with probabilities, not free text, and they are cheap, so you can ask many questions over many examples. Before, we could try this with normal LLMs too, but making the training data cost too much and you cannot trust those digits from textual response. Now each answer can become a feature. You can train a simple decision tree on labeled data, use feature importance to see which questions really matter, read the rules the tree learned, and write those rules back into one short prompt. So the same decision API plays two roles: it generates the features for training, and at runtime it makes the decision itself, following the trained rules as its instructions. The prompt is not guessed anymore. It is trained, and every sentence has evidence behind it.

I work with XR applications that guide, teach, and test students on step-by-step procedures. One opportunity I’m exploring is using TypeSafe’s JEV AI to help these applications make more informed decisions about guidance and evaluation.

JEV evaluates context and returns structured decisions or scores. An XR application could use those results to:

  • Select the right assistance: a visual highlight, a hint, or a demonstration.

  • Interpret voice requests such as “Explain that again” or “Why is this step necessary?”
  • Evaluate a student’s spoken explanation against an instructor-defined rubric.
  • Recommend targeted practice based on recurring mistakes.
  • Flag unclear evidence or repeated difficulties for instructor review.
  • For example, imagine a student learning to assemble a mechanical component.

The XR application verifies the selected part, placement, sequence, and torque through its interaction data and programmed rules. It then asks:

“Why must these fasteners be tightened in this sequence?”

Speech recognition converts the answer into text. JEV evaluates that answer against approved criteria, helping the application decide whether the student should continue, receive an explanation, or practice the concept again.

That creates an opportunity to assess both procedural performance and the reasoning behind it.

The architecture matters: JEV currently works with text and structured data, so XR interactions, sensor observations, and speech transcripts must be prepared before evaluation. Assessment criteria should be validated against instructor judgments, with uncertain results routed for review.

I see potential here for more responsive coaching and more useful evidence of student understanding.

The Jev versus small-model argument gets misleading the moment one route is handed the answer in its input.

Take a refund-status case. A typed Jev Choice receives a clean object: settlement complete, bank trace present, deadline elapsed. A small Qwen or Haiku route receives the original customer email and must find those facts itself. Measuring only the model-call milliseconds makes the first route look faster by excluding its retrieval and state-preparation work. Reversing the inputs could distort the result the other way.

TypeSafe's documentation describes Jev as a bounded Choice, Score or Noul judgment over supplied state; its coding-agent guidance explicitly places generative work around the decision. Qwen publishes small open-weight models, and Anthropic markets a fast Haiku tier. None of those vendor descriptions is an accepted-work benchmark for this refund process.

I would freeze raw cases and a labeled acceptance contract. Run deterministic lookup, Jev plus its necessary evidence and writing path, and a named small generative route. For each, count retrieval, preparation, model calls, retries, manual review, wrong-branch cost and end-to-end p95. Preserve missing-state and out-of-scope cases, where a quick confident branch is costly. No route wins until the whole job is measured.

Start at the same evidence and end at the same accepted outcome. Then compare.

author_headline: Senior Software Consultant & Architect | AI & Data Science | Cloud & Microservices | Java, Python | GCP (x2), Azure (x2), OpenShift | Full-Stack (React, Angular) | Technical Delivery
text:
Not every AI task needs a reasoning model.

Bespoke Labs just open-sourced Nimble, a 9B model designed for a very specific problem: making fast, typed decisions from text.

Instead of asking an LLM to generate an answer, explain its reasoning, and then parse JSON, Nimble works differently.

You provide:

• The text to evaluate
• A schema
• The allowed answers

Nimble selects the answer directly from the model's logits and returns probabilities for each choice. No generated reasoning. No JSON parsing. No long output.

That makes it particularly interesting for:

→ Request routing
→ Policy enforcement
→ Classification
→ Guardrails
→ Content decisions
→ Agent/tool selection
→ Enterprise workflow decisions

And the model is based on Qwen3.5-9B, fine-tuned with contrastive data curated for these decision tasks.

How does it compare?

On Bespoke Labs' 3,880-example evaluation across 13 public datasets:

Jev 1.13: 76.0%
Nimble 9B: 75.7%
Tev1 4B: 73.3%
Tev1 0.8B: 63.5%

On their 324-example held-out evaluation:

Jev: 93.2%
Nimble 9B: 90.1%
Qwen3.8-27B: 84.9%
Qwen3.5-9B: 66.4%
Gemma 3 270M: 28.7%

The interesting part isn't simply the accuracy.

It's the design philosophy.

A general-purpose LLM is optimized to generate.

Nimble is optimized to decide.

That can make a lot of sense when your application already knows the possible outcomes and you don't need an explanation from the model.

There are also important limitations: the current release is text-only, schemas are flat, each field must be boolean or an enum, and the model cannot generate arbitrary text. The latest checkpoint supports up to 8,192-token prompts and up to 255 choices per field.

For enterprise AI, I think this is an interesting direction:

Use large reasoning models for complex problems.
Use small decision models for the millions of simple decisions happening around them.

That's potentially a very different way to build AI systems.

The model and training recipe are available here:

"Bespoke Labs Nimble on GitHub" (https://reference-url-citation.invalid/4)

Underneath the RLCD headline, Forbes' Lance Eliot names the pattern that actually matters. Jev isn't generative AI. It's a rules-based, bounded-decision tool that other software, including generative AI, can call on for a specific, narrow job.

That's a small data point in a much bigger shift already underway. The most durable AI systems won't be one giant model doing everything. They'll be generative models paired with narrower, deterministic or semi-deterministic components, each doing the part of the job it's actually good at.

Generation is good at producing options, language, and drafts. On its own, it's not good at guaranteeing a decision stayed inside a set of approved choices, or that a control actually fired when it was supposed to.

It's the whole reason I built Gaia Tech Solutions around a governance layer that sits on top of whatever model a client already uses, instead of a model of its own. The model does the generating. The governance layer does the guaranteeing. Worth asking which one you're actually getting when someone pitches you an AI system this year.

author_headline: AI Governance & Risk Management Leader | DoCRA Practitioner | vCISO | Litigation Support
text:
TypeSafe's new tool, Jev, claims to avoid hallucination. Worth reading the fine print on what that claim actually covers.

Jev constrains its output to a predefined set of choices and attaches a calibrated confidence score to each one. That design genuinely kills one failure mode. The system can't invent an answer that was never on the list.

A different failure mode survives untouched. The system can still pick the wrong option from that list, and it can do it confidently.

Avoiding hallucination and avoiding wrong answers are two different guarantees, and a tool that solves the first one hasn't solved the problem most people hear when they read "avoids hallucination." Constrained-choice error is a real category, with real consequences, any time the decision on that list is the wrong one.

Before I sign off on a bounded-decision AI tool for a client, I want to know one thing. When it's confidently wrong, how do you find out, and what does it cost by the time you do?

text:
Nem toda decisão precisa de um LLM

Duas siglas surgiram nas últimas semanas e merecem atenção de quem trabalha com dados e IA: Jev e Laya. 

Os dois são motores de decisão, e não modelos de chat. Você entrega um texto (e-mail, ticket, código) junto com perguntas fechadas, e eles devolvem uma decisão com probabilidade. Não geram texto livre, então não há alucinação de resposta e a latência é baixíssima. 

🔹 Jev (TypeSafe AI): serviço hospedado, pesos fechados, cerca de 240 ms por chamada. Vai melhor de fábrica, sobretudo quando há muitas opções e na calibração. 

🔹 Laya (Convai Innovations): código aberto (Apache 2.0), 421M de parâmetros, roda local, na casa de 33 ms. Permite fine-tuning e custa zero por token. 

O que me chamou atenção: no benchmark Banking77 (77 intenções), o Jev fez 0,87 contra 0,43 do Laya sem ajuste. Já em um benchmark de decisões tipadas, o Laya especializado chegou a 0,766 contra 0,727. Ou seja, o desempenho depende muito de ajustar o modelo ao seu caso. 

E vale lembrar: os números de velocidade e acurácia vêm, em boa parte, dos próprios fabricantes. 

💡 Minha leitura: para classificação, roteamento e triagem em pipelines de dados, usar um modelo pequeno e especializado antes de acionar um LLM grande pode reduzir custo, latência e risco. Antes de adotar qualquer um dos dois, teste com os seus dados.

text:
Some of the LLM calls in my agentic investigation service never needed an LLM. They needed what Jev does faster and cheaper: return a bounded answer. I'm eager to incorporate it into that service as it expands beyond bail bonds agency use, and into the solutions I build for clients.

If you want a more robust explanation, I'll post a handy YouTube video in the comments, but here's the quick rundown:

🧠 Jev is a decision model. It reads language the way an LLM does but works as a classifier, a kind of machine learning (ML) that long pre-dates LLMs. 

🎯 Responses are bounded, not the unstructured strings returned by an LLM's token generation. 
❓You hand Jev a question and specify which of 3 primitive types to return: 
    ☑️ A single choice from a defined set of answers (passed in with the question) 
    📊 Ranking within an ordered scale (Mildly annoyed, Annoyed, Angry...) 
    🎲 Probability the answer is "Yes" expressed as a number between 0 and 1 
    ⚡ When a bounded response does fit the use case, Jev gets there with far less compute than an LLM does.

Software development often demands bounded answers, and much of the risk of incorporating LLMs into solutions is due to their unbounded, and sometimes wacky, responses. Jev is not a replacement for an LLM, so much as a better tool to reach for when the outcome you need either can or outright should be bounded. 

An example workflow where both Jev and an LLM earn their place. An email is received on a general customer service email address and needs to be routed to the appropriate department and prioritized based on customer sentiment. Jev wins for both of these assessments: there is a bounded list of departments available and a ranked scale can be defined for customer sentiment. 

Now let's say Jev identifies a customer email with the highest ranking of anger as the sentiment and the company SOP is to immediately send a contextualized response to that customer assuring them a manager is looking into their issue and will reach out soon. An LLM is (currently) the only option to generate that email.

I've been kicking myself a bit for not diving into ML earlier. I went pretty deep into statistical modeling in college so I'm coming in with a lot of the basics. Jev is a nice stepping stone into ML for me.

author_headline: Marketing Operations & Automation Manager | HubSpot, ABM & GTM Systems | Data Analytics
text:
Can an AI model that only picks answers, and never writes them, qualify B2B leads? I tested Jev from @TypeSafe on 1,097 company websites to find out.

Some background: I'm building a lead pipeline in Python with Claude Code. Its first stage, which is live, reads a company's website with Firecrawl and uses OpenAI models through OpenRouter to answer one question: does this company have a specific capability in-house? If it does, it's a target. So far it has qualified 1,107 companies at about 13 cents per lead. Enrichment and automation come next.

Jev is a different kind of model. You give it content and typed questions (yes/no, pick one, rate on a scale), and it returns calibrated probabilities. It costs $0.0007 per company, about 28 times less than my LLM step.

What I did 👇

• Turned my qualification rules into 32 small typed questions, plus one "does it make this itself?" question for each target product found on a company's pages.
• Ran Jev on 1,097 websites I'd already crawled. My own code, not Jev, turned the answers into verdicts.
• Scored it against my human-reviewed results, and set the pass mark before every run.

What I found 👇

✅ On batches it was never tuned on, it found 90% of my confirmed leads
✅ 99% of the companies it flagged were real leads
❌ Asked to rule companies out, it was wrong too often to trust
❌ It gives no proof sentence, so it can't replace the step that quotes the evidence

What made the difference 👇

1. Clean input. Half of what I first sent was menus and link addresses. Stripping them was the biggest gain.

2. Small questions. "Does it make X itself?", asked once per product, beat one "which product does it make?" question.

3. Code makes the decision. Jev observes; my rules decide.

My take: Jev is a strong fit when the question is narrow and clearly defined, like "does this company do X in-house?", and the evidence is on the page. It's not the tool for ruling things out, because a missing sentence doesn't mean a missing capability; sometimes the page that proves it was simply never crawled.

So it doesn't replace my pipeline. At under a tenth of a cent per company, it's a very cheap second opinion that points the expensive model at the right companies first.

The whole test cost $0.85.

author_headline: System Engineer @ Infosys | Building Agentic AI Systems | LLMs • Multi-Agent Systems • Intelligent Memory • Production AI
text:
What if the next big step in AI technology doesn't even involve text generation? I've been researching Jev, a new type of AI model created by TypeSafe AI that approaches AI differently than traditional LLMs. Rather than asking "Generate a response," you ask "Decide what to do next." Jev was developed to handle specific types of bounded, typed decisions. 
Some examples include: → Classify → Route → Rank → Score → Choose → Return confidence For instance, if an AI-based customer service system received the following message: "My Stripe integration has stopped working for three days and I'm losing sales," a decision model could determine the correct team to assign this issue to, the severity of the user's frustration, and how urgent it is. The most exciting aspect of Jev is that the application defines all possible answers before they occur.
Thus, if the application has defined the acceptable teams as: Billing | Technical | Sales The model will not be able to return: Legal This does not imply that Jev is always correct. It implies that while the **interface is limited**, the decision process remains probabilistic. Why is this significant for Agentic AI? Many Agentic workflows include numerous small decisions throughout: Should I use this tool? Which model should respond to this request? Does this action require human approval? Is this document applicable? Should I continue with this workflow? Does this agent trace require human review? Today we typically rely on large language models (LLMs) to make these decisions. Essentially, Jev's method is: LLM → generates Decision model → decides This creates a layer of decision making around LLM-based systems. 
Example applications include: User Request → Jev → Model Router → LLM Agent → Jev → Policy Check → Tool The overall concept is not that Jev replaces LLMs. It is that **AI systems will be composed of multiple specialized models**, with generative models completing open-ended reasoning tasks and decision models performing rapid, bounded judgments. There are however important considerations. Even with Jev, there is no guarantee that it will make the right decision. A probability is not a certainty. Poorly labeled data or poorly constructed options may result in poor automation.
Additionally, high-risk actions should remain protected by deterministic rules, permissions, and human intervention.
Therefore, I would view Jev as: ❌ “The next LLM replacement” I would view it as: A potential new primitive for building AI systems. The key question now is: How many decisions within today's AI applications require a complete generative model?

author_headline: Machine Learning & AI Research Engineer at Parascript
text:
What comes after JEV?

My bet: generalized pairwise interactions.

JEV has popularized the idea that classification doesn't need to be expressed through autoregressive language generation.

You can keep the flexibility of a general-purpose model without expressing the result through generated language.

And pairwise interactions seem like a natural next step.

Give a model a set of objects and define the relationship in natural language:

“Do these records refer to the same entity?”

Instead of calling an LLM for every pair, or asking it to generate the final grouping autoregressively, get the complete interaction matrix in one pass:
Y[i,j] = F(x[i], x[j] | prompt)

This primitive appears everywhere:
→ matching and entity resolution  
→ ranking and relevance  
→ deduplication and clustering  
→ contradiction and entailment  
→ temporal and other relationships

And the efficiency gain could be enormous.

Today, exhaustive pairwise reasoning means many model calls or many judgments generated sequentially.

A native Pairwise operation could keep that dimension parallel all the way to the output.

And this computational shape is remarkably natural for transformers, which already spend much of their computation modeling interactions between elements.

But this is where the idea gets broader.

LLMs gave us two things at once:
→ programmable semantics  
→ a general-purpose output representation: natural language

Almost any task can be described in language, and almost any result can be expressed in it.

That flexibility is exactly what made LLMs universal.

But it comes at a cost: natural language is a terribly inefficient representation for many computations.

ML has spent decades discovering efficient representations for recurring problem shapes.

So perhaps the next step is not to give up LLM universality, but to give universal models native machinery for these recurring computational primitives.

Natural language can still specify what we want, without requiring the answer to be serialized back into language when another representation fits the problem better.

Classification may be one primitive.

Pairwise interaction may be another.

And eventually these may not even be separate models or APIs. They could become native capabilities of universal AI, first as outputs and eventually as intermediate reasoning operations.

OpenAI's newly announced Decisions API (https://lnkd.in/gAD5BCxb) feels like another step in this direction: classification, routing, and action selection exposed as dedicated model operations.

Language made the model universal.

Native primitives can make that universality efficient.

author_headline: IT Infrastructure & Security Engineer | Networking, Active Directory, pfSense, IAM
text:
I cut my AI pipelines cost from $340/month to $5 — with Jev 🤖 

I had a classifier processing ~12,000 records a day. The architecture was the obvious one: a cheap filter up front, an LLM deciding the rest. Projected cost: $340/month. A queue that never cleared.

The cheap filter was an embeddings layer — the classic vector matrix, comparing each item against a reference profile. It made sense on paper: fast, cheap, no paid API involved.

But before looking for a cheaper LLM, I measured what I already had. I compared what the embeddings said against real decisions that had already been made. The answer was nearly identical for what mattered and what didnt — the layer wasnt discriminating anything. It was burning time, tokens, and money to return, in practice, a guess. 

The systems aggregate metrics still looked healthy. Thats why nobody had noticed. And thats why nearly all the volume was falling straight through to the most expensive layer.

I replaced the embeddings with Jev, from TypeSafe AI — released just weeks ago. It doesnt compare vectors or generate text. It returns a calibrated probability for a structured question. Fast enough to run on nearly the entire volume, cheap enough to disappear from the bill. The LLM, which used to decide everything, was left with what a text model actually does well: writing the justification for approved items and resolving the few genuinely ambiguous cases.

Along the way, two mistakes of mine that mattered more than any new model: 

I almost threw out a good model because the label I tested it against was wrong. I was conflating this isnt the right category with this is the right category, but I chose not to pursue it — different questions, different answers. Measuring both with the same ruler failed a model that actually worked.

And I was using the same confidence cutoff to approve and to discard. Getting a discard wrong costs an opportunity that doesnt come back. Getting an approval wrong costs someone thirty seconds of reading. Treating both as the same risk was the real bug.

$340 → $5 a month. Same volume.

But the lesson isnt about Jev. Its about measuring every layer in isolation before swapping anything out — especially the layer youd fall back on if the new one doesnt work.

If youre building something similar — triage, moderation, scoring, any pipeline that decides at scale — heres the question worth asking: is your smart layer actually deciding, or just looking like it is?

text:
𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 (𝗖𝗟𝗠-𝟴𝗕): 𝗔 𝗡𝗲𝘄 𝗪𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

Most LLMs make decisions by generating tokens.

But what if an AI agent doesn’t need to generate an answer at all?

Researchers from Stanford and NVIDIA Research introduced 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 (𝗖𝗟𝗠𝘀), a new class of “System One” models designed for fast and generalizable decision-making.

The first released model is 𝗖𝗟𝗠-𝟴𝗕.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗖𝗟𝗠-𝟴𝗕 𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁:

Instead of generating a sequence of tokens, CLM connects:

→ The current 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗲
→ The available 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

It learns embeddings for both and uses contrastive learning to determine which action best matches the current state.

So the problem becomes less about:

“Generate the next token.”

And more about:

“Which action best matches this situation?”

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗲:

• 60M Nemotron Q&A pairs for pre-training
• 30M synthetic hard negatives for mid-training
• 1M agentic trajectories for post-training

The model uses an InfoNCE-based contrastive objective to pull correct state-action pairs closer together while pushing incorrect pairs apart.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁: 𝗖𝗟𝗠-𝟴𝗕 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀.

Because states and actions are disaggregated, frequently reused actions can be encoded once and reused across different states.

This can significantly reduce the computation required for repeated agent decisions.

𝗥𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀:

The researchers report that CLM-8B performs comparably to Jev across computer-use, gaming, and tool-calling tasks while achieving up to 9× lower latency.

For agentic coding verification, lightweight fine-tuning achieved:

→ 81.6% on DeepSWE
→ 87.6% on Terminal-Bench 2.1

The paper also reports substantially faster inference for these verification workloads.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗜 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀:

Agentic systems constantly make small decisions:

• Which tool should I call?
• Which action should happen next?
• Which candidate solution is better?
• Which route should the workflow take?
• Is this candidate worth selecting?

Using a large generative model for every bounded decision can introduce unnecessary latency.

CLM takes a different approach:

𝗗𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 → 𝗘𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗱𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 → 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

This is an interesting direction for building faster agentic workflows where decisions are bounded and the candidate actions are known in advance.

The project is also open source, making it possible to experiment with the architecture and integrate CLM-8B into agent systems.

🔗 [Explore the CLM-8B GitHub repository](https://lnkd.in/d2bEBt8Q)

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗶𝗴 𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗮:

Not every AI decision needs generation.

Sometimes, the fastest path to an action is simply learning how well the current state matches the available choices.

text:
🚀 A small change in how we use LLMs could make AI applications significantly faster.

I’ve been looking into Jev and the idea behind its speed is quite interesting.

For example.

Imagine you’re building an AI system for a bank. A customer sends this message:

“My debit card was blocked, and I need to make an urgent payment. Can you help?”

Your system needs to determine whether this request belongs to Card Services, Fraud Prevention, or General Support.

A conventional LLM might generate a response explaining its decision. But if all you need is the correct department, generating an entire sentence is unnecessary.

Here’s where things get interesting.

Traditional LLMs generate text one token at a time.

Even a relatively short response requires multiple sequential decoding steps. The model generates a token, processes it alongside the previous context, and then generates the next one.

Now imagine handling thousands of these requests simultaneously. Those repeated generation steps can add up.

Jev approaches the problem differently.

Instead of generating a response, it treats the task as a selection problem.

You provide the customer’s message and the possible categories. The model makes a single forward pass and calculates the probabilities associated with each option.

For example:

* Card Services: 85%
* Fraud Prevention: 12%
* General Support: 3%

The system can then route the request based on the predicted result.

No need to generate a lengthy explanation just to select a category.

That’s the interesting part of Jev.

It’s not necessarily about building a bigger or more powerful model. It’s about changing the way we use an existing model to solve a specific problem.

For tasks such as classification, intent detection and structured decision-making, avoiding autoregressive text generation can substantially reduce latency.

Of course, the actual speedup depends on the model, hardware and workload. Not every AI task can be converted into a simple selection problem.

But this raises an interesting question for anyone building AI applications:

Are we sometimes using generative AI when all we really need is predictive AI?

As someone working on LLM inference optimization, I find this distinction particularly interesting. There’s still a lot of room to improve how efficiently we serve AI workloads.

text:
Stop using 70-billion-parameter generative LLMs to make binary decisions.

If you're building AI agents, you've likely seen this antipattern:
Every time an agent needs to decide whether to store a memory, route a tool, or evaluate sentiment, it spawns an autoregressive LLM prompt.

You wait 800ms to 2 seconds.
You pay per token.
And when the context window fills with junk, the system degrades.

Daniel Kahneman described human cognition as two systems:
• System 1: Fast, instinctive, automatic, and calibrated.
• System 2: Slow, deliberate, sequential, and logical.

Generative LLMs are fundamentally System 2.  They generate thoughts token-by-token.  Forcing them to act like System 1 for routine routing and classification is slow, expensive, and fragile.

That's why the AI engineering world is paying close attention to Jev (developed by TypeSafe AI and Diogo Almeida).

Jev represents a shift toward dedicated System 1 decision primitives:
Instead of "auto-regressively" generating a conversation, we evaluate state against schema-constrained choices in parallel.

We integrated a Jev-style decision engine directly into SULCUS, replacing legacy heuristic and slow LLM evaluators with three core primitives:

1. Noul (Gate):
A fast, calibrated probability threshold that asks, "Is this message an ephemeral conversational filler or a persistent directive worth storing?"
Evaluated in under 5 milliseconds.

2. Choice (Routing):
Classification across schema.  "Does this memory represent an objective fact, an architectural constraint, a personal preference, or an entity relationship?"
Output is a typed category with confidence metrics.

3. Score (Rating):
Continuous rating across ordered tiers to determine importance and decay curves.

The architectural outcome?
Sub-5ms evaluation latency in-process in Rust.
Culls evaluation costs associated with LLM calls.
Zero schema drift or hallucination as the output is typed by definition.
Classification is retrained on your feedback for better classification.

LLMs should be used for reasoning, synthesis, and deep conversation.

How are you handling routing and memory classification in your agent stacks today?

Cloudflare released Clef and Clef-flash, a family of open-source decision models, and debuted a new reinforcement learning platform for fine-tuning these models for agentic workflows.

• Clef includes a vision encoder, allowing it to take in images and classify visual content. This is a unique property compared to Jev, which currently only supports text classification.
• Clef models are hosted on Workers AI, leveraging Cloudflare's edge GPUs. This infrastructure provides low network latency, enabling the models to be placed in the hot path for agents making real-time decisions.
• Clef uses Qwen as a base model and performs a prefill-only pass, scoring valid schema choices in parallel. This non-autoregressive approach makes it significantly faster than traditional token-by-token LLM generation.

text:
No Wscout, estou trabalhando para que o assistente não dependa apenas de uma IA tentando interpretar livremente tudo o que o usuário escreve. A ideia é utilizar o JEV como camada de decisão, transformando linguagem natural em dados estruturados antes de chegar às regras e fontes do sistema.

O fluxo, de forma simplificada, funciona assim:
Pergunta → JEV → Backend → Dados → Resposta

O usuário pode simplesmente perguntar:“Quando joga o Palmeiras?”
O JEV identifica e estrutura informações como intenção, entidade, mercado, período e contexto. 

A partir daí, o backend resolve as entidades, aplica as regras necessárias e consulta apenas a fonte responsável pela informação. Isso também muda bastante a questão de custos.

Em aplicações com IA, cada contexto desnecessariamente grande, cada chamada adicional e cada processamento que poderia ter sido resolvido pelo próprio backend representa consumo. Por isso, nem tudo precisa ser entregue para um modelo de IA resolver.

Quando consigo transformar primeiro a solicitação em uma estrutura previsível, posso:

• reduzir o volume de contexto enviado aos modelos• evitar chamadas desnecessárias
• consultar diretamente dados que já existem no Wscout
• deixar regras determinísticas no backend
• utilizar IA somente nas etapas em que ela realmente agrega valor
• tornar o custo por interação mais controlável conforme o número de usuários cresce.

Ou seja: não é apenas uma discussão sobre inteligência. É também arquitetura, latência e custo operacional.
Outro ponto interessante aparece na continuidade da conversa.
Depois de perguntar sobre um jogo, o usuário pode simplesmente escrever:
“E os escanteios?” Isoladamente, a frase possui pouca informação. 
Mas mantendo estado, entidades e contexto estruturados, o sistema consegue entender sobre qual partida ou time a pergunta continua falando sem reconstruir toda a conversa do zero.
Esse é um dos objetivos que estou perseguindo no Wscout: usar modelos inteligentes onde existe incerteza e usar software determinístico onde já existe uma regra. Colocar IA em uma interface é relativamente simples.

Fazer IA conversar corretamente com contexto, entidades, regras de negócio, banco de dados, diferentes fontes e ainda manter o custo sustentável em escala é onde a engenharia começa a ficar realmente interessante. Mais uma evolução na arquitetura do Wscout, um projeto WIPdata.

text:
Toda semana o feed elege uma IA nova que muda tudo. Essa semana o eleito é o Jev.

Se você não viu: é um modelo novo, de um ex-pesquisador da OpenAI, que não escreve texto. Ele só decide. Você dá a situação e as opções, ele devolve a escolha com um grau de confiança, em menos de um segundo, por uma fração do custo de um LLM. Genuinamente interessante.

Mas não foi assim que ele chegou na sua timeline. Chegou como "a IA que aposenta o ChatGPT", "o fim do Claude", "quem não usar ficou para trás".

E no outro extremo mora a turma oposta: a que decidiu que isso tudo é moda passageira. Viu uma resposta errada em 2023, encerrou o assunto, e vai "esperar a tecnologia amadurecer" antes de encostar. Enquanto espera, o mercado aprende.

A minha posição é bem menos empolgante que as duas.

Estou testando o Jev, sim. Fora da produção. Num ambiente separado, medindo força, fraqueza, limite e custo. Nada que tem cliente rodando chega perto dele até o teste provar que merece. O próprio anúncio da ferramenta admite que os números divulgados são o teto do cenário ideal e que a demo é simplificada. Quem leu o anúncio sabe disso. Quem leu só o feed, não.

E aqui entra a reflexão que eu queria trazer.

Existe um custo invisível nessa troca constante. Antes de escrever isso aqui, fui atrás dos números para ver se era só implicância minha.

Não era. A psicologia estuda isso faz tempo: quando você pula de um contexto para outro, um pedaço da cabeça fica preso no anterior. Tem medição apontando uns 23 minutos para o cérebro voltar ao foco de verdade depois de cada troca. E estimativas de que esse pinga-pinga come até 40% de um dia produtivo.

Agora aplica isso a trocar de stack, de modelo, de ferramenta, a cada novidade. A conta não fecha. Nunca fechou.

Um dos últimos livros que li foi Nação Dopamina, e gostei bastante. Ele explica exatamente esse mecanismo: nosso cérebro recompensa novidade com um pico de prazer imediato. Dominar alguma coisa não dá pico nenhum: é lento, repetitivo, silencioso. E o feed amplifica o desequilíbrio, porque anunciar que você já usa a ferramenta nova rende status hoje. Entregar resultado com a ferramenta que você domina não rende post.

Só que resultado vem de profundidade. A mesma IA, na mão de quem a conhece de verdade, entrega um trabalho que a ferramenta nova na mão de um turista não entrega. E ignorar tudo, esperando a moda passar, só garante que a profundidade vai ser do concorrente.

Então sigo acompanhando tudo. Lendo os anúncios, testando por fora, medindo.

E em produção, minha regra não muda: novidade só entra depois que prova. Cliente não é ambiente de teste.

text:
I’ve been thinking about what models like Jev mean for cold email and outbound in general, and I’m starting to think it’s in real trouble.

Most deliverability work is about how an email gets sent: sender reputation, domain warmup, inbox rotation, infrastructure provider, dedicated IPs, authentication, spintax, etc..

All of that gets you past spam filters. But if inboxes start running cheap classifiers that judge what an email actually says, none of it helps much. And I know email/content classifiers aren’t new, but they just got the upgrade of a lifetime.

A sender with a spotless reputation on premium infrastructure could still get sorted into “cold pitch” and ignored. I wouldn’t be surprised if inbox providers like Google are already building this into their next classification update.

If that happens, I’d expect a lot of teams to move budget into cold calling (even as Apple cracks down there too) and drop email altogether.

Email filtered by content, calls screened by default. I don’t have a clear answer for what comes next but my theory is that whatever people are doing right now for outbound will have nothing to do with what they will be doing in 12 months…

text:
Three companies shipped the same kind of model this quarter, and none of them will write you a sentence on purpose.

TypeSafe's Jev started it in September: a System One model trained only to decide, not to talk. Yes or no, pick one of five, score zero to one. No chat. No explanation. No tool calls. On 1,357 labeled test decisions across 13 languages it hit 98.5% accuracy against a frontier Gemini model's 99%, but did it in 329 milliseconds against 1,598, and TypeSafe only charges for the input tokens.

Cloudflare answered this week with Clef and Clef-flash, open sourced under Apache 2.0, built on Qwen, and trained to be Jev-API compatible so switching over is a config change, not a rewrite. Across 43 benchmarks Clef posted a 209 millisecond median latency against Jev's 524, though Jev still wins some of the harder decision-specific evals. Perplexity answered the same week with pplx-decider-v1-27b through a new Decisions API, 4 cents per million input tokens, free output, 85.71% across its benchmark suite.

What catches my attention is the shape, not the vendor. None of these models can read an image carefully, write a reply, or call a tool, and that is the point. A support routing call, a fraud flag, a content classification, a ticket triage decision, none of that needed 200 billion parameters guessing at prose. It needed a probability distribution and a threshold.

This is what happened to computing once general purpose processors got good enough that someone noticed most of the work was narrow and repetitive, and a specialized chip could do it faster and cheaper. Decision models are that moment for the parts of an agent pipeline that were never actually generative to begin with.

The constraint nobody's pricing in yet: every one of these still needs a real language model sitting next to it for the reply. Jev's own documentation says so directly. You don't replace your LLM with a decision model, you split the pipeline into the part that decides and the part that talks, and that split is a harder architecture change than swapping an API key.
